questions.stem: The dilatancy test is used to identify:
questions.solution:
**Fine-grained soil.**

**Why.** **Coarse-grained soils (4.75 mm to 80 mm) can be identified VISUALLY** — their particles are large enough to see, and their shape (angular, flaky, rounded) can be judged by eye.

> **Fine-grained soils cannot.** Silt and clay both look like fine powder, so a field test is needed to tell them apart — and that is what the dilatancy test provides.

**How the test is performed:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | A **wet pat of soil** is placed in the palm |
| **2** | The hand is **shaken or jarred** sharply |
| **3** | Observe whether **water appears** on the surface, giving a shiny appearance |
| **4** | **Squeeze** the pat and observe whether the water disappears |

**Reading the result:**

| Reaction | Soil |
|---|---|
| **QUICK** — water appears rapidly on shaking, vanishes on squeezing | **SILT** (or fine sand) |
| **SLOW** | Silty clay |
| **NONE** | **CLAY** |

> **The physical reason is permeability.** Silt is permeable enough for water to move through it quickly under vibration; **clay is not**, so nothing happens however hard it is shaken.

> **That single difference — how fast water can move — is what the test detects**, and it is the same property that distinguishes silt and clay in almost every other respect too.

**The full set of FIELD identification tests for fine soils:**

| Test | Silt | Clay |
|---|---|---|
| **DILATANCY (shaking)** | **Quick reaction** | **No reaction** |
| **DRY STRENGTH** (crush a dried lump) | **Low — crumbles easily** | **High — hard to break** |
| **TOUGHNESS** (roll a thread at the plastic limit) | **Weak, crumbly thread** | **Tough, stiff thread** |
| Shine (rub with a knife) | Dull | **Shiny** |

> **Dilatancy and dry strength give OPPOSITE readings**, which is why they are used together: **silt is quick to dilate and weak when dry; clay is the reverse.** A soil that shows quick dilatancy AND high dry strength has been misread.

**Why field identification still matters** despite laboratory testing:

> **It costs nothing and takes a minute**, and it tells the engineer on site whether the material being placed matches what was assumed. **A laboratory result arrives days later, by which time the fill is in place.**

**The laboratory classification** that follows: **IS 1498 / USCS** uses the **particle size distribution** for coarse soils and the **PLASTICITY CHART** (plasticity index against liquid limit, with **A-line: I_p = 0.73(w_L − 20)**) for fine soils.

> **Above the A-line = CLAY; below = SILT or organic.** The chart is the laboratory equivalent of the field tests above, and it separates the same two materials by the same underlying property.

examTip.trick: **Coarse soils can be identified by EYE; fine soils cannot.** So every field identification test — dilatancy, dry strength, toughness — exists to separate **silt from clay**, which look identical.
examTip.trap: **Dilatancy and dry strength read OPPOSITE ways**: silt gives a **quick** dilatancy reaction and **low** dry strength; clay gives **none** and **high**. A soil showing both quick dilatancy and high dry strength has been misread.
examTip.mnemonic: **The underlying property is PERMEABILITY** — silt lets water move under vibration, clay does not. The same difference explains almost every other contrast between them.

questions.stem: The maximum size of a grain of silt is about:
questions.solution:
**About 0.06 mm** — within the silt range, whose upper bound is **0.075 mm**.

**The particle size classification (IS 1498):**

| Class | Size range |
|---|---|
| **Boulder** | **> 300 mm** |
| **Cobble** | **80 – 300 mm** |
| **GRAVEL** | **80 – 4.75 mm** |
| **SAND** | **4.75 – 0.075 mm** |
| **SILT** | **0.075 – 0.002 mm** |
| **CLAY** | **< 0.002 mm** |

> **0.06 mm lies between 0.002 and 0.075**, so it is silt ✓ — and it is the only option that does. The others (0.2, 0.5, 1 mm) are all **sand**.

**The two boundaries worth memorising above all:**

> **0.075 mm — the SAND/SILT boundary**, and it is also the **75 micron sieve**, the finest standard sieve. **It separates "coarse" from "fine" soils**, and it is the sieve below which sieving stops working and sedimentation analysis takes over.

> **0.002 mm (2 microns) — the SILT/CLAY boundary.**

**Why 0.075 mm matters so much practically:**

| Above 0.075 mm | Below 0.075 mm |
|---|---|
| **SIEVE analysis** | **HYDROMETER / sedimentation** analysis (Stokes' law) |
| Coarse-grained | Fine-grained |
| Classified by **GRADING** (C_u, C_c) | Classified by **PLASTICITY** (the A-line chart) |
| Generally free draining | Low permeability |

> **The classification method itself changes at 0.075 mm**, which is why it is the single most important number in the table.

**A caution about "clay":**

> **Clay-SIZE and clay-MINERAL are different things.** A particle below 2 microns is clay-sized, but **plasticity comes from the clay MINERALS** (kaolinite, illite, montmorillonite) and their electrochemical interaction with water — not merely from being small.

> **Finely ground rock flour is clay-sized but NOT plastic**, and it behaves as a silt. That is exactly why fine soils are classified by **plasticity** rather than by size.

**The clay minerals, in ascending order of trouble:**

| Mineral | Structure | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Kaolinite** | 1:1, strongly bonded | **Stable, low activity** |
| **Illite** | 2:1, potassium bonded | Intermediate |
| **MONTMORILLONITE** | 2:1, **weakly bonded — water enters between layers** | **HIGHLY expansive** |

> **Montmorillonite is what makes BLACK COTTON SOIL swell and shrink**, causing the differential settlement and cracking that makes such ground so difficult to build on — and it is why those soils are stabilised with **lime**.

examTip.trick: Two boundaries carry the whole table: **0.075 mm (sand/silt)** and **0.002 mm (silt/clay)**. Only 0.06 mm falls between them — the other three options are all sand.
examTip.trap: **0.075 mm is where the CLASSIFICATION METHOD changes** — sieving above, hydrometer below; grading above, plasticity below. That is why it matters far more than the number suggests.
examTip.mnemonic: **Clay-SIZE is not clay-MINERAL.** Rock flour is under 2 microns but not plastic. Plasticity comes from the minerals — and **MONTMORILLONITE** is the expansive one behind black cotton soil.

questions.stem: What is the number of satellites in the fully operational GPS constellation?
questions.solution:
**24 satellites.**

**The GPS constellation:**

> **24 satellites, four each in six orbital planes inclined at 55°**, spaced **60° apart in longitude**. The arrangement guarantees that **at least four satellites are visible from anywhere on Earth at any time**.

> In practice more are flown — currently about **31 operational** out of 38 placed — to provide redundancy and improve accuracy.

**The number needed for a FIX is a different question, and worth knowing:**

| Requirement | Satellites |
|---|---|
| **Stationary object** | **3 minimum** |
| **MOVING object / general 3-D fix** | **4 minimum** |

> **Why four and not three?** Three satellites give three range equations for three unknowns (x, y, z) — but the receiver's **CLOCK ERROR is a fourth unknown**. A receiver cannot carry an atomic clock, so its time offset must be solved for too.

> **The fourth satellite solves the clock**, which is why every GPS receiver needs four. **That is the single most elegant idea in satellite positioning**: the system gives you precise time for free, as a by-product of solving for position.

**The other global systems:**

| System | Country | Satellites |
|---|---|---|
| **GPS** | **United States** | 31 operational |
| **GLONASS** | **Russia** | 24 |
| **BeiDou** | **China** | 35 |
| **Galileo** | **Europe** | 22 |

> A modern receiver uses **several constellations at once (GNSS)**, which greatly improves availability in obstructed terrain — a real advantage in Nepal's valleys, where sky visibility is limited.

**Survey methods and their accuracy:**

| Method | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| **Single point (autonomous)** | 5 – 10 m |
| **DGPS (differential)** | **1 – 3 m** |
| **RTK (real time kinematic)** | **1 – 2 cm** |
| Static post-processed | **Millimetres** over long observation |

> **The huge jump from metres to centimetres comes from DIFFERENTIAL working** — a second receiver on a known point measures the errors common to both, and those cancel. **Most GPS error is common to nearby receivers**, which is precisely why differencing works so well.

**Sources of error:**

| Error | Note |
|---|---|
| **IONOSPHERIC delay** | **The largest** — reduced by dual-frequency receivers |
| Tropospheric delay | Modelled |
| **MULTIPATH** | Signals reflected off buildings and ground — **not removed by differencing** |
| Satellite clock and orbit | Small; corrected by ephemeris |
| **Satellite GEOMETRY (DOP)** | **Poor geometry degrades a fix even with perfect ranges** |

> **DOP (dilution of precision) is the same "strength of fix" idea as the well-conditioned triangle in triangulation** — satellites clustered together fix a position poorly, exactly as two rays crossing at a shallow angle do.

> **Multipath is the error that differencing cannot remove**, because it is local to each antenna — which is why GPS performs badly close to buildings and cliffs however good the equipment.

examTip.trick: **24 in the constellation, but only 4 needed for a fix** — and the fourth solves the **receiver's CLOCK error**, not a geometric unknown. Read which number the question wants.
examTip.trap: The source's own explanation discusses the **minimum for a fix (4)** while keying the **constellation size (24)**. Since 4 is not among the options, the question must be asking about the constellation.
examTip.mnemonic: **DOP is the satellite version of the well-conditioned triangle** — clustered satellites fix a position badly, just as shallow-crossing rays do. And **MULTIPATH is the error differencing cannot remove**.

questions.stem: The number of codes of conduct in the NEC, as updated in 2079 BS, is:
questions.solution:
**11.**

> **Before the 2079 amendment there were 8 codes of conduct; the amendment raised the number to 11.**

> Note that a paper set **before** that amendment keys **8**, and one set after keys **11** — so the date of the sitting decides the answer. **Both numbers are worth knowing for exactly that reason.**

**What the code of conduct requires** — the substance that matters more than the count:

| Obligation | Content |
|---|---|
| **PUBLIC SAFETY** | **Hold the safety, health and welfare of the public paramount** |
| **Competence** | Practise only within the field and level for which one is qualified |
| **Honesty and integrity** | No misrepresentation of qualifications or of work done |
| **Confidentiality** | Protect the client's information |
| **Conflict of interest** | Disclose any interest affecting judgement |
| **No secret commissions** | Neither offer nor accept |
| **Respect for colleagues** | No malicious injury to another engineer's reputation |
| **Continuing development** | Maintain and update competence |
| **Compliance with law and codes** | Including the building code |
| **Proper documentation** | **Sign only work actually done or supervised** |

**The provision that overrides all others:**

> **Public safety comes before the client's instructions and before the engineer's own interest.**

> Every professional code in the world places it first, and it is what gives an engineer both the **duty and the standing to refuse unsafe work** — a protection for the engineer as much as an obligation on them.

**The breach most often committed:**

> **Signing drawings one did not prepare or supervise.** It is treated seriously precisely because **the signature is the public's only assurance that a competent person took responsibility** for the design.

**Enforcement:**

| Sanction | Effect |
|---|---|
| Warning or reprimand | Minor breaches |
| **Suspension** of registration | For a period |
| **REMOVAL from the register** | **Ends the right to practise** |

> **Because registration is a legal requirement to practise, removal from the register ends the career** — which is what gives the Council's disciplinary power real force, and why the code is not merely aspirational.

**The Council block worth learning as a unit:** Act **2055 (1998 AD)**, Regulations **2057**, **21 members**, chairman **15 years**, VP and Registrar **10 years**, **2 nominated by the Council itself**, **5 elected from the NEA**, NEA President **ex officio**, **70%** for institutional affiliation, **3 months** to reconstitute after dissolution.

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION represents.** NEC registration is compulsory; NEA membership is voluntary.

examTip.trick: **8 before the 2079 amendment, 11 after.** The date of the sitting decides which is keyed — so learn both numbers and read the question's era.
examTip.trap: The count is the least important part. **Public safety overrides the client's instructions and the engineer's own interest** — that is the provision most likely to appear in a scenario question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Signing drawings you did not prepare or supervise is a disciplinary offence** — the commonest real breach, because the signature is the public's only assurance that someone competent took responsibility.

questions.stem: The moment of inertia of a semicircle about its base is:
questions.solution:
**πR⁴/8** about the base (the diameter).

**Why.** The base of a semicircle is the **diameter of the full circle**, and a semicircle is exactly **half** of that circle. So its second moment about that axis is **half the circle's**:

> **I_circle about a diameter = πR⁴/4** (equivalently πD⁴/64)
> **I_semicircle about its base = ½ × πR⁴/4 = πR⁴/8** ✓

> **Halving works here because the base axis passes through the circle's centroid**, so both halves contribute equally. **That reasoning does not work for the centroidal axis of the semicircle**, which is a different line.

**The two semicircle values, which the options deliberately offer together:**

| Axis | Second moment |
|---|---|
| **About the BASE (diameter)** | **πR⁴/8 = πD⁴/128** |
| **About its own CENTROIDAL axis** (parallel to the base) | **R⁴(π/8 − 8/9π) = 0.11 R⁴** |

> **Options (c) and (d) are the SAME value written two ways** — the exact expression and its decimal. Both are the **centroidal** value, not the base value.

> Recognising that two options are identical is itself informative: **neither can be the intended answer**, which halves the field immediately.

**Why the centroidal value is smaller:**

> **I_base = I_centroid + A d²**, and the added term is always positive — so the **centroidal axis always gives the MINIMUM** second moment. Here **d = 4R/3π ≈ 0.424R**, the centroid distance of a semicircular area from its diameter.

> Check: **0.11R⁴ + (πR²/2)(4R/3π)² = 0.11R⁴ + 0.283R⁴ = 0.393R⁴ = πR⁴/8** ✓

**The quarter circle**, from the source's own note — both values are **half** those of the semicircle:

| Axis | Quarter circle |
|---|---|
| **About the base** | **πR⁴/16 = πD⁴/256** |
| About its centroidal axis | **0.055 R⁴** |

**Standard second moments worth carrying:**

| Shape | About the centroid | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh³/12** | **bh³/3** |
| **Triangle b × h** | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** |
| **Circle diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| **Semicircle** | **0.11 R⁴** | **πR⁴/8** |

**Standard centroid positions:**

| Shape | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Triangle** | **h/3 from the base** |
| **Semicircular AREA** | **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r** |
| Semicircular arc | 2r/π |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** |
| Solid cone | h/4 from the base |

> **Note the difference between the semicircular AREA (4r/3π) and the semicircular ARC (2r/π)** — a lamina and a wire are different problems, and the two constants are frequently swapped.

examTip.trick: The base of a semicircle **is the circle's diameter**, so its I is exactly **half the circle's: ½ × πR⁴/4 = πR⁴/8**. Halving works because the axis passes through the circle's centroid.
examTip.trap: **Options (c) and (d) are the SAME value written two ways** — the exact expression and its decimal — and both are the **CENTROIDAL** value, not the base one. Two identical options can never be the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Quarter circle values are HALF the semicircle's** (πR⁴/16 about the base, 0.055R⁴ centroidal). And keep the semicircular **AREA (4r/3π)** apart from the **ARC (2r/π)** — a lamina is not a wire.

questions.stem: If the speed of the overtaken vehicle is 80 km/h, then the design speed is:
questions.solution:
**96 km/h.**

**Working.** In overtaking sight distance analysis, the **overtaking vehicle travels faster than the one it overtakes** by a standard margin:

> **Speed of overtaking vehicle (the design speed) = speed of overtaken vehicle + 16 km/h**
> **= 80 + 16 = 96 km/h** ✓

> The margin of **16 km/h ≈ 4.5 m/s** is the IRC convention, and it represents the **relative speed** at which the manoeuvre is completed.

**Why a relative speed is needed at all:**

> Overtaking takes time, and the distance covered depends on **how much faster** the overtaking vehicle is going. **If the two travelled at the same speed the manoeuvre could never be completed.**

**Overtaking sight distance:**

> **OSD = d₁ + d₂ + d₃**

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **d₁** | Distance travelled during the **reaction time** (2 s) while the driver decides |
| **d₂** | Distance travelled during the **actual overtaking manoeuvre** |
| **d₃** | Distance travelled by the **OPPOSING vehicle**, at design speed |

> **d₃ is what makes OSD so long.** On a two-lane two-way road, the overtaking vehicle uses the opposing lane, so the clear distance must also cover whatever an oncoming vehicle travels in the same time.

> **On a divided carriageway d₃ vanishes**, and the required distance drops to roughly two thirds — which is one of the significant safety advantages of a divided road.

**The scale of OSD:**

| Design speed | SSD | OSD |
|---|---|---|
| 50 km/h | ~60 m | ~235 m |
| **80 km/h** | **~120 m** | **~470 m** |
| 100 km/h | ~180 m | ~640 m |

> **OSD is roughly FIVE times SSD.** That is why overtaking zones cannot be provided continuously, and why roads are marked with **overtaking-prohibited** sections rather than the reverse.

> Where full OSD cannot be provided, **INTERMEDIATE sight distance = 2 × SSD** is used as a compromise, giving at least some overtaking opportunity.

**Overtaking ZONES** are the practical provision:

> Marked stretches where OSD is available, with **advance signs** before them. IRC recommends the zone length be at least **three times OSD, desirably five times** — because a driver needs to see the opportunity, decide, and complete the manoeuvre well before the zone ends.

**The other sight distances:**

| Type | Governs |
|---|---|
| **Stopping (SSD)** | **The absolute minimum on every road**; **SSD = vt + v²/2gf**, t = 2.5 s, f = 0.35–0.40 |
| **Overtaking (OSD)** | Two-lane two-way roads |
| **Headlight** | **VALLEY (sag) curves** at night |
| Intersection | Junction visibility |

> **SUMMIT curves are governed by SIGHT distance; VALLEY curves by HEADLIGHT distance.** A sag curve looks unobstructed by day — its problem appears only after dark.

examTip.trick: **Design speed = overtaken vehicle's speed + 16 km/h.** The 16 km/h (≈4.5 m/s) is the relative speed at which the manoeuvre is completed — without a speed difference, overtaking could never finish.
examTip.trap: **OSD is about FIVE times SSD** — 470 m against 120 m at 80 km/h. That is why overtaking zones are the exception, and why **intermediate sight distance (2 × SSD)** exists as a compromise.
examTip.mnemonic: **d₃ — the opposing vehicle's distance — is what makes OSD so long, and it VANISHES on a divided carriageway.** That single fact is a large part of the safety case for dividing a road.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a type of load-bearing wall?
questions.solution:
**A panel wall** — which is a **NON-load-bearing** wall used in framed structures.

**The classification:**

| Load-bearing walls | Non-load-bearing walls |
|---|---|
| **Solid masonry wall** | **PANEL wall** |
| **Cavity wall** | Partition wall |
| **Faced wall** | Curtain wall |
| **Veneered wall** | Infill wall |

> **A panel wall fills a bay in a framed structure** — the frame carries the load, and the wall carries only its own weight and the wind on its face.

**The distinction that matters structurally:**

| | **LOAD-BEARING** | **FRAMED** |
|---|---|---|
| Carries floors and roof | **The WALLS** | **The FRAME** (columns and beams) |
| Wall thickness | Increases with height | Constant — walls are only enclosure |
| Openings | **Restricted** — they interrupt the load path | Free |
| Height | Practically limited | Unlimited |
| Alteration later | **Difficult and dangerous** | Easy — walls can be removed |

> **The practical consequence: in a load-bearing structure you cannot remove a wall.** Owners do it anyway, and it is a common cause of failure in Nepali buildings that were originally masonry.

**Faced versus veneered — the pair most often confused:**

| | **FACED wall** | **VENEERED wall** |
|---|---|---|
| Facing material | **BONDED to the backing and acts with it structurally** | **Attached for APPEARANCE only** |
| Structural action | The two act **together** | The veneer carries nothing |

> **A faced wall's facing is part of the wall; a veneer is decoration.** The words sound interchangeable and are not.

**Cavity walls** deserve a note because they are load-bearing despite appearing to be two thin walls:

> Two leaves separated by a **50–100 mm cavity**, tied together with **wall ties**. Their advantages:

| Advantage | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **DAMP resistance** | The cavity **breaks the capillary path**; water crossing the outer leaf runs down the cavity face |
| **Thermal insulation** | The air gap, or insulation within it |
| Sound insulation | The discontinuity |
| Lighter than a solid wall of equal performance | — |

> **The cavity must be kept CLEAR.** Mortar droppings bridging it provide a path for water straight across — the same **bridging** failure that defeats a DPC, and for the same reason.

> **Effective thickness of a cavity wall = ⅔(t₁ + t₂), or the thicker leaf, whichever is greater** — a slenderness provision worth carrying, since it is a common examination point.

**Masonry design essentials:** slenderness **SR = h_e/t_e ≤ 27** in cement mortar; **h_e = 0.75H** with both ends restrained; **piers and cross walls increase the effective thickness**; and in an earthquake **unreinforced masonry fails OUT OF PLANE**, cured by **horizontal bands at plinth, sill, lintel and roof** plus vertical bars at corners (NBC 109 and 202).

examTip.trick: A **panel wall fills a bay in a FRAMED structure** — the frame carries the load, the wall carries only itself and the wind. Everything else listed is a genuine load-bearing type.
examTip.trap: **FACED versus VENEERED**: a faced wall's facing is **bonded and acts structurally**; a veneer is **appearance only**. The words sound interchangeable and are not.
examTip.mnemonic: **In a load-bearing structure you cannot remove a wall** — a common and dangerous alteration in older Nepali buildings. And keep a cavity **CLEAR**: mortar droppings bridge it exactly as they defeat a DPC.

questions.stem: Before plastering, the surface has to be:
questions.solution:
**Rough.**

**Why.** Plaster adheres to a background largely by **MECHANICAL KEY** — it grips into the irregularities of the surface. A smooth surface offers nothing to grip, and the plaster **debonds and falls off in sheets**.

**The preparation:**

> **All mortar joints are raked out and the brick surface is scraped or scratched** to obtain a rough face. **The process of deliberately roughening a background before plastering is called HACKING.**

> On a smooth concrete surface — where scraping is not enough — hacking is done mechanically, or a **bonding agent or spatterdash coat** is applied instead.

**Why the joints are raked:**

> Raking the mortar joints to a depth of about **10–20 mm** creates a **continuous mechanical key** across the whole wall, not merely on the brick faces. It is the single most effective preparation step on masonry.

**The other options are real steps in the wrong place:**

| Option | Where it belongs |
|---|---|
| **Watered** | The surface **IS wetted** before plastering — but to stop the background **sucking water out of the plaster**, not as the primary requirement. A dry background causes the plaster to dry too fast and crack |
| Cemented | A **bonding coat** is used on smooth concrete, but it is a remedy for the absence of roughness, not the requirement itself |
| Smooth | The **opposite** of what is needed |

> **Wetting is genuinely necessary and is done alongside roughening** — but the question asks what the surface must **be**, and the answer is rough.

**Number of coats** (from the source's own note):

| Background | Coats |
|---|---|
| **Wood and metal** | **3 coats** — to seal the surface completely |
| **Stone and brick masonry** | **2 coats** |
| Low-cost construction | **1 coat** |

**Plaster thickness and mixes:**

| Location | Thickness | Mix |
|---|---|---|
| **Internal walls** | **12 mm** | 1:4 to 1:6 |
| **External walls** | **20 mm** (often two coats) | **1:4** — richer, for weather resistance |
| Ceilings | 6 mm | 1:3 |

**The common plaster defects and their causes:**

| Defect | Cause |
|---|---|
| **Cracking (crazing)** | Mix **too rich**, or **too rapid drying** |
| **Debonding / hollowness** | **Inadequate key** — the failure this question is about |
| **Blistering** | Late slaking of unhydrated lime particles |
| **Efflorescence** | **Soluble salts** carried to the surface by moisture |
| Peeling | Poor adhesion or damp background |
| Popping | Contaminant particles expanding |

> **A richer mix is not a better plaster.** More cement means more shrinkage and more cracking — which is why internal plaster is deliberately leaner than external.

**Curing** is the step most often skipped: plaster must be **kept damp for about 7 days**. **Plaster that dries too fast cracks**, and no amount of care in mixing compensates for a missed cure.

**IS 1661** is the relevant code for plastering.

examTip.trick: Plaster grips by **MECHANICAL KEY** — it needs irregularities to hold onto. **Raking the mortar joints** creates that key across the whole wall, and the process of roughening is called **HACKING**.
examTip.trap: **"Watered" is a real and necessary step** — the background is wetted so it does not suck water from the plaster. But it is done **alongside** roughening, not instead of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A richer mix is NOT a better plaster** — more cement means more shrinkage and more cracking, which is why internal plaster is leaner than external. And **cure for 7 days**: plaster that dries fast cracks.

questions.stem: The total strain energy stored in a body within the elastic limit is known as:
questions.solution:
**Resilience.**

**The family of related definitions**, which is exactly what this question tests:

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **STRAIN ENERGY** | The **internal work done in deforming a body** — **U = ½ × stress × strain × volume** |
| **RESILIENCE** | The **TOTAL strain energy stored within the ELASTIC limit** — the area under the load–deflection curve up to that limit |
| **PROOF RESILIENCE** | The **MAXIMUM** energy storable up to the elastic limit |
| **MODULUS OF RESILIENCE** | **Proof resilience PER UNIT VOLUME** — area under the **stress–strain** curve to the elastic limit |
| **TOUGHNESS** | Area under the stress–strain curve **TO FRACTURE** — **beyond** the elastic zone |

> **The discriminators are two: WITHIN the elastic limit versus TO FRACTURE, and TOTAL versus PER UNIT VOLUME.**

**Reading the options against those:**

| Option | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Toughness** | Measured **to FRACTURE**, not within the elastic limit |
| **Modulus of resilience** | **Per unit VOLUME**, not the total |

> **Both wrong options differ from the answer by exactly one of the two discriminators** — which is a well-constructed question.

**The physical distinction between resilience and toughness:**

| Property | Means |
|---|---|
| **RESILIENCE** | Ability to absorb energy **and RETURN it** — a **spring** |
| **TOUGHNESS** | Ability to absorb energy **before BREAKING** — resistance to fracture |

> **A material can be highly resilient and not tough** (glass, high-carbon spring steel), or **tough but not resilient** (mild steel, which yields early but absorbs enormous energy before fracture).

> **For structural engineering TOUGHNESS matters more**, because it measures the capacity to absorb energy in an overload — which is exactly what is wanted in an earthquake.

**Strain energy expressions:**

| Loading | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | **U = P²L/(2AE)** |
| **Bending** | **U = ∫M²dx/(2EI)** |
| **Torsion** | U = T²L/(2GJ) |
| Shear | U = ∫V²dx/(2AG) |

**Where strain energy is used in analysis:**

| Method | Statement |
|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO's second theorem** | **∂U/∂P = deflection** in the direction of P |
| **Unit load method** | Virtual work |
| **Two-hinged arch** | The horizontal thrust H from **∂U/∂H = 0** |
| Indeterminate structures generally | Minimum strain energy |

> **Castigliano's theorem is the most useful of these for hand analysis** — differentiate the strain energy with respect to a load and you get the deflection under it directly. Where no load acts at the point of interest, a **dummy load** is applied and set to zero afterwards.

**SUDDEN and IMPACT loading** are the practical application of resilience:

| Loading | Stress produced |
|---|---|
| **Gradual** | **σ = P/A** |
| **SUDDEN** | **2P/A — TWICE the gradual value** |
| **Impact from height h** | **σ = (P/A)[1 + √(1 + 2AEh/PL)]** |

> **A suddenly applied load produces twice the stress of the same load applied gradually**, because the body must absorb the load's full potential energy before coming to rest. **That factor of two is a genuine and often-forgotten design consideration.**

examTip.trick: Two discriminators separate the whole family: **WITHIN the elastic limit vs TO FRACTURE**, and **TOTAL vs PER UNIT VOLUME**. Each wrong option differs by exactly one of them.
examTip.trap: **Toughness goes to FRACTURE; modulus of resilience is PER UNIT VOLUME.** Both are real quantities — the question is which discriminator the wording matches.
examTip.mnemonic: **Resilience = a spring (absorbs and RETURNS); toughness = resistance to breaking.** For structures toughness matters more — it is what absorbs earthquake energy. And a **SUDDEN load gives TWICE the stress** of a gradual one.

questions.stem:
Which of the following measures are used by a risk-averse person to minimize risk?

**A.** Diversification of resources  **B.** Insurance of risk event  **C.** Total cost of resources  **D.** Value of information of risk event
questions.solution:
**A, B and D only** — diversification, insurance, and the value of information.

**Why each of the three works:**

| Measure | How it reduces risk |
|---|---|
| **A. DIVERSIFICATION of resources** | Spreading investment means a loss in one holding is **offset by gains in another** — the risks partly cancel |
| **B. INSURANCE of the risk event** | **TRANSFERS the financial impact** to the insurer for a known premium |
| **D. VALUE of information** | Gathering information **before deciding** reduces uncertainty and allows a better-informed choice |

**Why C is excluded:**

> **"Total cost of resources" is a MEASUREMENT, not a risk-reduction measure.** Knowing what something costs does nothing to reduce the variability of its outcome.

> **It is the odd one out on category** — the other three are actions taken to manage risk; this is simply an accounting quantity. Spotting that settles the question without evaluating each combination.

**Diversification deserves a note because its mechanism is subtle:**

> It works only when the risks are **imperfectly correlated**. Two investments that rise and fall together provide **no diversification at all**.

> **"Don't put all your eggs in one basket" is only useful if the baskets can fall independently** — which is why diversifying across the same sector achieves much less than diversifying across different ones.

**The four standard risk responses**, for context:

| Response | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **AVOID** | Eliminate the risk by changing the plan or scope |
| **TRANSFER** | Shift the impact to a third party — **insurance**, bonds, fixed-price subcontracts |
| **MITIGATE** | **REDUCE** the probability or the impact |
| **ACCEPT** | Absorb it — with a **contingency reserve** (active) or by monitoring (passive) |

> **Insurance is TRANSFER, not reduction.** It does not stop the flood; it pays for it. **And the residual risk always remains with the project** — a subcontractor who goes bankrupt hands the risk straight back.

**What risk means in this context:**

> **RISK is the VARIABILITY of the outcome** — measured by the **standard deviation** — not simply the chance of loss. It is dispersion in **both** directions.

> **A risk-averse person accepts a lower expected return for lower variability.** That preference is what all three correct measures serve.

**And the fundamental relationship:**

> **Higher risk demands higher expected return**, with the ordering following **claim priority in liquidation**: **debt → preference shares → equity last**, which is exactly why equity is riskiest and commands most.

**RISK versus UNCERTAINTY** is worth keeping apart: **RISK** is where probabilities are **known or estimable**; **UNCERTAINTY** is where they are not. **Most large infrastructure decisions involve genuine uncertainty**, which is why judgement remains essential and why sensitivity analysis — showing which assumption the decision turns on — is usually more valuable than a single probability-weighted number.

examTip.trick: **"Total cost of resources" is a MEASUREMENT, not a risk measure** — it is the odd one out on category. Spotting that identifies the excluded item without evaluating each combination.
examTip.trap: **Insurance is TRANSFER, not reduction** — it does not stop the flood, it pays for it. And the **residual risk stays with the project**: an insurer who disputes, or a subcontractor who fails, hands it back.
examTip.mnemonic: **Diversification works only if the risks are imperfectly CORRELATED.** Eggs in different baskets help only if the baskets can fall independently — which is why diversifying within one sector achieves little.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not generated during wastewater treatment?
questions.solution:
**Potable water.**

**Why.** **Potable water is water fit for HUMAN CONSUMPTION.** A conventional wastewater treatment plant produces water clean enough to **discharge to a watercourse**, but **not clean enough to drink**.

> The distinction is between **CLARIFIED** water — treated effluent, low in solids and BOD — and **POTABLE** water, which must additionally be free of **pathogens, dissolved chemicals and toxins** to drinking water standards.

**What a wastewater plant does produce:**

| Product | Description |
|---|---|
| **Clarified (treated) effluent** | The main liquid output — discharged to a river or reused for irrigation |
| **SLUDGE** | Settled solids from primary and secondary treatment |
| **SCUM** | Floating material — oil, grease, light solids — skimmed off |
| **Screenings and grit** | From preliminary treatment |
| **BIOGAS** | From anaerobic digestion — 60–70% methane |

**Why treated effluent is not drinkable:**

| Remaining | Note |
|---|---|
| **PATHOGENS** | Secondary treatment removes most but not all; **disinfection is a separate step** |
| **Dissolved salts** | Not removed by biological treatment at all |
| **Nutrients** (N, P) | Need tertiary treatment |
| Trace organics, pharmaceuticals | Largely unaffected |

> **Biological treatment removes ORGANIC MATTER, not dissolved minerals.** No amount of settling or aeration reduces salinity, and that is one reason treated effluent cannot simply be redirected to supply.

**Water REUSE is nevertheless real and increasing:**

| Use | Treatment needed |
|---|---|
| **Irrigation, landscaping** | Secondary plus disinfection |
| Industrial cooling | Secondary plus filtration |
| **Groundwater recharge** | Advanced |
| **Direct potable reuse** | **Advanced: membranes, reverse osmosis, advanced oxidation, UV** — and multiple barriers with continuous monitoring |

> **Direct potable reuse is technically achievable and is practised in a few water-scarce cities**, but it requires treatment far beyond a conventional plant, and **multiple independent barriers** so that no single failure can reach consumers.

> **The barrier principle is the key idea**: safety comes from having several independent processes each capable of removing the hazard, so that one failing does not compromise the whole.

**The conventional treatment train and what each stage removes:**

| Stage | Units | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary** | Screens, grit chamber, skimming | Coarse and inert material |
| **PRIMARY** | Primary sedimentation | **~60% SS, ~35% BOD** |
| **SECONDARY** | **Biological** — activated sludge, trickling filter | **~85–95% BOD overall** |
| **Tertiary** | Filtration, nutrient removal, **disinfection** | Residual solids, N and P, pathogens |

> **PRIMARY is physical; SECONDARY is BIOLOGICAL.** No amount of settling removes **dissolved** BOD, which is exactly why biological treatment cannot be skipped — and why the two stages are not interchangeable.

**Sludge is the by-product that dominates operating cost:**

> **Sludge handling is often the largest single cost in a wastewater plant.** Its sequence is **thickening → stabilisation (digestion) → CONDITIONING → dewatering → disposal**, and **conditioning with polymer is what makes dewatering work at all** — raw sludge holds its water tenaciously.

examTip.trick: **Clarified ≠ potable.** A wastewater plant produces water fit to **discharge**, not to drink — the remaining pathogens, dissolved salts and nutrients are the gap between the two.
examTip.trap: **Biological treatment removes ORGANIC matter, not dissolved minerals.** No amount of settling or aeration reduces salinity — which is why treated effluent cannot simply be redirected to supply.
examTip.mnemonic: **PRIMARY is physical, SECONDARY is BIOLOGICAL** — settling never removes **dissolved** BOD. And potable reuse, where practised, relies on **multiple independent barriers** so no single failure reaches consumers.

questions.stem: What type of material is most likely to be transported as suspended load?
options: depends on the "energy" of the stream
questions.solution:
**It depends on the energy of the stream.**

**Why no single material can be named.** Whether a particle travels as **suspended load or bed load** depends on the balance between two things:

| Force | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The particle's SETTLING velocity** | Tends to make it fall to the bed |
| **The stream's TURBULENT velocity fluctuations** | Tend to keep it aloft |

> **A particle stays in suspension when the upward turbulent velocity exceeds its settling velocity.**

> **Both sides of that comparison vary** — settling velocity with particle size, and turbulence with the stream's energy. **So the same material can be suspended in a flood and bed load in low flow.**

**The practical illustration:**

| Flow condition | Behaviour of sand |
|---|---|
| **Low flow** | Rolls along the bed — **bed load** |
| **High flow (flood)** | Carried in **suspension** |

> **In a Himalayan river in full monsoon flood, even gravel moves as bed load and coarse sand travels in suspension** — quantities that would be immovable in the dry season.

> **That is why the option naming a material is wrong however plausible it sounds**: clay is *usually* suspended and gravel *usually* bed load, but neither is a rule.

**The modes of sediment transport:**

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| **BED LOAD** | **Rolling, sliding and SALTATING** along the bed |
| **SUSPENDED LOAD** | Held aloft by **turbulence** |
| **WASH LOAD** | Very fine material, **always in suspension**, and **unrelated to the bed** — it comes from the catchment, not the channel |

> **Wash load is worth distinguishing**: its concentration depends on **what the catchment supplies**, not on the stream's hydraulics. **A stream cannot be said to have a capacity for wash load** — it carries whatever arrives.

**The criterion for motion at all — SHIELDS:**

> **θ = τ₀/[(γ_s − γ)d]**, with the critical value **θ_c = 0.056** in fully turbulent flow.

> **τ_c = 0.056(γ_s − γ)d ≈ 0.9 N/m² per millimetre of grain size**, compared against the bed shear **τ₀ = γRS**.

> **It is the SHEAR STRESS at the bed, not the mean velocity, that moves a grain** — which is why the tractive force method superseded the velocity-based regime theories of Kennedy and Lacey.

**Why it matters so much in Nepal:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Reservoir sedimentation** | Trap efficiency 90–99%; dead storage fills far faster than international norms assume |
| **TURBINE EROSION** | **Quartz sand at high velocity cuts runners** — a Pelton needle can lose its profile in one monsoon |
| Canal silting | Requires silt excluders and ejectors |
| Bridge scour | **The leading cause of bridge failure worldwide** |
| Channel instability | Aggradation and degradation |

> **The suspended load usually dominates by MASS, but it is the coarse BED LOAD that damages turbines and fills reservoirs** — which is exactly why a **gravel trap comes before the settling basin**: coarse first, fine second.

**The defences in order along the water's path:** intake siting (outer bank, surface draw) → **trash rack** → **gravel trap** → **settling basin** → flushing.

> **Intake siting removes more sediment than any structure downstream, and it costs nothing** — placing the intake on the **outside of a bend**, where the helical secondary current sweeps bed load to the inside.

examTip.trick: The answer is a **comparison, not a material**: a particle stays suspended when the **turbulent velocity exceeds its settling velocity**. Both sides vary, so the same sand is bed load in low flow and suspended in flood.
examTip.trap: Naming a material feels like the "real" answer, but clay is only *usually* suspended and gravel only *usually* bed load. In a monsoon flood even gravel moves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Suspended load dominates by MASS; coarse BED LOAD does the damage** — eroding turbines and filling reservoirs. Hence **gravel trap before settling basin**: coarse first, fine second.

questions.stem: The best suited material for stabilization of black cotton soil is:
questions.solution:
**Hydrated lime.**

**Why black cotton soil needs stabilising:**

> It contains **MONTMORILLONITE**, an expansive clay mineral whose layers are weakly bonded, so **water enters between them**. The soil therefore **swells when wet and shrinks when dry**, with large volume changes.

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Differential settlement** | The ground moves unevenly under a structure |
| **Cracking** of buildings and pavements | The classic damage |
| **Seasonal heave and subsidence** | Repeated every year with the monsoon cycle |
| Very low strength when wet | — |

> **It is not weakness that makes black cotton soil difficult — it is MOVEMENT.** A soil that swells and shrinks destroys a structure however strong it is when tested.

**How lime stabilisation works** — four mechanisms, in order of time:

| Mechanism | Effect | Timescale |
|---|---|---|
| **1. CATION EXCHANGE** | **Calcium replaces sodium** on the clay surfaces, reducing the double layer | **Immediate** |
| **2. FLOCCULATION** | Particles aggregate into larger crumbs — **plasticity index falls sharply** | Hours |
| **3. Carbonation** | Lime reacts with CO₂ | Slow |
| **4. POZZOLANIC reaction** | Lime + clay silica/alumina → **cementitious compounds** | **Weeks to months — the strength gain** |

> **The immediate benefit is workability; the long-term benefit is strength.** Cation exchange and flocculation happen within hours and transform an unworkable plastic clay into a friable material that can be compacted. **The pozzolanic reaction then cements it over months.**

> **Lime stabilisation actually gains strength for years** — an unusual and valuable property.

**The essential requirement:**

> **Lime works on CLAYEY soils and does nothing for sands**, because the pozzolanic reaction needs the clay's own **silica and alumina** to react with. **There must be clay present for lime to work.**

**Matching the stabiliser to the soil** — the discrimination this question requires:

| Soil | Stabiliser | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **CLAYEY (including black cotton)** | **LIME** | Cation exchange plus pozzolanic reaction |
| **Granular / sandy** | **CEMENT** | Hydrates independently of the soil |
| Sandy, low cohesion | **BITUMEN** | **Waterproofs and binds** — needs a granular skeleton |
| Dusty roads | **Calcium chloride** | **Hygroscopic — retains moisture**, a dust palliative, not a structural stabiliser |
| Fine sands | Sodium silicate | Chemical grouting |

> **LIME for CLAY, CEMENT for SAND** is the essential pairing, and it is the reverse of what many candidates assume.

> **Bitumen is wrong here for a specific reason**: it works by waterproofing and binding granular particles. **Applied to a plastic clay it cannot coat the fine particles and the clay's own water defeats it.**

**Alternatives to stabilisation** where black cotton soil is met:

| Approach | Note |
|---|---|
| **REMOVE and replace** with selected fill | Simple, effective, expensive |
| **CBR / cushion layer** of granular material | Isolates the structure from movement |
| **Deep foundations** through the active zone | Piles or piers below seasonal moisture change |
| **Under-reamed piles** | The standard Indian solution — the bulb **anchors against uplift** during swelling |

> **Under-reamed piles deserve mention**: swelling soil grips a pile shaft and **lifts it**, so an ordinary pile can be jacked upward. **The under-ream bulb resists that uplift**, which an ordinary shaft cannot.

**Note the source's own remark**: a **rigid pavement** is preferred over a flexible one on black cotton soil, because the slab **bridges over** the differential movement rather than following it.

examTip.trick: **LIME for CLAY, CEMENT for SAND** — the reverse of what most people assume. Lime needs the clay's own **silica and alumina** for the pozzolanic reaction, so it does nothing in sand.
examTip.trap: **It is MOVEMENT, not weakness, that makes black cotton soil difficult.** It swells and shrinks seasonally, destroying structures that its strength alone would carry comfortably.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lime gives immediate WORKABILITY (cation exchange, flocculation) and long-term STRENGTH (pozzolanic reaction over months).** And **under-reamed piles** resist the uplift that swelling soil exerts on a plain shaft.

questions.stem: Which soil is formed by the deposition of silt brought down by the rivers?
questions.solution:
**Alluvial soil.**

> **"Alluvial" means deposited by flowing water.** The name itself carries the answer — alluvium is river-borne sediment laid down where the flow slows enough to drop it.

**Where it forms:**

| Location | Note |
|---|---|
| **River flood plains** | Deposited during overbank flooding |
| **Deltas** | Where the river meets a standing water body |
| **Alluvial fans** | Where a steep stream emerges onto a plain and loses velocity abruptly |
| Coastal plains | Some reworked by wave action |

> In the subcontinent, alluvial soils are formed mainly by the **Indo-Gangetic-Brahmaputra river system** — and in Nepal they constitute the **TERAI**, the country's most productive agricultural land.

**Engineering characteristics of alluvium:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRATIFIED** — layered | Deposited in episodes, each flood laying its own bed |
| **Highly VARIABLE laterally** | A sand lens can pinch out within metres |
| Generally fine grained | Silts, fine sands, clays |
| **High water table** | Usually |
| **Loose to medium dense** | Recently deposited, not preloaded |

> **The lateral variability is the engineering problem.** A borehole gives the profile **at that point only** — and in alluvium the profile a few metres away can be quite different.

> **That is why a single borehole is never adequate on alluvial ground**, and why investigation spacing must be closer than on more uniform deposits.

**And the seismic consequence:**

> **Loose, saturated, fine sand and silt in a recent alluvial deposit is the classic LIQUEFACTION material.** Under earthquake shaking the pore pressure rises until the effective stress reaches zero and the soil behaves as a liquid.

> **The Terai has extensive liquefaction-susceptible ground**, and it was observed in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. **Assessment is by (N₁)₆₀ from the SPT.**

**The other soil types named:**

| Soil | Formation |
|---|---|
| **BLACK (cotton) soil** | Weathering of **basaltic lava**; contains **montmorillonite** — **expansive** |
| **RED soil** | Weathering of crystalline rock; **iron oxide** gives the colour |
| **Forest soil** | Formed in situ under forest cover; **high organic content** |
| Laterite | Leaching in high rainfall; hardens on exposure |

> **Note the fundamental division: alluvial soil is TRANSPORTED; the others are RESIDUAL** — formed in place by weathering of the underlying rock.

**Transported versus residual is the classification that matters most in geotechnics:**

| | **RESIDUAL** | **TRANSPORTED** |
|---|---|---|
| Formed | **In place**, by weathering | **Elsewhere**, then deposited |
| Grading | Grades into the parent rock with depth | **Distinct layers**; no relation to the rock beneath |
| Particle shape | Angular | **Rounded** by transport |
| Predictability | Follows the geology | **Depends on the depositional history** |

> **The transporting agent leaves its signature**: **alluvial** (water) is stratified and sorted; **AEOLIAN** (wind) is uniformly fine and very loose; **GLACIAL till** is unsorted with everything from clay to boulders; **COLLUVIAL** (gravity, on slopes) is angular, loose and often unstable.

> **Recognising the depositional environment predicts the engineering behaviour** before a single test is done — which is why the geological history of a site is worth establishing first.

examTip.trick: **"Alluvial" means deposited by flowing water** — the name carries the answer. The other three are **residual** soils, formed in place by weathering.
examTip.trap: **Lateral variability is alluvium's engineering problem** — a sand lens can pinch out within metres, so one borehole is never adequate. Investigation spacing must be closer than on uniform ground.
examTip.mnemonic: **The transporting agent leaves its signature**: water = stratified and sorted; **wind = uniformly fine and loose**; **glacier = unsorted, clay to boulders**; **gravity = angular and unstable**. The history predicts the behaviour.

questions.stem: When two column loads are unequal, which of the possible footings can be provided?
questions.solution:
**A trapezoidal combined footing.**

**The governing principle** for any footing carrying more than one column:

> A footing bears **uniformly** only when its **CENTROID coincides with the RESULTANT of the column loads**. Otherwise the pressure is non-uniform and the footing **tilts**.

**Why a trapezoid:**

| Situation | Shape |
|---|---|
| Loads **equal**, or space available beyond the lighter column | **RECTANGULAR** combined footing |
| **Loads UNEQUAL and space constrained at both ends** | **TRAPEZOIDAL** — the **wider end under the HEAVIER column** |
| Columns far apart | **STRAP** footing |

> A trapezoid **puts more area under the heavier load** without extending further — achieving the correct centroid position within the available length. **A rectangle long enough to do the same would have to project beyond the boundary.**

> The source notes the typical case precisely: **the outer column carries the heavier load and there is a space limitation beyond it.**

**The geometry:**

> **A = (b₁ + b₂)L/2 = ΣP/q_allowable**
> **x̄ = (L/3)(2b₂ + b₁)/(b₁ + b₂)** from the b₁ end

> **A trapezoid is only feasible if the resultant falls between L/3 and L/2 from the heavy end.** Outside that range a rectangle or strap footing is needed — a real constraint, not a formality.

**Why the other options are wrong here:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Strap footing** | For a **BOUNDARY column** whose footing cannot be centred, linked by a beam to an interior one — a different problem |
| **Raft / Mat** | **The SAME thing under two names**; used when footings would cover **more than about half the plan area** — a soil capacity question, not an unequal-load one |

> **That raft and mat are synonyms is itself the tell**: two of the four options describe the same foundation, so neither can be the intended answer. **Recognising that halves the field immediately.**

**The structural surprise in a combined footing:**

> It spans as a **beam loaded UPWARD by the soil**, so it **HOGS between the columns** and the **main steel goes in the TOP face** — the reverse of an isolated footing.

> **That is a classic and serious detailing error**, and it follows directly from noticing which way the load acts.

**A strap footing's mechanism**, since it is the near-miss:

> The **strap beam is a rigid link** carrying moment from the eccentric boundary footing to the interior one. **The strap itself does not bear on the soil** — it is deliberately kept clear, or cast on a compressible layer, so that all the bearing happens at the two pads.

> **A strap beam resting on the ground defeats the whole design**, because it then attracts bearing pressure and the load distribution assumed in the calculation no longer holds.

**Design sequence for any footing:**

> **1.** Size the base from the **safe bearing capacity** using **SERVICE** loads. **2.** Compute the **FACTORED** soil pressure for the structural design. **3.** Check **one-way shear at d** and **two-way (punching) shear at d/2**. **4.** Design the flexural steel. **5.** Check development length.

> **Using factored loads for the bearing check applies the safety factor twice** and produces a footing far larger than necessary — a common and expensive error.

examTip.trick: **Raft and mat are the SAME foundation under two names** — two of the four options are identical, so neither can be the answer. That alone halves the field before any reasoning.
examTip.trap: A **STRAP** footing solves a different problem — a column at a **property boundary** whose footing cannot be centred. It is not about unequal loads.
examTip.mnemonic: **Wide end under the heavy column, so the centroid lands under the resultant.** And a combined footing is loaded **UPWARD by the soil**, so it **HOGS** — main steel in the **TOP**, the reverse of an isolated footing.

questions.stem: Algae in a pond:
options: float in the water during day time and sink during night time
float in the water during night time and sink during day time
float in the water during day time and night time
sink in the water during day time and night time
questions.solution:
**Float by day, sink by night.**

**The mechanism is buoyancy from photosynthetic oxygen:**

| Time | Process | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **DAY** | **Photosynthesis produces oxygen**, which is trapped as bubbles in and around the algal cells | **Buoyancy increases — the algae FLOAT** |
| **NIGHT** | No photosynthesis; **respiration CONSUMES the accumulated oxygen** and releases CO₂ | **Buoyancy is lost — the algae SINK** |

> **The algae are not swimming — they are being lifted by their own oxygen bubbles.** That single picture explains the whole daily cycle.

**The consequence for the water body — the DIURNAL DO SWING:**

| Time | Dissolved oxygen |
|---|---|
| **Afternoon** | **SUPERSATURATED** — photosynthesis outpaces respiration |
| **Just before dawn** | **MINIMUM — can approach zero** |

> **The pre-dawn minimum is when fish kills occur**, and it is why a DO sample taken in the afternoon can be dangerously misleading. **A water body must be judged on its pre-dawn DO, not its daytime value.**

**Why algae are a problem in a water supply:**

| Problem | Note |
|---|---|
| **Taste and odour** | The commonest complaint |
| **CLOGS FILTERS** | Shortens filter runs substantially |
| **Chlorine demand** | Consumes disinfectant |
| **Trihalomethane precursors** | Organic matter reacting with chlorine |
| **Toxins** | Some blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) release genuine toxins |
| DO swings | Stress on aquatic life |

**Control measures:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **COPPER SULPHATE** | **The standard algicide** — about 0.3 mg/l |
| Chlorination | Pre-chlorination |
| **Nutrient control** | **Treats the CAUSE** — algae bloom because of nitrogen and phosphorus |
| Covering the reservoir | Removes the light |
| Mixing / destratification | — |

> **EUTROPHICATION is the underlying problem**, and it is driven by **nutrients — principally PHOSPHORUS**. Algicides treat the symptom; **only nutrient control treats the cause**, which is why tertiary treatment for phosphorus removal matters upstream of any reservoir.

**The algae's one useful role**, worth knowing for the contrast:

> In a **WASTE STABILISATION POND**, the algae–bacteria symbiosis is the treatment mechanism itself: **algae produce the oxygen that aerobic bacteria need**, and the bacteria produce the CO₂ and nutrients the algae need.

> **The same organism that is a nuisance in a water supply reservoir is the working element of a stabilisation pond** — a good illustration that "pollution" is a matter of context.

examTip.trick: The algae are **lifted by their own oxygen bubbles** from photosynthesis — produced by day, consumed by respiration at night. Not swimming, just buoyancy.
examTip.trap: **DO is at its MINIMUM just before dawn, not at night's start.** An afternoon sample shows supersaturation and is dangerously misleading — fish kills happen pre-dawn.
examTip.mnemonic: **Copper sulphate treats the SYMPTOM; nutrient (phosphorus) control treats the CAUSE.** And the same algae that foul a reservoir are the working element of a **waste stabilisation pond**.

questions.stem: For controlling the growth of algae, the chemical generally used is:
questions.solution:
**Copper sulphate (CuSO₄).**

> It is the standard **ALGICIDE**, applied at about **0.3 mg/l**, and often used **routinely through the summer months** whether or not a bloom has yet appeared — because prevention is far easier than clearing an established bloom.

**Why copper works:**

> **Copper ions are toxic to algae at concentrations far below those harmful to humans or fish.** That wide margin is what makes it usable in a drinking water reservoir at all.

> The dose must nonetheless be controlled: too little is ineffective, and too much harms fish and accumulates in the sediment.

**A caution on timing:**

> **Killing a heavy bloom suddenly releases the algae's cell contents** — causing a **taste and odour episode** and a **DO crash** as bacteria decompose the dead mass. **Treating early, at low algal density, avoids both.**

**Why each other chemical is wrong — each has a real and different job:**

| Chemical | Its actual purpose |
|---|---|
| **ALUM — Al₂(SO₄)₃** | **COAGULANT**. Destabilises colloids so they flocculate and settle |
| **BLEACHING POWDER — Ca(OCl)₂** | **DISINFECTANT**. Kills pathogens; **raises pH** |
| **LIME — Ca(OH)₂** | **Softening** (lime–soda process); **pH correction**; coagulation aid |

> **All four are genuine water treatment chemicals**, which is what makes this a real test of function rather than of recognition.

**Alum deserves a note since it is the most-used of the four:**

> **Al₂(SO₄)₃·18H₂O + alkalinity → Al(OH)₃ floc**

> **The reaction CONSUMES alkalinity and lowers the pH**, so a water of low natural alkalinity needs **lime added with the alum** — which is one reason lime and alum are dosed together.

> **Optimum coagulation pH is 6.5–8.5**, and the dose is fixed by a **JAR TEST**, not by calculation, because it depends on the raw water's particular colloids.

**The coagulation sequence and its counter-intuitive requirement:**

| Stage | Mixing | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| **RAPID (flash) mix** | **Violent** | **30–60 seconds** |
| **FLOCCULATION** | **GENTLE** | **20–40 minutes** |

> **The gentle stage is gentle for a reason: violent mixing would TEAR the flocs apart** as fast as they form. The whole art of flocculation is stirring hard enough to bring particles together and softly enough not to break what has formed — expressed as the **velocity gradient G**, high for rapid mix and low for flocculation.

**And the reason coagulation is needed at all:**

> **Colloids carry a NEGATIVE surface charge and repel each other**, so they never settle on their own — they would remain suspended indefinitely. **Alum's trivalent Al³⁺ neutralises that charge**, letting the particles approach and aggregate.

> **Rapid sand filters strain FLOCS, not colloids** — which is exactly why coagulation must precede filtration, and why a rapid filter without coagulation is close to useless.

examTip.trick: All four are genuine treatment chemicals with **different jobs**: alum **coagulates**, bleaching powder **disinfects**, lime **softens and corrects pH**, copper sulphate **kills algae**. Match function, not familiarity.
examTip.trap: **Treat algae EARLY.** Killing a heavy bloom releases the cell contents, causing a taste-and-odour episode and a DO crash as the dead mass decomposes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid mix VIOLENT for 30–60 s; flocculation GENTLE for 20–40 min** — stir hard enough to bring particles together, softly enough not to tear the flocs apart.

questions.stem: In a parallel combination of pipes, which of the following holds?
options: Discharge is same in all pipes
Head loss is same in all pipes
Total head loss is sum of head loss in each pipe
Velocity is same in all pipes
questions.solution:
**The head loss is the same in all pipes.**

**Why.** Pipes in parallel connect the **same two points**. Since head loss is the **difference in energy between those two points**, and both ends are common, **every parallel path must experience the same head loss** — whatever its length, diameter or roughness.

> **The discharges then ADJUST so that each pipe's head loss comes out equal.** A larger or smoother pipe simply carries more flow.

**Series versus parallel — exact mirror images:**

| | **SERIES** | **PARALLEL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Discharge** | **SAME in each pipe** | **ADDS: Q = Q₁ + Q₂ + …** |
| **Head loss** | **ADDS: h = h₁ + h₂ + …** | **SAME across each** |

> Options (a) and (c) are the two **SERIES** properties, offered here to see whether the pair is understood or merely half-remembered.

**The electrical analogy makes it unforgettable:**

| Hydraulics | Electricity |
|---|---|
| Discharge Q | Current |
| Head loss h | Voltage |
| Pipe resistance | Resistance |

> **Series adds resistance; parallel reduces it** — exactly as resistors do. **Parallel elements share a voltage; series elements share a current.**

**Why option (d) is wrong even though it sounds close to (b):**

> **Equal head loss does NOT mean equal velocity.** From **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**, two pipes of different diameter or length reach the same h_f at **different velocities**. Only if the pipes were identical would the velocities match.

**The head loss relation:**

> **h_f = fLV²/(2gD) = fLQ²/(12.1 D⁵)**

> **h_f ∝ Q²** and **h_f ∝ 1/D⁵** — and the fifth power is what makes diameter such a powerful variable. **A 10% larger pipe cuts the head loss by nearly 40%.**

**Working a parallel problem:**

> Set **h₁ = h₂**, express each in terms of its own Q, and combine with **Q = Q₁ + Q₂**. Two equations, two unknowns.

> For **two IDENTICAL pipes**, each carries **Q/2**, so each loses **(1/2)² = 1/4** of the single-pipe head loss — which is why an equivalent single pipe of the same D and f is only **L/4** long.

**Why parallel (looped) networks are used despite being harder to analyse:**

| | **Branched (dead end)** | **LOOPED (parallel)** |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis | **Determinate** — simple | **Indeterminate** — needs **Hardy Cross** |
| Reliability | A break cuts off everything downstream | **Water reaches any point by more than one route** |
| **Water quality** | **STAGNATION at dead ends** | Continuous circulation |
| Fire fighting | Poor | Good — flow from several directions |

> **The stagnation problem is decisive for water quality**: at a dead end the chlorine residual decays to zero, sediment accumulates, and bacteria regrow. **Dead ends are where contamination shows up first**, and they need a **scour valve and regular flushing**.

examTip.trick: Parallel pipes join the **same two points**, so they must share the **same energy difference** — the same head loss. The discharges then adjust to make that true.
examTip.trap: Options (a) and (c) are the two **SERIES** properties. **Series: same Q, losses add. Parallel: same loss, Q adds.** Exact mirror images, and constantly swapped.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal head loss ≠ equal velocity** — from h_f = fLV²/2gD, different diameters reach the same loss at different speeds. The **electrical analogy** (current/voltage/resistance) keeps series and parallel straight.

questions.stem: As the benefit-cost ratio of a project increases, the attractiveness of the project increases. But the minimum value of the benefit-cost ratio for acceptance of a project should be:
questions.solution:
**One.**

> **B/C ≥ 1 is the acceptance criterion**, so the **minimum acceptable value is exactly 1** — the break-even point at which discounted benefits just equal discounted costs.

**Reading the ratio:**

| B/C | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **> 1** | Benefits exceed costs — **worth doing** |
| **= 1** | **Exactly break even — the MINIMUM acceptable** |
| **< 1** | Costs exceed benefits — reject |

> Note the precision the question demands: the project is acceptable when B/C is **greater than OR EQUAL TO** one, so the **minimum value** is **1**, not "greater than one".

> **Option (c) states the condition for the project to be attractive; option (b) states the minimum acceptable value.** The question asks for the minimum, which is the boundary itself.

**The formula:**

> **B/C = PW of benefits ÷ PW of costs**

> **Both must be DISCOUNTED to present worth.** Comparing undiscounted totals over a long life is meaningless, since benefits typically accrue for decades after the costs are incurred.

**Why B/C is the standard method for PUBLIC projects:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compares benefit against public expenditure directly** | Intuitive for a budget holder |
| **Handles non-monetary benefits** once valued | Time savings, lives saved, health |
| Widely required by funding agencies | — |

**Its weakness — the SCALE problem, shared with IRR:**

> **B/C is a RATIO, so it favours small efficient projects over large valuable ones.**

| Project | Cost | Benefit | B/C | Net benefit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 1 crore | 2 crore | **2.0** | 1 crore |
| **B** | 10 crore | 15 crore | 1.5 | **5 crore** |

> **A has the higher ratio; B adds five times the value.**

> **For MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE projects, INCREMENTAL analysis is required**: compare the **extra benefit against the extra cost** of the larger option. Here **ΔB/ΔC = 13/9 = 1.44 > 1**, so the increment is justified and **B should be chosen**.

> **Choosing on the raw ratio would pick the wrong project** — the same error IRR makes, and for the same reason.

**A further ambiguity peculiar to B/C:**

> **A recurring cost can be treated either as a COST (in the denominator) or as a NEGATIVE BENEFIT (in the numerator)** — and the two give **different ratios for the same project**.

> The **NET benefit is unaffected**, which is one more reason NPV is the more robust measure. **The convention must be stated**, and comparisons must use the same convention throughout.

**The appraisal methods compared:**

| Method | Discounted? | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **NPV** | Yes | **≥ 0; choose the HIGHEST** — the theoretically correct method |
| **IRR** | Yes | > MARR |
| **B/C** | Yes | **≥ 1** — standard for public projects |
| **Payback** | **No** | Shorter is better — a **liquidity** measure only |

> **The DISCOUNT RATE is the assumption that most often decides a public appraisal.** A high rate discounts distant benefits almost to nothing, making **long-lived infrastructure look poor** — which is why the rate is genuinely contested and why sensitivity analysis on it is essential.

examTip.trap: The question asks for the **MINIMUM acceptable value**, which is the boundary itself: **1**. Option (c) states when a project is attractive; option (b) states the minimum. Read which is wanted.
examTip.trick: **B/C shares IRR's SCALE problem** — a ratio favours small efficient projects over large valuable ones. For mutually exclusive choices use **INCREMENTAL analysis**: ΔB/ΔC > 1 justifies the larger option.
examTip.mnemonic: **A recurring cost can go in the denominator OR as a negative benefit in the numerator — giving different ratios for the same project.** The net benefit is unaffected, which is why **NPV is more robust**.

questions.stem: The abrasion test is conducted to find:
questions.solution:
**Hardness** of the aggregate.

**The property–test–code table**, which is exactly what this question requires:

| Property | Test | Code |
|---|---|---|
| **Crushing strength** | **Crushing test** | IS 2386 (part 4) |
| **HARDNESS** | **LOS ANGELES ABRASION test** | **IS 2386 (part 5)** |
| **TOUGHNESS** | **Aggregate IMPACT test** | IS 2386 (part 4) |
| **DURABILITY** | **SOUNDNESS test** (accelerated weathering) | IS 2386 (part 5) |
| Shape factors | Shape test | IS 2386 (part 1) |
| Specific gravity, porosity | Specific gravity and water absorption | IS 2386 (part 3) |
| **Adhesion to bitumen** | **Stripping value** | IS 6241-1971 |

> **Every distractor here is a real aggregate property with its own test** — so the question is a straight four-way match, and knowing the table answers it directly.

**The three that are easiest to confuse:**

| Test | Applies | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **CRUSHING** | **GRADUALLY applied** compressive load | Resistance to crushing |
| **IMPACT** | **SUDDEN shock** — a falling hammer | **TOUGHNESS** |
| **ABRASION** | **RUBBING and grinding** | **HARDNESS / wear resistance** |

> **Gradual load → crushing; sudden shock → impact/toughness; rubbing → abrasion/hardness.** Three loading modes, three tests, three properties.

**The LOS ANGELES abrasion test:**

> The aggregate is rotated in a steel drum with **abrasive charge (steel balls)** for a set number of revolutions. **The percentage passing a 1.7 mm sieve afterwards is the LA value.**

| Limit | Application |
|---|---|
| **≤ 30%** | Wearing course |
| ≤ 40% | Base course |
| ≤ 50% | Sub-base |

> **The LA test is the most comprehensive single aggregate test**, because the tumbling drum applies **abrasion, impact AND grinding together** — which is why it is preferred internationally over the separate crushing and impact tests.

**The ATTRITION test** is distinguished in the source's own note:

> It tests resistance to **mutual rubbing or grinding of the aggregate mass** under traffic — closely related to abrasion but measuring wear between the particles themselves rather than against a charge.

**The organising principle for the whole family:**

> **All these values measure DAMAGE, so LOWER is always better.** Crushing value, impact value, abrasion value, soundness loss, water absorption and flakiness index alike — a smaller number is a better aggregate.

> **The single exception is the stripping test**, where **retention above 95%** is wanted — because it measures what is **kept**, not what is lost.

**And the property that governs long-term safety:**

> **POLISHED STONE VALUE** — the skid resistance an aggregate retains after years of trafficking. **Some aggregates polish smooth and become dangerously slippery when wet** despite passing every strength test — a durability property invisible in initial testing, and the reason wearing course aggregate is specified differently from base course aggregate.

examTip.trick: Three loading modes give three tests: **GRADUAL load → crushing; SUDDEN shock → impact (toughness); RUBBING → abrasion (hardness).** Match the mode to the property.
examTip.trap: Every distractor is a **real property with its own test** — strength (crushing), toughness (impact), durability (soundness). This is a four-way match, not a guess.
examTip.mnemonic: **All these values measure DAMAGE, so LOWER is better** — with one exception: the **stripping test wants retention above 95%**, because it measures what is kept. And **LA abrasion is the most comprehensive single test**, combining all three mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which type of hazard is an earthquake and landslide?
questions.solution:
**Geological (geophysical) hazards.**

**The classification by originating process:**

| Hazard type | Origin | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **GEOLOGICAL / geophysical** | **Processes within the Earth's crust or mantle** | **Earthquakes, landslides**, volcanic eruptions, ground subsidence |
| **METEOROLOGICAL** | **Weather and atmospheric conditions** | Hurricanes, tornadoes, droughts, hailstorms |
| **HYDROLOGICAL** | **Water processes** | Floods, storm surges, tsunamis |
| **BIOLOGICAL** | **Living organisms** | Pandemics, epidemics, pest infestations |

> **The discriminator is WHERE THE PROCESS ORIGINATES**, not what it damages. An earthquake originates in the crust, so it is geological however much water it may displace.

**Primary and secondary effects:**

| Earthquake | Effects |
|---|---|
| **PRIMARY** | Ground shaking, surface rupture, ground displacement |
| **SECONDARY** | **Landslides, tsunamis, soil LIQUEFACTION**, fires, dam failure |

> **A tsunami is triggered by an earthquake but classified as HYDROLOGICAL**, because the hazard itself is a water process. **The trigger and the hazard can belong to different categories** — which is exactly why the classification is by process, not by cause.

**Nepal's hazard profile** makes this more than a taxonomy exercise:

| Hazard | Note |
|---|---|
| **EARTHQUAKE** | The whole country is seismically active; 2015 Gorkha the most recent major event |
| **LANDSLIDE** | **The most frequent hazard by number of events** — steep slopes, fragile geology, monsoon rainfall |
| **FLOOD** | Terai and river valleys |
| **GLOF** — glacial lake outburst flood | A distinctly Himalayan hazard |
| Fire, drought, epidemic | — |

> **Landslides deserve emphasis because they are both a geological hazard AND a monsoon-triggered one** — the slope is prepared by geology and triggered by rainfall. **The distinction between PREDISPOSING factors and TRIGGERS is the basis of landslide hazard mapping.**

**The terminology that must be kept apart:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HAZARD** | The **potentially damaging EVENT** |
| **EXPOSURE** | **What lies in its path** — people, buildings, infrastructure |
| **VULNERABILITY** | **How badly the exposed elements would be affected** |
| **RISK** | **Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability** |

> **Engineering cannot reduce the hazard — an earthquake will happen regardless.** What engineering reduces is **VULNERABILITY**, by making structures able to withstand it. **Planning reduces EXPOSURE**, by keeping development off hazardous ground.

> **That is the whole logic of disaster risk reduction**, and it explains why building codes and land use planning are complementary rather than alternative measures.

**The four risk responses** apply equally here: **AVOID** (do not build on the hazardous site), **MITIGATE** (design to resist), **TRANSFER** (insurance), **ACCEPT** (with contingency). **Avoidance through siting is almost always the cheapest**, and almost always the hardest to enforce.

examTip.trick: Classify by **WHERE THE PROCESS ORIGINATES**, not by what it damages. An earthquake starts in the crust — geological — however much water it displaces.
examTip.trap: **A tsunami is triggered by an earthquake but classified as HYDROLOGICAL**, because the hazard itself is a water process. Trigger and hazard can belong to different categories.
examTip.mnemonic: **RISK = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability.** Engineering cannot reduce the hazard — it reduces **VULNERABILITY**; planning reduces **EXPOSURE**. That is why codes and land use planning are complementary.

questions.stem: As the duration of the unit hydrograph increases:
questions.solution:
**Both — the base period increases AND the peak ordinate decreases.**

**The reasoning, which links the two:**

> **The total volume under a unit hydrograph is FIXED** — it always represents **one unit depth (1 cm) of effective rainfall** over the catchment, whatever its duration.

| Step | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Duration increases** | The same 1 cm falls over a **longer time**, so **intensity decreases** |
| **Base period increases** | Base = **rainfall duration + time for catchment runoff to complete**, so a longer rainfall lengthens it |
| **Volume is constant** | **Volume ≈ ½ × base × peak** |
| **Therefore** | **Base up × Peak down = constant** — the **peak MUST fall** |

> **The peak falls because the base widens and the area is fixed.** The two effects are not independent observations — one forces the other.

> **That single constraint — constant volume — is the key to every unit hydrograph question.**

**Comparing durations:**

| Duration | Shape |
|---|---|
| **SHORT (e.g. 2-hour)** | **Higher, sharper peak; shorter base** |
| **LONG (e.g. 12-hour)** | **Lower, flatter peak; longer base** |

> **A short-duration unit hydrograph is the more critical for design**, because it produces the higher peak discharge — which is why the design storm duration is chosen carefully rather than conveniently.

**What a unit hydrograph is:**

> The **direct runoff hydrograph from ONE UNIT DEPTH of effective rainfall**, falling **uniformly over the catchment** in a **specified duration**.

> **Quoting a unit hydrograph without its duration is meaningless** — a 6-hour UH and a 12-hour UH for the same catchment are different curves.

**Deriving it:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Take the observed flood hydrograph |
| **2** | **SEPARATE the base flow** → direct runoff hydrograph (DRH) |
| **3** | Volume under the DRH ÷ catchment area = **effective runoff DEPTH** |
| **4** | **Divide every DRH ordinate by that depth** |

**The three assumptions:**

| Assumption | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Time invariance** | Same rainfall always gives the same hydrograph shape |
| **LINEARITY** | **2 cm gives ordinates 2× those of 1 cm, with the SAME time base** |
| **Superposition** | Hydrographs from successive rainfall blocks simply add, offset in time |

> **Linearity is the assumption doing all the work, and it is only approximately true.** Real catchments respond **non-linearly** — a very large storm produces a proportionally **faster and peakier** response, because overland flow depths and velocities increase.
