> **So a UH derived from moderate storms UNDERESTIMATES the peak of an extreme event** — which matters greatly, since extreme events are what design concerns.

**Changing duration:** the **S-CURVE** method converts a UH to **any** duration; simple **superposition** works only for integer multiples.

**For an ungauged catchment** — the common Nepali case — a **SYNTHETIC unit hydrograph** (Snyder's, SCS) is derived from catchment characteristics: area, length, slope and length to the centroid.

examTip.trick: **The VOLUME is fixed at one unit depth**, and volume ≈ ½ × base × peak. So a longer base **forces** a lower peak — the two effects are one consequence, not two observations.
examTip.trap: Both (a) and (b) are individually true, so "both" is correct. On a question where two options are each defensible, check whether a combined option is offered before choosing one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Short duration → higher, sharper peak** — and that is the critical case for design. **LINEARITY is the weak assumption**: a UH from moderate storms **underestimates** an extreme event's peak.

questions.stem: Plastic bitumen is generally used for:
questions.solution:
**Filling cracks** in masonry structures, and stopping leakage.

**What plastic bitumen is:**

> A mixture of **bitumen, a thinner (solvent), and a suitable INERT FILLER** — with the filler making up about **40 to 45 percent**.

> **The heavy filler content is what makes it "plastic"** — a stiff, putty-like consistency that can be pressed into a crack and stays where it is put, rather than flowing out.

**Why that suits crack filling:**

| Requirement | How plastic bitumen meets it |
|---|---|
| **Stays in place** | The filler gives body; it does not run |
| **Remains flexible** | Accommodates continued movement of the crack |
| **Waterproof** | Bitumen is impervious |
| **Adheres to masonry** | The thinner allows it to wet the surface |
| **Applied cold** | The thinner makes it workable without heating |

> **A crack that is still moving needs a FLEXIBLE filler**, not a rigid one. **Filling a live crack with cement mortar simply cracks the mortar** — which is why a bituminous product is used at all.

**The bitumen product family**, since each option names a real material:

| Product | Composition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **PLASTIC bitumen** | Bitumen + thinner + **40–45% filler** | **Crack filling, leak stopping** |
| **Bitumen (paving grades)** | Straight-run bitumen, graded by penetration | **Road pavement** |
| **CUTBACK bitumen** | Bitumen + **volatile solvent** | **Prime and tack coats**, surface dressing in cold weather |
| **BITUMEN EMULSION** | Bitumen droplets **dispersed in water** | Cold application; prime and tack coats; patching |
| **Blown (oxidised) bitumen** | Air blown through hot bitumen | Roofing, waterproofing, joint filling |
| **Bituminous paint** | Bitumen in solvent | Protective coating |
| **Joint filler / sealant** | Various | Expansion joints |

> **The other three options are all genuine bitumen applications** — which is what makes this a real discrimination rather than a recognition test.

**Cutback versus emulsion** is the pair worth knowing, since both allow cold application:

| | **CUTBACK** | **EMULSION** |
|---|---|---|
| Bitumen dispersed in | **Volatile SOLVENT** (kerosene, naphtha) | **WATER** |
| Sets by | **Evaporation of solvent** | **"BREAKING"** — water separates and drains or evaporates |
| Grades | RC (rapid), MC (medium), SC (slow) curing | RS, MS, SS setting |
| Environmental | **Solvent is lost to the atmosphere; flammable** | **Much better — water based** |

> **Emulsions have largely displaced cutbacks** on environmental and safety grounds: a cutback releases its solvent into the air and is a fire risk, while an emulsion releases only water.

> **Emulsions can also be applied to a DAMP surface**, which a cutback cannot — a real advantage in a monsoon climate where a genuinely dry surface may be unobtainable.

**And the general bitumen requirements**, for context: **moisture ≤ 0.2%** (it flashes to steam at the ~150 °C working temperature), **ductility ≥ 50 cm**, **penetration in tenths of a millimetre**, and adequate **stripping resistance** — the last being the failure that destroys bituminous pavements when water gets between binder and aggregate.

examTip.trick: **40–45% inert FILLER is what makes it "plastic"** — a stiff putty that stays where it is pressed instead of flowing. That consistency is exactly what a crack needs.
examTip.trap: **All four options are genuine bitumen applications**, so this tests which product does which job — not whether bitumen is used in roads.
examTip.mnemonic: **A live crack needs a FLEXIBLE filler** — cement mortar in a moving crack simply cracks again. And **EMULSIONS have displaced CUTBACKS**: water instead of solvent, and they work on a damp surface.

questions.stem: The final setting time of ordinary Portland cement is:
questions.solution:
**10 hours (600 minutes)** — the maximum permitted.

**The two limits, which run in OPPOSITE directions:**

| Limit | Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **INITIAL setting time** | **NOT LESS THAN 30 minutes** | Time to **mix, transport, place and compact** |
| **FINAL setting time** | **NOT MORE THAN 600 minutes (10 hours)** | So the work can proceed — formwork, curing, the next lift |

> **A minimum on the first, a maximum on the second.** That asymmetry is the most-tested point in the topic, and option (b), 30 minutes, is the initial value offered here to catch a reversal.

**What each means:**

> **INITIAL SET** — the time from adding water until the paste **starts to lose its plasticity**.
> **FINAL SET** — the time until it **completely loses plasticity and attains enough firmness to resist a definite pressure**.

**Measured by the VICAT apparatus:**

| Attachment | Test | Criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **Plunger (10 mm)** | Standard consistency | Penetrates to **5–7 mm from the bottom** |
| **Needle (1 mm²)** | **Initial set** | Needle **fails to penetrate** to within 5–7 mm of the bottom |
| **Needle + annular attachment** | **Final set** | The **annulus leaves no impression** |

> All are performed on a paste of **standard consistency** (about **26–33% water**), so that different cements are comparable — **without a fixed water content, setting times would be meaningless**, since a wetter paste always sets more slowly.

**Setting times by cement type:**

| Cement | Initial | Final |
|---|---|---|
| **Ordinary Portland (OPC)** | **30 min** | **600 min** |
| **Rapid hardening** | **30 min** | **600 min** |
| **High alumina** | **3.5 hours** | **5.5 hours** |
| **Low heat** | **1 hour** | 600 min |

> **Rapid hardening cement has EXACTLY the same setting times as OPC.** It does **not** set faster — it develops **STRENGTH** faster, reaching in **3 days** what OPC reaches in 7. That distinction is examined constantly.

> **High alumina cement is the odd one out**: it sets slowly but hardens extremely fast, gaining in 24 hours what OPC needs 28 days for — which is why it is used for emergency and refractory work.

**Why gypsum is in cement at all:**

> **C₃A hydrates almost instantly and would cause a FLASH SET** — the cement would stiffen in the mixer. **Gypsum (2–3%) is interground with the clinker purely to retard it.**

> **That is the entire reason gypsum is present**, and it connects directly to the setting time limits this question asks about.

**Factors affecting setting time in practice:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Temperature** | **Hot weather ACCELERATES setting** — a real problem in the Terai |
| Water content | More water, slower set |
| **Fineness** | Finer cement sets and hydrates faster |
| **Admixtures** | **Retarders** for hot weather and long hauls; **accelerators** for cold |
| Age / storage | **Old cement sets slower and is weaker** — it absorbs atmospheric moisture |

> **Cement should be used within about 3 months of manufacture**, and stored off the ground in a dry store. **Air-set lumps that cannot be crushed between the fingers indicate cement that has already begun to hydrate** and should be rejected.

examTip.trap: The two limits run **OPPOSITE ways**: initial set has a **MINIMUM of 30 min**, final set a **MAXIMUM of 600 min**. Option (b) is the initial value, offered to catch a reversal.
examTip.trick: Reason from site practice: you need **time to place** (minimum on initial set) and you need to **get on with the work** (maximum on final set).
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid hardening cement does NOT set faster** — same 30/600 as OPC; it gains **strength** faster. **High alumina** is the exception: slow set, extremely fast hardening. And **gypsum exists solely to retard C₃A**.

questions.stem: What are the dimensions of kinematic viscosity of a fluid?
questions.solution:
**L²T⁻¹.**

**Derivation.** Kinematic viscosity is **dynamic viscosity divided by density**:

> **ν = μ/ρ = (ML⁻¹T⁻¹)/(ML⁻³) = M⁰L²T⁻¹ = L²T⁻¹** ✓

> **The mass dimension CANCELS** — which is exactly what "kinematic" means. **A kinematic quantity involves only length and time**, never mass or force.

> **That is why the name is a memory aid rather than a label**: kinematics is the study of motion without reference to mass, and this viscosity has no M in it.

> **Option (c), ML⁻¹T⁻¹, is DYNAMIC viscosity** — the near-miss, and the one that retains the mass dimension.

**The two viscosities:**

| | **DYNAMIC (absolute) μ** | **KINEMATIC ν** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | **τ = μ(du/dy)** | **ν = μ/ρ** |
| Dimensions | **ML⁻¹T⁻¹** | **L²T⁻¹** |
| SI unit | **Pa·s (N·s/m²)** | **m²/s** |
| CGS unit | **poise** | **stokes** |
| Water at 20 °C | **1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s** | **1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s** |

> **Water's kinematic viscosity of 10⁻⁶ m²/s is worth memorising** — it appears in every Reynolds number calculation.

**Where kinematic viscosity appears:**

> **Re = VD/ν** — the Reynolds number, and the reason ν is so widely used: it is the **combination in which viscosity actually enters the flow equations**, since inertia depends on ρ and viscous resistance on μ.

> **ν is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to inertia**, which is why it, rather than μ alone, decides whether a flow is laminar or turbulent.

**Reynolds number ranges:**

| Flow | Pipe | Open channel |
|---|---|---|
| **Laminar** | **Re < 2000** | Re < 500 |
| Transitional | 2000 – 4000 | 500 – 2000 |
| **Turbulent** | **Re > 4000** | Re > 2000 |

> Note the **open channel values use the HYDRAULIC RADIUS** rather than the diameter, which is why the thresholds differ by a factor of about four (**D = 4R** for a full circular pipe).

**How temperature affects the two viscosities differently:**

| Fluid | Viscosity with rising temperature |
|---|---|
| **LIQUIDS** | **DECREASES** — thermal agitation overcomes cohesion |
| **GASES** | **INCREASES** — more molecular momentum exchange |

> **The opposite behaviour reflects opposite mechanisms**: a liquid's viscosity comes from **cohesion** between molecules, which heat weakens; a gas's comes from **molecular momentum transfer**, which heat intensifies.

> **That is why hot oil flows freely while hot air is more viscous than cold** — counter-intuitive but entirely consistent once the mechanism is known.

**Dimensional analysis** is worth a note since this question is an instance of it:

> **BUCKINGHAM's π theorem**: with **n variables** and **m fundamental dimensions**, there are **(n − m) dimensionless groups**.

> The standard groups all express a **ratio of forces to inertia**: **Reynolds (viscous), Froude (gravity), Euler (pressure), Weber (surface tension), Mach (elastic)**.

> **Which group governs tells you which force matters**: **Froude for open channel and ship models**, **Reynolds for pipe and submerged flow** — and a model cannot generally satisfy both at once, which is the central difficulty of hydraulic modelling.

examTip.trick: **"KINEMATIC" means no mass** — kinematics studies motion without reference to mass. So the answer must contain only **L and T**, and only one option does.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), ML⁻¹T⁻¹, is DYNAMIC viscosity** — the one that keeps the mass dimension. Dividing by density is what removes it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water: ν = 10⁻⁶ m²/s** — memorise it for every Reynolds number. And viscosity moves **opposite ways with temperature**: liquids thin (cohesion weakens), gases thicken (momentum exchange rises).

questions.stem: The fine for violating a patent right is:
questions.solution:
**Five hundred thousand rupees (Rs 500,000).**

> A fine of **up to Rs 500,000** applies for committing the offence itself, while **an ATTEMPT or ABETMENT** of the same offence attracts a fine of up to **Rs 250,000** — half the amount.

> **Option (b) is that attempt/abetment figure**, offered here to catch a candidate who remembers a number but not which offence it attaches to.

**Intellectual property in Nepal:**

| Right | Protects | Governed by |
|---|---|---|
| **PATENT** | An **INVENTION** — a new and useful process, machine or composition | **Patent, Design and Trademark Act 2022 BS (1965)** |
| **DESIGN** | The **appearance/shape** of an article | Same Act |
| **TRADEMARK** | A **mark distinguishing goods or services** | Same Act |
| **COPYRIGHT** | **Original literary, artistic and creative works** | **Copyright Act 2059 BS** |

**Copyright penalties differ**, and the source notes them explicitly:

> **First infringement of COPYRIGHT: imprisonment up to 6 months and a fine of Rs 10,000 to Rs 100,000, or both.**

> **Note that copyright carries a possible custodial sentence while the patent provision here is a fine** — the two regimes are not parallel, which is worth knowing when a question specifies one or the other.

**Why intellectual property matters to an engineer:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design drawings and reports** | **Copyright** normally vests in the author unless the contract assigns it |
| **Proprietary construction methods and products** | May be **patented** — using them requires license |
| **Software** | Licensed, not owned; unlicensed use is infringement |
| **Consultancy deliverables** | The contract should state **who owns the design** and who may reuse it |

> **The ownership of design documents is a routine source of dispute**, and it is settled by the contract, not by default assumption. **An engineer who assumes they may reuse a design prepared for one client on another project may be infringing.**

**The distinction between the rights, which is the substance worth carrying:**

> **A PATENT protects an IDEA embodied in an invention** — and requires it to be **new, non-obvious and useful**. It must be **registered**, lasts a limited term, and in exchange the invention is **published** so others may learn from it.

> **COPYRIGHT protects the EXPRESSION, not the idea.** It arises **automatically on creation** without registration, and lasts far longer — but it does not prevent anyone from independently expressing the same idea differently.

> **That difference — idea versus expression, registered versus automatic — is what most intellectual property questions turn on.**

**And the professional obligation that connects to it:**

> The NEC code of conduct requires **honesty and integrity** and **no misrepresentation of work done**. **Presenting another's design as one's own is both an infringement and a disciplinary offence** — and the latter is the more serious for an engineer, since **removal from the register ends the right to practise**.

examTip.trap: **Rs 250,000 is the ATTEMPT or ABETMENT figure — half the Rs 500,000 for the offence itself.** Remembering a number without which offence it attaches to is exactly what this question punishes.
examTip.trick: Note that **copyright carries possible imprisonment (6 months) plus Rs 10,000–100,000**, while the patent provision here is a fine. The two regimes are not parallel.
examTip.mnemonic: **A PATENT protects the IDEA (registered, examined, limited term); COPYRIGHT protects the EXPRESSION (automatic, no registration, long term).** Most IP questions turn on that distinction.

questions.stem: Who published the moment distribution method?
questions.solution:
**Hardy Cross**, in **1930**.

**What he contributed.** The method analyses indeterminate structures by **successive approximation**: the **internal moments at the joints are distributed and balanced until the joints have rotated to their final positions.**

> **His insight was that the simultaneous equations of the slope deflection method need never be written down.** Release one joint at a time, distribute the unbalanced moment, carry over, and repeat until the corrections become negligible.

> **That turned a problem requiring the solution of many simultaneous equations into one requiring only arithmetic** — and it made the analysis of multi-storey frames practical decades before computers.

**The procedure:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Compute **fixed end moments** with all joints locked |
| **2** | Compute **distribution factors DF = K/ΣK** at each joint |
| **3** | **Release a joint**; distribute the out-of-balance moment in proportion to DF |
| **4** | **CARRY OVER half** to the far end |
| **5** | Repeat until negligible |

**The two constants:**

| Constant | Far end **FIXED** | Far end **PINNED** |
|---|---|---|
| **Carry-over factor** | **½** | **0** |
| **Stiffness K** | **4EI/L** | **3EI/L** |

> **Using the modified stiffness 3EI/L for a pin-ended member removes the carry-over to that end entirely**, which for an end span saves a great deal of work.

**The others, and what each is actually known for:**

| Name | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **CASTIGLIANO** | **Strain energy theorems** — **∂U/∂P = deflection**; a **FORCE (flexibility)** method |
| **BERNOULLI** | **Fluid energy equation**; also the **Euler–Bernoulli beam theory** |
| **EULER** | **Column BUCKLING — P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**; also the Euler equations of inviscid flow |

> **All four are genuine names in structural and fluid mechanics**, so the question tests attribution rather than recognition.

> **Note Castigliano is the near-miss in a meaningful sense**: his method also analyses indeterminate structures, but it is a **FORCE method** — unknowns are redundant forces — while moment distribution is a **DISPLACEMENT method**.

**The two families:**

| | **FORCE (flexibility)** | **DISPLACEMENT (stiffness)** |
|---|---|---|
| Unknowns | **Redundant FORCES** | **Joint DISPLACEMENTS** |
| Number | **Static** indeterminacy D_s | **Kinematic** indeterminacy D_k |
| Methods | Consistent deformation, **Castigliano**, three-moment, column analogy | **Slope deflection, MOMENT DISTRIBUTION, matrix stiffness** |

> **Choose whichever has fewer unknowns** for hand analysis: a continuous beam usually has fewer redundant forces, a multi-storey frame fewer joint rotations.

> **All modern software uses the STIFFNESS method** — it assembles automatically from element matrices and needs no judgement about which redundants to release. **Moment distribution is its hand ancestor**, and understanding it is the best preparation for understanding what the software does.

examTip.trick: **Hardy Cross, 1930** — and remember why it mattered: it removed the need to solve simultaneous equations, making multi-storey frame analysis practical before computers.
examTip.trap: **Castigliano also analyses indeterminate structures**, but by a **FORCE method** (unknowns are redundant forces). Moment distribution is a **DISPLACEMENT method** — the opposite family.
examTip.mnemonic: **Carry over ½ to a fixed end, 0 to a pinned one; stiffness 4EI/L fixed, 3EI/L pinned.** Using 3EI/L for end spans removes the carry-over entirely.

questions.stem: The hydraulic radius in a wide rectangular channel of bed width 'b' metres, if the flow depth is y, is:
questions.solution:
**R ≈ y** — the hydraulic radius of a **WIDE** rectangular channel equals its **depth**.

**Derivation.** For a rectangular channel:

> **Area A = b y**
> **Wetted perimeter P = b + 2y**
> **R = A/P = by/(b + 2y)** — the **exact** expression, which is option (a)

> **For a WIDE channel, y ≪ b**, so the **2y** term is negligible against b:

> **P = b + 2y ≈ b**
> **R = by/b = y** ✓

**The word "WIDE" is doing all the work in this question.**

> **Option (a) is the exact expression and is always true** — but the question specifies a wide channel, which is precisely the condition under which it simplifies. **The simplification is the point being tested.**

> A question giving no width condition would have (a) as its answer; **this one gives the condition, so it wants the approximation.**

**When is a channel "wide"?**

> Conventionally when **b/y > about 10**. At that ratio, **P = b + 2y = 12y against b = 10y**, so R = 10y²/12y = **0.83y** — within about 17% of y, and the error falls rapidly as the ratio grows.

**Why the simplification is genuinely useful:**

> **Natural rivers and large canals are almost always wide in this sense.** Taking R = y removes the width from every calculation, so **Manning's equation becomes a relation in depth alone**:

> **V = (1/n) y^{2/3} S^{1/2}** and **q = V y = (1/n) y^{5/3} S^{1/2}** per unit width

> **That is the standard form used in flood routing, sediment transport and gradually varied flow analysis** — and it is why the approximation is worth recognising rather than merely tolerating.

**Why option (b), y/2, is wrong here but tempting:**

> **R = y/2 is the value for the MOST EFFICIENT rectangular section**, where **b = 2y**. It is a real and much-quoted result — for **every** most-efficient section, **R = y/2**.

> **But an efficient section is NARROW (b = 2y), not wide.** The two conditions are opposite ends of the same range, which is exactly why both values are offered.

**The efficient sections, for contrast:**

| Shape | Most efficient proportions | R |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangular** | **b = 2y** | **y/2** |
| **Trapezoidal** | **Half-hexagon**, side slope 1:√3 | **y/2** |
| **Any shape** | **SEMICIRCLE** — theoretical optimum | **y/2** |

> **The most efficient section has the LEAST wetted perimeter for a given area**, hence the greatest R and the greatest discharge.

> **So a wide channel is hydraulically INEFFICIENT** — it has a large perimeter for its area. Wide channels exist because of topography, sediment regime and construction practicality, **not because they carry water well.**

**And the Manning scaling worth carrying:**

> **S ∝ n²** at constant V and R — **doubling the roughness quadruples the slope required**, which is the whole economic case for lining.

examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the EXACT expression and is always true** — but the question says **WIDE**, which is the condition under which it simplifies to y. The word is doing all the work.
examTip.trick: **Wide means b/y > about 10**, so P = b + 2y ≈ b and R = by/b = **y**. Natural rivers and large canals are almost always wide in this sense.
examTip.mnemonic: **R = y/2 belongs to the MOST EFFICIENT section (b = 2y) — a NARROW channel.** Wide and efficient are opposite ends of the range, which is why both values appear as options.

questions.stem: The annual depreciation in a hydropower plant is:
questions.solution:
**0.5 to 1.5% per year.**

**Depreciation rates by plant type:**

| Plant | Annual depreciation |
|---|---|
| **HYDROPOWER** | **0.5 – 1.5%** |
| **Wind power** | **0.5 – 1.5%** |
| **Diesel** | **5 – 8%** |
| **Thermal** | **10 – 25%** |

> **The ordering reflects PLANT LIFE directly** — a low depreciation rate means a long life, since depreciation writes off the capital over that life.

**Why hydropower depreciates so slowly:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very long life — 50 to 100 years** | Civil works (dam, tunnel, intake) last longest of all |
| **No combustion** | No high-temperature corrosion or thermal cycling |
| **Few moving parts**, slow speeds | A turbine turns at a few hundred rpm |
| Simple, robust machinery | — |

> **A thermal plant burns fuel at high temperature**, so its boilers, tubes and turbines suffer **corrosion, erosion and thermal fatigue** continuously — a fundamentally more destructive environment, and hence a **10–25%** rate implying a life of a decade or so for major components.

**The structure of the two costs is opposite**, and this is the point that matters:

| | **HYDRO** | **THERMAL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Capital cost** | **VERY HIGH** | Lower |
| **Running cost** | **NEAR ZERO — no fuel** | **HIGH — fuel dominates** |
| Life | **50 – 100 years** | 25 – 30 years |
| Depreciation | **Low** | High |
| Gestation | **LONG** | Shorter |

> **Hydro's economics are almost entirely front-loaded**: pay once, then generate for generations at negligible marginal cost.

**The consequence that follows, and it is significant:**

> **Hydropower is acutely sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE.** Its benefits stretch over 50–100 years, and **a high discount rate reduces distant benefits almost to nothing**.

> **At 12%, a benefit 50 years away is worth about 0.3% of its face value.** A project delivering value for a century is then judged almost entirely on its first two decades.

> **That single assumption often decides whether a hydropower project appears viable** — more than any engineering input does. It is why the choice of discount rate for public infrastructure is genuinely contested, and why sensitivity analysis on it is essential.

**The three depreciation methods**, for completeness:

| Method | How it writes off value |
|---|---|
| **Straight line** | Equal **AMOUNT** each year: **(C − S)/n** |
| **Declining balance** | Fixed **PERCENTAGE** each year — **faster early**, closest to how plant really loses value |
| **SINKING FUND** | A uniform annual deposit **accumulating at interest** to the replacement cost |

> **Only the sinking fund method actually PROVIDES the money** rather than merely recording the loss — which is why it is used in valuation and lease agreements.

> **A = (F × i)/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** is the sinking fund deposit.

**And the related valuation terms:** **scrap value** (dismantled materials, ~10% of cost), **salvage value** (still usable), **year's purchase = 100/rate of interest**, and **capitalised value = net annual income × YP**.

> **A lower interest rate gives a HIGHER year's purchase and a higher valuation** — the same discounting logic seen from the other side.

examTip.trick: **Depreciation rate is the inverse of plant LIFE.** Hydro lasts 50–100 years, so 0.5–1.5%; thermal burns fuel at high temperature and lasts 25–30, so 10–25%.
examTip.trap: Hydro's costs are **front-loaded**: very high capital, near-zero running cost. That is the opposite of thermal, where fuel dominates — and it changes how the two should be appraised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Hydro is acutely sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE** — at 12%, a benefit 50 years out is worth 0.3% of face value. That assumption decides viability more often than any engineering input.

questions.stem: A sinking fund is:
options: The fund for rebuilding a structure when its economic life is over
The total sum to be paid to the municipal authorities by the tenants
A part of the money kept in reserve for providing additional structures and structural modifications
questions.solution:
**A fund accumulated to rebuild or replace a structure when its economic life is over.**

**How it works:**

> A **uniform annual amount** is set aside and **accumulates at compound interest**, so that the total at the end of the asset's life equals the replacement cost.

> **A = (F × i)/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]**

> where A is the annual deposit, F the amount required, i the interest rate and n the life. The bracketed expression is the **sinking fund factor**, one of the standard compound interest factors.

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a real but different fund:**

| Option | What it actually describes |
|---|---|
| "To meet maintenance costs" | **MAINTENANCE** — a recurring annual expense funded from income |
| "Paid to municipal authorities" | **RATES or TAXES** |
| "Reserve for additional structures" | A **CAPITAL RESERVE** or contingency, for **expansion** rather than replacement |

> **The discriminator is REPLACEMENT AT END OF LIFE, not upkeep during it.**

> Option (b) is the natural wrong answer, because "setting money aside for a building" sounds like maintenance. **But maintenance is spent continuously and funded from revenue; a sinking fund is accumulated for a single future event.**

**The three depreciation methods compared:**

| Method | How it writes off value | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Straight line** | Equal **AMOUNT** each year: **(C − S)/n** | Simplest |
| **Declining balance** | Fixed **PERCENTAGE** each year | **Faster early** — closest to how plant really loses value |
| **SINKING FUND** | Uniform annual deposit **accumulating at interest** | **The only one that PROVIDES the money** |

> **That last distinction is the substance of the concept.** Straight line and declining balance are **accounting** methods — they record the loss of value on paper. **A sinking fund is a financial arrangement that actually sets money aside**, which is why it appears in valuation and in lease agreements rather than merely in the accounts.

**Where it is used in practice:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Property valuation** | Deducted from gross income to give the net |
| **Lease agreements** | The lessee contributes to a fund for eventual renewal |
| **Bond redemption** | Accumulating to repay principal at maturity |
| Plant replacement | Industrial asset management |

**The related valuation terms**, which are examined together:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Scrap value** | Value of the **dismantled materials** — about **10%** of cost |
| **Salvage value** | Value of the asset **still standing and usable** |
| **Book value** | Original cost less accumulated depreciation |
| **YEAR'S PURCHASE (YP)** | **100 ÷ rate of interest** |
| **Capitalised value** | **Net annual income × YP** |

> **A LOWER interest rate gives a HIGHER year's purchase and therefore a higher valuation** — which is why property values rise when interest rates fall, and it is the same discounting arithmetic seen from the investor's side.

> Note that **scrap and salvage are different**: scrap is what the **materials** fetch once the structure is demolished; salvage is what the **asset** fetches while still usable. The two are frequently swapped.

examTip.trap: "To meet maintenance costs" is the natural wrong answer. **Maintenance is recurring and funded from income; a sinking fund accumulates for a single future REPLACEMENT.**
examTip.trick: The sinking fund is unique among the depreciation methods in that it **actually provides the money**, rather than merely recording a loss of value on paper.
examTip.mnemonic: **A = Fi/[(1+i)ⁿ − 1].** And keep **SCRAP (dismantled materials, ~10%)** apart from **SALVAGE (still usable)** — the two are frequently swapped.

questions.stem: The unit of measurement of odour is:
questions.solution:
**TON — Threshold Odour Number.**

**What it measures:**

> The **DILUTION RATIO at which the taste and odour become just barely detectable.**

> **TON = (volume of sample + volume of odour-free dilution water) ÷ volume of sample**

> A sample requiring five-fold dilution before the odour disappears has **TON = 5**.

> **A higher TON means a stronger odour**, since more dilution was needed — and the number is a ratio, so it is dimensionless.

**The limits:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Acceptable** | **1 TON** |
| **Cause for rejection** | **3 TON** |

**Measured with an OSMOSCOPE or OLFACTOMETER** — but note that **the detector is the human nose**. There is no instrument that measures odour objectively, which makes this one of the few genuinely subjective parameters in water quality.

> **A panel of testers is used** to reduce individual variation, and testers must be free of colds and must not have smoked or eaten recently.

**Sources of taste and odour in water:**

| Source | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Inorganic salts** | **Na, Ca, Mg**, iron, manganese |
| **Organic dissolved impurities** | Decaying vegetation |
| **Dissolved gases** | **H₂S (rotten eggs), CO₂** |
| **ALGAE** | The commonest cause of seasonal complaints |
| Industrial discharges | Phenols in particular — and **phenol + chlorine gives an intense medicinal taste** at trace levels |

> **The phenol-chlorine reaction is worth knowing**: chlorophenols are detectable at **parts per BILLION**, so a trace industrial discharge upstream can make a whole supply undrinkable without exceeding any other parameter.

**Why the other units are wrong — each is a real unit for something else:**

| Unit | Measures |
|---|---|
| **NTU** — Nephelometric Turbidity Unit | **TURBIDITY** — scattered light at **90°** to the incident beam |
| **FTU** — Formazin Turbidity Unit | **TURBIDITY** — formazin is the reference standard |
| **ppm** — parts per million | **CONCENTRATION** of a dissolved substance |

> **NTU and FTU both measure turbidity** — two of the four options are units for the same property, which tells you neither is the intended answer. **JTU (Jackson Turbidity Unit)** is the older visual unit, using a candle beneath a tube.

**Why removing odour matters despite being an aesthetic parameter:**

> **People who dislike the taste of treated water turn to untreated sources.** An unpalatable safe supply can therefore be **less protective of health than a palatable one**, because it is not used.

> **That is why aesthetic parameters carry standards at all**, and it is a genuinely important point in a rural water supply context.

**Treatment for taste and odour:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **AERATION** | Removes **dissolved gases** — H₂S, CO₂ — and oxidises iron and manganese |
| **ACTIVATED CARBON** | **Adsorbs organic** taste and odour compounds — the most effective general method |
| Ozonation | Oxidises the compounds |
| **Algae control** | Copper sulphate — treats the commonest cause |
| Breakpoint chlorination | Destroys some odour compounds |

> **Aeration for gases, activated carbon for organics** — matching the method to the cause is what makes treatment effective, since neither works on the other's problem.

examTip.trick: **NTU and FTU are BOTH turbidity units** — two of the four options measure the same property, so neither can be the answer. That halves the field immediately.
examTip.trap: **TON is a DILUTION RATIO measured by the human nose** — the only genuinely subjective water quality parameter. Acceptable **1 TON**, reject at **3 TON**.
examTip.mnemonic: **AERATION for dissolved gases, ACTIVATED CARBON for organics** — neither works on the other's problem. And an unpalatable safe supply is less protective than a palatable one, because people abandon it.

questions.stem: The densification of a soil by means of mechanical manipulation is called:
questions.solution:
**Compaction.**

**The definition:** the process in which **soil particles are forced into a denser state by MECHANICAL means**, decreasing the **air voids** and hence the porosity.

**COMPACTION versus CONSOLIDATION — the distinction that matters most:**

| | **COMPACTION** | **CONSOLIDATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expels** | **AIR** | **WATER** |
| **Applies to** | **Partially saturated** soil | **FULLY SATURATED** soil |
| **Cause** | **MECHANICAL energy** — rolling, ramming, vibration | **Sustained LOAD** |
| **Time** | **INSTANTANEOUS** | **TIME-DEPENDENT — years** |
| **Where** | **Artificial** — an engineering operation | **Natural** — a response to loading |
| Equipment | Rammer, roller, vibrator | None — it just happens |

> **Compaction expels AIR in minutes by machine; consolidation expels WATER over years under load.** Those two sentences separate them completely, and the pair is examined constantly.

**The three stages of consolidation**, from the source's own note:

| Stage | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Immediate** | Expulsion of **air** and lateral expansion, if partly saturated |
| **PRIMARY** | **Expulsion of pore water** — the main settlement |
| **SECONDARY (creep)** | **Gradual readjustment of clay particles** into a more stable configuration — occurs over a very long time |

> **Secondary consolidation continues after all excess pore pressure has dissipated**, which is why it cannot be predicted from the pore pressure at all — and why it dominates the long-term settlement of **organic soils and peat**.

**Why the other options fail:**

| Option | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Compressibility** | A **PROPERTY** (a_v, m_v, C_c), not a process |
| **Compression** | The general act of reducing volume — too broad, and not specifically mechanical |
| **Soil stabilization** | Improving soil by **adding a material** (lime, cement, bitumen) — chemical, not mechanical |

> **Stabilisation is the meaningful near-miss**: it also improves soil, but by **adding something**. **Compaction adds nothing — it only rearranges what is there.**

**The compaction curve and its key result:**

> Plotting dry density against moisture content gives an inverted-U curve with a peak:

> **MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY (MDD) at the OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT (OMC).**

| Side of the peak | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **DRY of optimum** | **Flocculated** structure; **higher strength, more permeable, more brittle** |
| **WET of optimum** | **Dispersed** structure; **lower strength, less permeable, more ductile** |

> **The choice of which side to compact on is a real design decision**: an **earth dam CORE is compacted WET of optimum** for low permeability and ductility (so it can deform without cracking), while a **road subgrade is compacted at or slightly dry of optimum** for strength.

> **Compacting the same soil on either side of OMC produces materially different engineering behaviour at the same density** — which is why specifications state a moisture range, not merely a density.

**The tests and field control:**

| Test | Compactive effort |
|---|---|
| **Standard Proctor** | 2.6 kg rammer, 310 mm drop, 3 layers × 25 blows |
| **MODIFIED Proctor** | **4.89 kg rammer, 450 mm drop, 5 layers × 25 blows** — much greater energy |

> **Greater compactive effort gives a HIGHER MDD at a LOWER OMC** — the peak moves up and to the left. That relationship is worth knowing because it explains why heavier plant needs drier soil.

> **Field control is by RELATIVE COMPACTION** — field dry density as a percentage of MDD, typically **95–100%** required — measured by the **sand replacement** or **core cutter** method, or a nuclear density gauge.

**And the compaction plant matched to the soil:** **smooth wheeled** and **vibratory** rollers for granular soils; **SHEEPSFOOT** rollers for cohesive soils, because the feet **knead the clay and compact from the bottom of the layer up**; **pneumatic tyred** rollers for a range of soils.

examTip.trick: **Compaction expels AIR in minutes by MACHINE; consolidation expels WATER over years under LOAD.** Two sentences separate them completely — and the pair is examined constantly.
examTip.trap: **Stabilisation is the meaningful near-miss** — it also improves soil, but by **ADDING** lime, cement or bitumen. Compaction adds nothing; it rearranges what is there.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dam CORE compacted WET of optimum** (low permeability, ductile); **road subgrade at or DRY of optimum** (strength). Same soil, same density, materially different behaviour — which is why specifications give a moisture range.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an enlarging scale?
questions.solution:
**5 : 1.**

**The convention:**

> **Scale = length in the DRAWING : corresponding ACTUAL length**

> **The drawing's dimension is stated FIRST.** That single convention decides every scale question.

| Scale type | Form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **ENLARGING** | **x : 1** where x > 1 | The drawing is **LARGER** than the object |
| **FULL SIZE** | **1 : 1** | Same size |
| **REDUCING (diminishing)** | **1 : x** where x > 1 | The drawing is **SMALLER** than the object |

> **5 : 1 means 5 mm on the drawing represents 1 mm of the object** — five times larger ✓

> All three other options are of the form **1 : x**, so all three are **reducing** scales.

**When each is used:**

| Scale | Application |
|---|---|
| **Enlarging (2:1, 5:1, 10:1)** | **SMALL components** — watch parts, instrument details, thread profiles |
| **Full size (1:1)** | Ordinary machine parts |
| **Reducing** | **Almost all civil engineering** — buildings, sites, maps |

**Standard reducing scales in civil work:**

| Scale | Use |
|---|---|
| **1 : 1000, 1 : 2000** | **Site and layout plans** |
| **1 : 100, 1 : 200** | **Building plans, sections, elevations** |
| **1 : 50** | Detailed plans |
| **1 : 20, 1 : 10, 1 : 5** | **Construction DETAILS** — connections, reinforcement |
| 1 : 25 000, 1 : 50 000 | Topographic maps |

> **Note that a "large scale" map shows a SMALL area in great detail** (1:1000), while a **"small scale" map shows a LARGE area** (1:50 000). **The terminology is the reverse of the intuition**, and it catches people constantly — the reason being that 1/1000 is a larger fraction than 1/50 000.

**Representative fraction (RF):**

> **RF = 1/denominator** — a dimensionless ratio, so it is **independent of the units** used. A scale of 1:1000 is 1:1000 whether measured in metres or feet.

> **That unit independence is why RF is preferred for maps**, where different users may work in different units.

**The drawing convention that must accompany a scale:**

> **A GRAPHICAL (bar) scale should be drawn on the sheet**, not only a stated ratio.

> **The reason is practical: drawings are photocopied, scanned and reproduced at altered sizes.** A stated "1:100" becomes wrong the moment the sheet is reduced; **a drawn bar scale reduces with the drawing and stays correct.**

> **Dimensions should always be read from the figures written on the drawing, never scaled off it** — which is why drawings carry the note "do not scale". The bar scale is for approximate checking, not for taking dimensions.

**Related drawing standards:** lettering heights **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm** in a **√2** progression matching the A-series paper sizes (**A0 = 1 m²**); **vertical 90° or inclined 75°** lettering, **only one style per drawing**; and the **projection symbol** in the title block, since **a drawing read in the wrong angle system is a mirror image of the intended part**.

examTip.trick: **The DRAWING's dimension is stated FIRST.** So **x : 1 enlarges** and **1 : x reduces**. Three of the four options are 1 : x, leaving only one candidate.
examTip.trap: **A "LARGE scale" map shows a SMALL area** (1:1000) and a "small scale" map a large area (1:50 000) — the reverse of intuition, because 1/1000 is the larger fraction.
examTip.mnemonic: **Always draw a GRAPHICAL bar scale**, because drawings get photocopied at altered sizes and a stated ratio then lies. And **never scale off a drawing** — read the written dimensions.

questions.stem: Shear modulus is defined as the ratio of:
questions.solution:
**Shear stress ÷ shear strain.**

> **G = τ/θ = (F/A)/θ** — also called the **MODULUS OF RIGIDITY**, denoted G (or η).

**Why stress over strain:**

> **Every MODULUS is stress ÷ strain.** A modulus measures **stiffness** — how much stress is needed to produce a given deformation. **Its reciprocal is a COMPLIANCE or COMPRESSIBILITY.**

> **The word "modulus" therefore settles the direction of the ratio**, and option (b) is that ratio inverted.

**The three elastic moduli:**

| Modulus | Symbol | Definition | Deformation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Young's (elastic)** | **E** | **Normal stress ÷ normal strain** | **Change in LENGTH** |
| **Shear (rigidity)** | **G** | **Shear stress ÷ shear strain** | **Change in SHAPE** |
| **Bulk** | **K** | **Volumetric stress ÷ volumetric strain** | **Change in VOLUME** |

> **Length, shape, volume** — three kinds of deformation, three moduli. That mapping makes the family easy to hold.

**Why options (c) and (d) are wrong:**

> Both mix **shear with longitudinal** quantities. **A modulus relates a stress to the strain it directly causes**, not to a strain in another mode.

> The ratio of **lateral to longitudinal strain** is a real quantity — **POISSON'S RATIO μ** — but it is a ratio of two **strains**, not of a stress to a strain, and it is dimensionless.

**The relations between the constants:**

| Relation |
|---|
| **E = 2G(1 + μ)** |
| **E = 3K(1 − 2μ)** |
| **E = 9KG/(G + 3K)** |
| **μ = (3K − 2G)/(6K + 2G)** |

> **Only TWO elastic constants are independent** for an isotropic material — given any two, the rest follow.

**Typical values:**

| Material | E (GPa) | G (GPa) | μ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Steel** | **200** | **80** | **0.30** |
| Aluminium | 70 | 26 | 0.33 |
| **Concrete** | **~25 (5000√f_ck)** | ~10 | **0.15 – 0.20** |

> **Check with E = 2G(1 + μ) for steel: 2 × 80 × 1.25 = 200 GPa** ✓ — a five-second verification that any of these values can be checked against.

> **Note G is roughly 0.4E** for most metals, which follows directly from μ ≈ 0.25–0.33.

**Where G is used:**

| Application | Relation |
|---|---|
| **TORSION** | **τ/r = T/J = Gθ/L**; angle of twist **θ = TL/GJ** |
| **Shear deflection** | Significant in **deep beams**, negligible in slender ones |
| Shear stress in beams | τ = VAȳ/Ib |
| **Soil dynamics** | **G_max** governs shear wave velocity and site response |

> **Torsional stiffness GJ depends enormously on the section type**: a **CLOSED** tube (J = 4A²t/s, Bredt) is **hundreds of times stiffer** than an **OPEN** section of the same weight (J = Σbt³/3).

> **That is why an I-beam is a poor torsion member and a box girder an excellent one** — and why curved bridges and decks carrying eccentric load use box sections.

**A note on soil:** **G_max**, the small-strain shear modulus, is the parameter governing **seismic site response** — and it falls sharply as strain increases, which is why the amplification of earthquake motion through soft ground is a non-linear problem.

examTip.trick: **Every MODULUS is stress ÷ strain** — the word itself fixes the direction. Its reciprocal would be a compliance or compressibility, which is what option (b) states.
examTip.trap: Options (c) and (d) mix **shear with longitudinal** quantities. A modulus relates a stress to the strain it **directly causes**. The lateral/longitudinal **strain** ratio is **Poisson's ratio**, a different thing entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **E changes LENGTH, G changes SHAPE, K changes VOLUME** — three deformations, three moduli. Check any pair with **E = 2G(1+μ)**: steel gives 2 × 80 × 1.25 = 200 GPa ✓.

questions.stem: Pick up the incorrect statement from the following regarding tunnel excavation:
options: Oxygen should not be less than 19.5%
Carbon dioxide should not be more than 0.5%
Hydrogen sulphide should not be more than 0.001%
questions.solution:
**"Oxygen should be LESS than 19.5%" is the incorrect statement.**

> **Options (a) and (d) are direct contradictions of each other**, so one of them must be the false one — and since oxygen is what workers breathe, the requirement is obviously a **MINIMUM**, not a maximum.

> **Spotting the contradictory pair identifies the answer immediately**, without knowing the other limits at all. **When two options state opposite things, one of them is the answer.**

**The tunnel atmosphere requirements:**

| Gas | Limit | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **OXYGEN** | **NOT LESS than 19.5%** | Below it, impaired judgement, then unconsciousness |
| **Carbon dioxide** | Not more than **0.5%** | Asphyxiant; causes rapid breathing and headache |
| **Hydrogen sulphide** | Not more than **0.001% (10 ppm)** | **Highly toxic** |
| Carbon monoxide | Not more than 50 ppm | Binds haemoglobin |
| Methane | Below the explosive limit | **Explosive at 5–15%** |

> **Normal air is about 20.9% oxygen**, so 19.5% is only a small reduction — the margin is deliberately tight because the effects of oxygen deficiency come on without warning.

**Why hydrogen sulphide is the most dangerous:**

> It smells of **rotten eggs at low concentration** — but **at higher concentrations it PARALYSES the sense of smell**.

> **The warning disappears exactly when the danger becomes lethal.** A worker who notices the smell fading may believe the air has cleared when in fact it has become far more dangerous.

> **That is why H₂S is monitored by instrument, never by nose**, and why its limit is expressed in parts per million rather than percent.

**Where these gases come from in a tunnel:**

| Gas | Source |
|---|---|
| **Oxygen depletion** | Consumed by workers, engines, oxidation of rock and timber |
| **CO₂ and CO** | **Blasting fumes**, diesel plant, combustion |
| **H₂S and METHANE** | **Released from the strata** — particularly organic-rich or coal-bearing rock |
| Radon | Some geological formations |
| **Dust (silica)** | Drilling and blasting — **SILICOSIS is a long-term hazard** |

> **Methane and H₂S emerge from the ground itself and cannot be predicted from the surface** — which is why **continuous monitoring**, not periodic testing, is the requirement.

**VENTILATION** is therefore the primary control:

| System | Note |
|---|---|
| **Blowing (forcing)** | Fresh air ducted to the face — **clears blasting fumes fastest** |
| **Exhausting** | Foul air drawn out |
| **Reversible** | Blow to clear the face, exhaust during mucking |

> **Ventilation frequently controls the ADVANCE RATE of a tunnel**, alongside muck removal — the cycle cannot restart until the face is clear of fumes.

**The other tunnelling hazards:**

| Hazard | Control |
|---|---|
| **Roof falls** | Prompt support — **rock bolts, shotcrete, mesh (NATM)** |
| **WATER inrush** | **Probe drilling ahead of the face** — the essential precaution |
| **Squeezing / swelling ground** | Flexible support, monitored convergence |
| Fire and explosion | Gas monitoring, non-sparking equipment |
| Dust | Wet drilling, ventilation, respirators |

> **Probe drilling ahead of the face is the single most valuable precaution in uncertain ground**, because a water or gas inrush encountered without warning gives no time to react — and in a tunnel there is only one way out.

examTip.trick: **Options (a) and (d) directly contradict each other**, so one must be the answer — and oxygen is obviously a **minimum**. Spotting a contradictory pair settles the question without knowing any other limit.
examTip.trap: **H₂S paralyses the sense of smell at dangerous concentrations** — the warning vanishes exactly when the risk becomes lethal. Hence instrument monitoring, never the nose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Normal air is 20.9% O₂; the limit is 19.5%** — a deliberately tight margin, because oxygen deficiency impairs judgement before it is noticed. And **probe drill ahead of the face**: in a tunnel there is one way out.

questions.stem: A raft foundation is called a floating foundation when:
options: A normal foundation which can raise and float during floods
A foundation floating on water like barges
A foundation in which new loads due to the structure are equal to the weight of the soil removed by excavation
A foundation cannot be floating type under any condition
questions.solution:
**When the new load imposed by the structure equals the weight of the soil removed by excavation.**

**The principle — and it is an elegant one:**

> **The soil at foundation level already carries the weight of the ground above it.** If you excavate a basement and the structure you build weighs **exactly the same as the soil you removed**, then the soil at that level experiences **NO NET CHANGE IN STRESS**.

> **No stress change means NO SETTLEMENT** — the structure is, in effect, "floating" in the excavation, buoyed by the stress it did not add.

> It is also called a **BALANCING RAFT** or **COMPENSATED FOUNDATION**, and it causes **theoretically zero settlement**.

**Note the name is metaphorical, not literal**, which is exactly what options (a) and (b) exploit:

> The foundation does **not** float on water. **It "floats" in the sense that Archimedes' principle is being applied to SOIL rather than to water** — the excavated soil plays the part of the displaced fluid.

> **That analogy is the whole idea**, and recognising it eliminates both literal-minded distractors at once.

**Degrees of compensation:**

| Type | Condition | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| **FULLY compensated** | Structure weight **=** excavated soil weight | **Theoretically zero** |
| **PARTIALLY compensated** | Structure weight **>** excavated soil weight | Reduced, but not zero |
| **Over-compensated** | Structure weight **<** excavated soil weight | **HEAVE — the ground rises** |

> **Over-compensation causes HEAVE**, which is a real problem in deep excavations in soft clay — the base of the excavation swells upward as the overburden is removed, and it must be accounted for in the construction sequence.

**When a floating foundation is used:**

> **On DEEP DEPOSITS OF SOFT COMPRESSIBLE CLAY**, where:

| Alternative | Problem |
|---|---|
| Shallow footings | **Excessive settlement** |
| Piles | **No competent stratum within reach** — the clay may be tens of metres deep |
| **Floating raft** | **Works precisely because it adds no stress** |

> **It is the solution when there is nothing firm to found on**, which is why it appears in cities built on deep alluvial or lacustrine deposits — including, in principle, parts of the Kathmandu valley.

**The practical difficulties**, which are considerable:

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Deep excavation** required | The heavier the building, the deeper the basement must be |
| **Dewatering and its consequences** | Lowering the water table **increases effective stress and settles the SURROUNDINGS** |
| **BASE HEAVE** during excavation | The excavation floor swells before the building is placed |
| **UPLIFT (flotation) when empty** | The completed basement may be **buoyant** if the water table is high and the building unloaded |
| Sequencing | The building must be constructed as the relief occurs |

> **The uplift check is genuinely important and easily forgotten**: a deep basement below the water table experiences **hydrostatic UPLIFT**, and an empty or lightly-loaded structure can float. **The dead load resisting uplift must be factored DOWN to 0.9**, not up — using 1.5 there hides the failure entirely.

**Raft foundations generally:**

> A raft is used when **footings would cover more than about half the plan area**, when bearing capacity is low, or when **differential settlement must be controlled** — because a raft **ties the columns together so they settle as one**, converting differential settlement into uniform settlement.

> **That is a raft's main virtue: it does not necessarily reduce total settlement, but it makes it uniform** — and it is **differential** settlement, not uniform, that damages buildings.

examTip.trick: **It is Archimedes applied to SOIL, not water** — the excavated soil plays the part of the displaced fluid. Recognising the metaphor eliminates both literal-minded distractors at once.
examTip.trap: **Over-compensation causes HEAVE** — remove more weight than you add and the ground rises. And a deep empty basement below the water table can **float**, so the resisting dead load is factored **DOWN to 0.9**.
examTip.mnemonic: **No stress change means no settlement.** It is the solution when there is **nothing firm to found on** — deep soft clay with no stratum within pile reach. And a raft's virtue is making settlement **uniform**, not smaller.

questions.stem: The maximum deflection in a fixed beam due to a point load P at the centre is:
questions.solution:
**PL³/192EI.**

**The standard deflection formulae** — and the pattern in them:

| Beam | Loading | Maximum deflection |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | **Central point load W** | **WL³/48EI** |
| **FIXED both ends** | **Central point load W** | **WL³/192EI** |
| **Simply supported** | **UDL w** | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| **FIXED both ends** | **UDL w** | **wL⁴/384EI** |
| **Cantilever** | **Point load at free end** | **WL³/3EI** |
| Cantilever | UDL | wL⁴/8EI |

**The pattern worth carrying:**

> **Fixing both ends reduces the deflection FOURFOLD for a point load** (48 → 192) and **FIVEFOLD for a UDL** (5/384 → 1/384).

> **Fixity is enormously effective against deflection**, because the end moments oppose the sagging curvature over the whole span.

**Why option (d), PL³/384EI, is the trap:**

> **384 belongs to the UDL cases**, not the point load. The number is real and familiar — it appears in both **5wL⁴/384EI** and **wL⁴/384EI** — but with **w (intensity) and L⁴**, never with P and L³.

> **Check the DIMENSIONS as a guard**: a UDL formula must contain **L⁴** because w has units of force per length. **A point load formula contains L³.** That check alone eliminates any confusion between the two families.

**Why option (c) is dimensionally wrong:**

> **PL²/16EI** has **L²**, which cannot give a deflection. **PL²/EI has the dimensions of an ANGLE (a slope), not a length.**

> Indeed **PL²/16EI is the slope at the support** of a simply supported beam under a central point load — a real quantity in the wrong place.

> **Deflection formulae always carry L³ (point load) or L⁴ (UDL); slope formulae carry L² or L³.** That is a reliable dimensional screen.

**The associated fixed-end moments**, which are the reason for the reduction:

| Loading | Fixed end moment | Midspan moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Central point load W** | **WL/8** | **WL/8** |
| **UDL w** | **wL²/12** | **wL²/24** |

> Compare with the simply supported values of **WL/4** and **wL²/8** — **fixity halves the maximum moment as well as cutting the deflection several-fold.**

> **That is the structural argument for continuity**, and it is why continuous construction dominates in reinforced concrete, where fixity is achieved simply by running the reinforcement through.

**The costs of fixity**, which must be stated alongside:

| Cost | Note |
|---|---|
| **SETTLEMENT sensitivity** | A support that settles or rotates induces **large moments** |
| **Temperature stresses** | The beam cannot expand freely |
| **HOGGING at supports** | Tension in the **TOP** — needs top steel there, adequately extended |
| Indeterminate | Harder to analyse |

> **A determinate beam develops no stress at all from support settlement; a fixed beam develops a great deal** — which is why fixity requires reliable foundations.

**Why deflection matters at all:**

> It is a **SERVICEABILITY** limit state, checked with **UNFACTORED** loads. IS 456 limits: **span/250** for total deflection, and **span/350 or 20 mm** (whichever is less) for deflection after partition construction.

> **For slabs and long-span beams, deflection usually governs the depth rather than strength** — which is why the **span/effective depth ratio** (cantilever 7, simply supported 20, continuous 26) is the first thing computed in a slab design, not the last.

examTip.trick: **Fixing both ends cuts deflection FOURFOLD for a point load (48 → 192) and FIVEFOLD for a UDL (5/384 → 1/384).** Learn the pattern, not four separate numbers.
examTip.trap: **384 belongs to the UDL cases**, with **w and L⁴** — never with P and L³. And **PL²/16EI has the dimensions of a SLOPE, not a deflection**. A dimensional check kills both wrong options.
examTip.mnemonic: **Point load → L³; UDL → L⁴.** Fixity also halves the moment (WL/4 → WL/8, wL²/8 → wL²/12 at supports) — but it makes the beam **sensitive to support settlement**, which a determinate beam is not.

questions.stem: NTU is the measure of:
questions.solution:
**Turbidity.**

**What NTU means:**

> **Nephelometric Turbidity Unit.** "Nephelometric" refers to the measurement principle: the instrument measures **light SCATTERED at 90° to the incident beam** by suspended particles.

> **The more particles, the more scattering, the higher the NTU.**

**The turbidity units and how they differ:**

| Unit | Basis |
|---|---|
| **NTU** | **Nephelometric** — scattered light at 90°. **The modern standard** |
| **FTU** | **Formazin** Turbidity Unit — formazin is the **reference standard suspension** |
| **JTU** | **Jackson** Turbidity Unit — the **historical VISUAL method**, using a candle beneath a tube until the flame could no longer be distinguished |

> **NTU and FTU are numerically equivalent**, both being calibrated against formazin; JTU is the obsolete visual method.

**What turbidity measures and why it matters:**

> It is the degree to which water **loses its transparency** because of suspended particles, and it gives an estimate of **TOTAL SUSPENDED SOLIDS (TSS)**.

| Consequence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SHIELDS pathogens from disinfection** | Micro-organisms hide **inside** particles, where chlorine cannot reach |
| **Consumes chlorine** | The organic fraction exerts a demand |
| **Fastest indicator of treatment failure** | A rise signals filter breakthrough immediately |
| Aesthetically objectionable | People reject cloudy water and turn to unsafe sources |

> **The shielding effect is decisive: chlorination of turbid water does not work reliably, however large the dose.** That is why the treatment sequence is always **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST** — filtration is what makes disinfection work.

**Limits:**

| Standard | Turbidity |
|---|---|
| **Nepal drinking water standard** | **5 NTU** |
| **WHO guideline** | **< 1 NTU** where disinfection is practised |
| Filter effluent (good practice) | **< 0.5 NTU** |

**The other options and their proper units:**

| Parameter | Unit |
|---|---|
| **Colour** | **Hazen units (Pt-Co scale)** — limit **5–15** |
| **Dissolved oxygen** | **mg/l** — saturation **9.08 mg/l at 20 °C** |
| **pH** | **Dimensionless** — a logarithmic scale, limit **6.5 – 8.5** |
| **Odour** | **TON** — Threshold Odour Number |

> **Note that pH has no unit at all**, being **−log₁₀[H⁺]** — a point worth remembering, since it is occasionally asked directly.

**Turbidity versus colour** is worth distinguishing, since both affect appearance:

| | **TURBIDITY** | **COLOUR** |
|---|---|---|
| Caused by | **SUSPENDED** particles | **DISSOLVED** substances (and colloids) |
| Removed by | **Coagulation, sedimentation, FILTRATION** | **Coagulation, activated carbon, oxidation** |
| Health significance | **Indirect but serious** — shields pathogens | Mainly aesthetic |

> **Turbidity is suspended and filterable; true colour is dissolved and is not.** That is why a water can be perfectly clear and still deeply coloured — as with the brown, organic-rich water of a peaty catchment.

**Key Nepali standard values as a block:** turbidity **5 NTU**, pH **6.5–8.5**, hardness **500 mg/l**, iron **0.3**, chloride **250**, **nitrate 50**, **fluoride 0.5–1.5 (a RANGE)**, **arsenic 0.05**, **E. coli ZERO per 100 ml**, residual chlorine 0.1–0.2 mg/l.

examTip.trick: **"Nephelometric" describes the METHOD** — scattered light at 90°. NTU and FTU are numerically equivalent (both calibrated to formazin); **JTU is the obsolete visual candle method**.
examTip.trap: Turbidity's real importance is that it **SHIELDS pathogens from chlorine** — so **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST**. A large chlorine dose does not compensate for turbid water.
examTip.mnemonic: **Turbidity is SUSPENDED (filterable); true colour is DISSOLVED (not).** Water can be perfectly clear and deeply coloured — as in a peaty catchment. And **pH has no unit at all**.

questions.stem: The influence line diagram for the reaction at the support of a cantilever beam is:
questions.solution:
**A rectangle** of height 1, extending across the whole span.

**Why.** A cantilever has **only ONE support**, so **that support must carry the entire load wherever it is placed.**

> A unit load anywhere on the span produces a **vertical reaction of exactly 1** at the fixed end.

> **The ordinate is therefore 1 at every position** — and a diagram with constant ordinate 1 across the span is a **RECTANGLE** ✓

**The reasoning is pure statics and needs no construction:**

> **ΣV = 0** requires the reaction to equal the applied load. **With no second support to share it, the reaction is always the full load.**

> **That is why the influence line is flat.** It is one of the few influence lines that can be written down instantly.

**The other cantilever influence lines**, for contrast:

| Quantity | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Vertical REACTION at the fixed end** | **RECTANGLE, ordinate 1 throughout** |
| **Fixing MOMENT at the support** | **TRIANGLE**, zero at the free end, **maximum L at the support** — linear |
| **Shear at a section** | **Rectangle of ordinate 1** over the portion **beyond** the section, zero elsewhere |
| **Moment at a section** | **Triangle** over the portion beyond the section |

> **Note the pattern: for a cantilever, load applied BETWEEN the section and the support has no effect on that section** — it is carried directly to the support without passing through. **Hence the zero region in the shear and moment influence lines.**

**Compare with a simply supported beam**, where the reaction is shared:

| Quantity | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | **Linear, 1 at A falling to 0 at B** |
| **Moment at a section** (a from left) | **Triangular**, peak **ab/L** |
| **Shear at a section** | Two parallel lines with a **UNIT STEP** at the section |

> **The simply supported reaction influence line is a triangle because the two supports share the load in proportion to the load's position.** A cantilever has no sharing, hence the rectangle.

**What an influence line IS**, since the concept underlies all of this:

> **One quantity, ONE FIXED section, MOVING load.** The horizontal axis is the **position of the LOAD**, not position along the beam.

> **That is what distinguishes it from a bending moment diagram**, in which the load is fixed and the section varies — even though the two can share the same triangular shape on a simple span.

**Using an influence line — two rules cover everything:**

| Load | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at the load's position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |

> And the placement rules follow: **point load → maximum ordinate; UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.**

> **Because a SHEAR influence line changes sign at the section, loading both sides partly cancels** — so maximum shear needs **one side loaded only**. That is the pattern-loading principle in its simplest form.

**For an INDETERMINATE structure** the influence line is a **CURVE** and cannot be found by statics — but **MÜLLER-BRESLAU's principle** gives its shape directly: **release the restraint corresponding to the quantity wanted, impose a unit displacement, and the deflected shape IS the influence line.**

examTip.trick: A cantilever has **only one support**, so it carries the **whole** load wherever the load sits. The ordinate is **1 everywhere** — a rectangle. Pure statics, no construction needed.
examTip.trap: The **fixing MOMENT** influence line for the same cantilever **is** a triangle (zero at the free end, L at the support). Read which quantity is asked — reaction or moment.
examTip.mnemonic: **One quantity, ONE fixed section, MOVING load** — the axis is the **load's position**, which is what separates an influence line from a bending moment diagram. And **Müller-Breslau** gives the shape for indeterminate cases.

questions.stem: Which part of Nepal is more susceptible to earthquake?
questions.solution:
**Eastern Nepal**, as keyed.

> The Council's material identifies eastern Nepal as the more susceptible region. **In practice the whole country is seismically active**, and the question is one of relative rather than absolute susceptibility.

**Why Nepal is seismic at all — the tectonic setting:**

> Nepal lies on the **collision boundary between the INDIAN and EURASIAN plates**. The Indian plate is moving north at about **45–50 mm per year** and **underthrusting** the Eurasian plate.

> **That convergence is what raised the Himalaya, and it is what makes the entire range one of the world's most active seismic belts.** The mountains and the earthquakes have the same cause.

**The major structures:**

| Fault | Position |
|---|---|
| **MFT — Main Frontal Thrust** | Southernmost, at the Siwalik front |
| **MBT — Main Boundary Thrust** | Between the Siwaliks and the Lesser Himalaya |
| **MCT — Main Central Thrust** | Between the Lesser and Higher Himalaya |
| **MHT — Main Himalayan Thrust** | **The master DÉCOLLEMENT** on which the others merge at depth |

> **The MHT is where the great earthquakes occur**, and the 2015 Gorkha earthquake (M 7.8) ruptured a segment of it.

**The SEISMIC GAP concept** is the reason regional susceptibility is discussed at all:

> Segments of the Himalayan front that **have NOT ruptured in a long time** have accumulated strain and are considered more likely to rupture next.

> **A long quiet interval on an active fault is a warning, not a reassurance** — which is the opposite of the intuitive reading, and it is the single most important idea in regional seismic hazard.

> **Western Nepal is widely discussed as such a gap**, not having had a great earthquake since 1505 — which is why sources differ on which region is "most" susceptible depending on whether they mean recent activity or accumulated strain.

**Major historical earthquakes:**

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| **1505** | Great western Nepal earthquake |
| **1833** | Central Nepal |
| **1934 (1990 BS)** | **Nepal–Bihar, M 8.0 — the most destructive in Nepali history** |
| **1988** | Udayapur, M 6.9 — eastern Nepal |
| **2015 (2072 BS)** | **Gorkha, M 7.8** |

**What the 2015 earthquake demonstrated** about vulnerability:

| Failure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SOFT STOREY** | Open ground floors for parking or shops, with infill walls above |
| **SHORT COLUMN** | Partial-height walls attracting large shear over a short length |
| **Unreinforced masonry OUT-OF-PLANE failure** | The dominant failure in traditional buildings |
| **Site AMPLIFICATION** | The **soft lacustrine basin of the Kathmandu valley amplified the shaking** |
| Poor detailing | 90° hooks, inadequate confinement, poor bar anchorage |

> **Configuration faults — soft storey and short column — cannot be corrected by strengthening members.** They must be avoided in the layout, which is why they are a planning matter as much as a structural one.

**Design provisions (IS 1893 / NBC 105):**

> **V_B = A_h × W**, with **A_h = (Z/2)(I/R)(S_a/g)** and **W = full dead load + 25–50% of imposed load.**

> **Earthquake force is proportional to MASS** — uniquely among load types, **reducing weight reduces the load directly**. Lighter roofing, lighter partitions, and no heavy tanks high up.

> And the detailing that delivers ductility: **STRONG COLUMN–WEAK BEAM**, **closely spaced ties in hinge zones**, and **135° hooks** — because a **90° hook opens out and becomes useless the moment the cover spalls**, which is exactly when it is needed.

examTip.trick: **The Himalaya and its earthquakes have the same cause** — the Indian plate underthrusting Eurasia at 45–50 mm/year. The whole country is active; the question is relative susceptibility.
examTip.trap: **A long quiet interval on an active fault is a WARNING, not a reassurance** — the seismic gap concept. That is the opposite of the intuitive reading and the key idea in regional hazard.
examTip.mnemonic: **Earthquake force follows MASS**, so lighter is safer — uniquely among loads. And **SOFT STOREY and SHORT COLUMN are configuration faults**: no amount of member strengthening fixes them, only layout does.

questions.stem: A fish ladder is provided on the side of:
questions.solution:
**The divide wall.**

**What a fish ladder is:**

> A structure at a weir or barrage that lets **fish migrate past the obstruction** — moving freely and safely up and down the river. It is provided on **headworks built on PERENNIAL rivers**, where fish migration is a year-round concern.

**Why beside the DIVIDE WALL:**

> The divide wall separates the **under-sluice pocket** from the weir bays. Placing the fish ladder alongside it puts it where:

| Advantage | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Flow is available year round** | The under-sluice section carries flow even at low river stages |
| **A defined, attractive current exists** | **Fish find the entrance by following the current** — the ladder must produce a flow they can detect |
| Conditions are relatively calm | The divide wall shelters it from the main weir discharge |

> **The attraction flow is the critical design requirement.** A fish ladder that fish cannot find is useless however well built — and finding it means detecting a current at the downstream entrance and following it.

> **That is why placement matters more than the ladder's internal design**, and why it goes beside the divide wall rather than at a convenient point on the bank.

**How a fish ladder works:**

> It converts a single large drop into a **series of small steps or pools**, each with a difference in level small enough for fish to swim or leap.

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Small drop per step** | Typically 150–300 mm |
| **Velocity within the fish's swimming ability** | Species-specific |
| **Resting pools** between steps | Fish cannot swim continuously |
| **Continuous flow** through the season of migration | — |

**The other components of a diversion headworks**, since the distractors are all real walls:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **DIVIDE WALL** | Separates the **under-sluice pocket** from the weir bays; the fish ladder sits beside it |
| **Under-sluices** | **Flush accumulated silt**; pass low flows |
| **Head regulator** | Controls flow **into the canal** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | Stops silt **ENTERING** the canal |
| **Guide banks** | Confine the river; **prevent outflanking** |
| **Launching apron** | Protects against scour |

**And the walls named in the options, each real but from elsewhere:**

| Wall | Where it belongs |
|---|---|
| **DIAPHRAGM wall** | A **deep reinforced concrete cut-off**, for excavation support and seepage control |
| **CORE wall** | The **impervious core of an EARTH DAM** |
| **WING wall** | Retains the approach embankment at a **bridge or culvert** abutment |

> **All four are genuine structures**, so the question tests whether the headworks layout is understood rather than whether the terms are recognised.

**The silt structures are worth keeping straight**, since they are constantly swapped:

> **SILT EXCLUDER excludes silt at the ENTRANCE** — it sits at the head regulator and stops silt getting into the canal.
> **SILT EJECTOR ejects silt from WITHIN the canal** — it sits downstream and removes what has already entered.

> **Prevention versus cure**, and the two names describe exactly that difference.

**Weir versus barrage**, the other standard distinction: a **weir's** pond level is fixed by its **crest**; a **barrage's** is controlled by **GATES**, so its upstream flooding can be released in a flood and its gates can flush silt. **Barrages dominate on large alluvial rivers** for exactly those reasons.

examTip.trick: **Fish find the ladder by FOLLOWING A CURRENT.** The divide wall's under-sluice pocket carries flow year round, so the entrance is detectable — placement matters more than internal design.
examTip.trap: **All four options are real walls** — diaphragm (deep cut-off), core (earth dam), wing (bridge abutment). The question tests the headworks layout, not vocabulary.
examTip.mnemonic: **Silt EXCLUDER excludes at the entrance; silt EJECTOR ejects from within the canal** — prevention versus cure, and the two are swapped constantly.

questions.stem: Which of the following is considered to be the highest quality construction in the group of black top pavements?
questions.solution:
**Bituminous concrete (BC)** — the highest quality black-top surfacing.

**Why it ranks highest:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **DENSE graded** — continuous grading from coarse to filler | Minimal voids; high stability |
| **Designed by the MARSHALL method** | Binder content, voids and stability all controlled |
| **Plant mixed** at controlled temperature | Uniform, verifiable proportions |
| **Impervious** when properly compacted | Protects the layers below |
| Excellent riding quality and durability | Used as the **wearing course** on high-traffic roads |

> **BC is at the top of a progression toward greater control**: spraying in place → premixing → precisely graded dense mixes designed by test.

**The black-top family, in ascending order of quality:**

| Treatment | Description |
|---|---|
| **Surface dressing (seal coat)** | Binder sprayed, chips spread and rolled — **a SEAL, not a structural layer** |
| **Penetration macadam** | **Aggregate laid and compacted first, binder sprayed INTO it** |
| **Bituminous carpet** | **Thin (20–25 mm) premix wearing course** — open graded, needs a seal coat |
| **Bituminous macadam (BM)** | Premixed, **open graded** — binder course |
| **Dense bituminous macadam (DBM)** | Premixed, **dense graded** — binder course |
| **BITUMINOUS CONCRETE (BC)** | **Premixed, dense graded, Marshall designed — WEARING course** |

**The two specialist materials in the options:**

| Material | Character |
|---|---|
| **MASTIC asphalt** | **Very high binder content with fine filler; laid HOT and POURED, needs NO compaction.** Impervious and durable — used for **bridge decks, footpaths and waterproofing**, but **expensive** and can be soft in hot weather |
| **SHEET asphalt** | **Fine aggregate and sand only, NO coarse aggregate** — a smooth surfacing, but with **low stability** because it lacks the coarse skeleton |

> **Both are genuine high-quality materials for particular purposes**, which is what makes them well-chosen distractors — but neither is the general-purpose highest-quality pavement course.

> **Sheet asphalt's weakness is instructive**: without coarse aggregate there is **no interlocking skeleton to carry the load**, so it relies entirely on the binder and deforms under heavy traffic. **The aggregate skeleton carries the load; the binder only holds it together.**

**What makes BC work — dense grading:**

> A **continuous grading** from coarse aggregate down through fine aggregate to mineral filler means the smaller particles **fill the voids between the larger ones**, producing a dense, interlocked, low-void mix.

| Marshall design target | Value |
|---|---|
| **Stability** | **≥ 9 kN** (heavy traffic) |
| **Flow** | **2 – 4 mm** |
| **Air voids** | **3 – 5%** |
| **Voids filled with bitumen** | 65 – 75% |

> **The 3–5% air void target is deliberate, not a tolerance**: below 3% the mix **bleeds** in hot weather with no room for the binder to expand; above 5% it is **permeable**, admitting water and air which oxidise the binder and cause **stripping and ravelling**.

**And the binder content is a genuine optimum:**

> **Too little binder → RAVELLING** (the mix loses cohesion and sheds aggregate). **Too much → BLEEDING and RUTTING** (the excess acts as a lubricant).

> **Adding more binder past the optimum makes the pavement worse**, which is the point candidates most often get backwards.

**Aggregate quality matters as much as the mix design**, since aggregate is **90–95% of the mix by weight**: **crushing and impact values ≤ 30%**, **flakiness ≤ 15%**, **water absorption < 2%**, and adequate **stripping resistance**.
