examTip.trick: The family runs toward **greater control**: sprayed in place → premixed → **dense graded and Marshall designed**. BC sits at the top because its grading, binder content and voids are all designed by test.
examTip.trap: **Mastic and sheet asphalt are genuine high-quality materials for particular jobs** — mastic for bridge decks and waterproofing, sheet for smoothness. Neither is the general-purpose best pavement course.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sheet asphalt has NO coarse aggregate, so no interlocking skeleton — hence low stability.** The aggregate carries the load; the binder only holds it together. And **3–5% air voids is a target, not a tolerance**.

questions.stem: The effective length of a battened column is increased by:
questions.solution:
**10%.**

> **The effective slenderness ratio of a battened column shall be taken as 1.1 times the maximum actual slenderness ratio** — an increase of **10%** — to account for **shear deformation effects**.

**Why the penalty exists:**

> A **battened column** is two or more separate components (channels, angles) connected at intervals by **BATTEN PLATES** — flat plates bolted or welded across the flanges.

> **The battens transmit shear through BENDING**, which is a flexible mechanism. The assembly therefore deforms more in shear than a solid section would, and that extra flexibility **reduces the buckling capacity**.

> **The code accounts for it by artificially increasing the slenderness ratio by 10%**, rather than by a separate shear analysis.

**The comparison with a LACED column, which is the point of the number:**

| | **BATTENED** | **LACED** |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | **Batten PLATES** perpendicular to the components | **Diagonal LACING bars**, forming triangles |
| Shear carried by | **BENDING of the battens** — flexible | **AXIAL force in the lacing** — stiff |
| **Effective length penalty** | **+10%** | **+5%** |
| Strength | Lower | **Higher for the same load and effective length** |
| Appearance / fabrication | Simpler | More members, more connections |

> **A laced column is stronger because triangulation carries shear AXIALLY**, and axial action is far stiffer than bending. **Its penalty is therefore only 5%, half the battened value.**

> **That contrast — bending versus axial load paths — is the reason for the two different numbers**, and it makes both worth remembering together rather than separately.

**The batten design rules** (from the source's own note):

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| **Spacing** | Such that the **component's slenderness ratio ≤ 50** |
| **Transverse shear** | Battens designed for **2.5% of the axial force** |
| **Thickness of batten plate** | **≥ 1/50 of the distance between innermost connecting bolts/rivets** |
| **Effective depth of END batten** | ≥ distance between the components' centroids, and **> twice the width of one component** |
| **Depth of INTERMEDIATE batten** | **¾ of the end batten depth** |

> **Note the end battens are deeper than the intermediate ones**, because shear is greatest at the ends of the column.

> **The 2.5% transverse shear provision is the essential one**: even a nominally axially loaded column has some shear from initial crookedness and accidental eccentricity, and the battens must be able to carry it.

**Why built-up columns are used at all:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Large radius of gyration for the material used** | Spreading the components apart increases I dramatically |
| **Long lengths** where a rolled section would be too slender | — |
| **Heavy loads** beyond available rolled sections | — |
| Convenient connection to bracing | — |

> **Spreading two channels apart increases I about the spread axis enormously** while using the same steel — the same principle that makes a hollow tube efficient, applied to available rolled sections.

**The general column relations** this sits within:

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**, **λ = L_e/r** with **r about the MINIMUM axis**, and effective lengths of **0.5L (fixed-fixed), 0.707L, 1.0L (pinned), 2.0L (cantilever)** — a **sixteen-fold** range in capacity.

> **Codes use higher values than the theory** (0.65L rather than 0.5L for fixed–fixed), because **a real fixed end always rotates a little.**

examTip.trick: **Battened +10%, LACED +5%.** Learn them as a pair — the difference exists because battens carry shear by **BENDING** (flexible) while lacing carries it **AXIALLY** (stiff).
examTip.trap: The penalty is applied to the **slenderness ratio (×1.1)**, which then feeds into the buckling capacity — it is not a 10% reduction in strength directly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Battens: spacing for component λ ≤ 50; designed for 2.5% of the axial force; END battens deeper than intermediate (¾).** Shear is greatest at the column ends, which is why.

questions.stem: Bending moment is independent of:
questions.solution:
**The beam section.**

**Why.** Bending moment is determined entirely by **EQUILIBRIUM** — by the applied loads, their positions, and the support reactions. **It is a STATICS quantity.**

> **The size and shape of the cross-section do not enter the equilibrium equations at all.** A 200 mm deep beam and a 600 mm deep beam spanning the same distance under the same load carry **exactly the same bending moment**.

> **What the section changes is the STRESS, not the moment:**

> **σ = M/Z** — the same M divided by a different section modulus gives a different stress.

> **That is the distinction the question turns on, and the source states it exactly: "bending stress is dependent on section but not bending moment."**

**Why the other three DO affect bending moment:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SPAN** | **M ∝ L² for a UDL** (wL²/8) and **∝ L for a point load** (WL/4) |
| **LOADING** | Magnitude, type and position all change M directly |
| **TYPE of beam** | Simply supported wL²/8; **fixed wL²/12 at supports**; cantilever wL²/2 — quite different |

> **All three are genuine dependencies**, so this is a clean four-way discrimination.

**The one important qualification:**

> **For a STATICALLY DETERMINATE beam, the section truly does not matter at all.**

> **For an INDETERMINATE beam it does — indirectly.** The distribution of moments depends on the **relative stiffness EI** of the members, so changing one member's section **redistributes** moment between members.

| | **Determinate** | **INDETERMINATE** |
|---|---|---|
| Moment depends on section? | **No — not at all** | **Yes, through relative EI** |
| Example | Simply supported beam, cantilever | Continuous beam, fixed beam, frame |

> **Making one member of a frame stiffer ATTRACTS more moment to it** — a genuinely important design consequence, and one that surprises people. **Strengthening a member can increase the load it must carry.**

> **The question's answer holds for the determinate case, which is what a bare "beam" question implies** — but the qualification is worth knowing, because it is the basis of moment distribution and of the whole stiffness method.

**The relations that govern bending moment:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Shear is the **SLOPE** of the moment diagram | dM/dx = V |
| **V = 0 marks a moment peak** | The turning point |
| **Change in M = AREA of the shear diagram** | The fastest hand method |

**And the diagram features:**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** |
| **COUPLE M** | **No change** | **JUMPS by M** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |
| **Internal hinge** | — | **M = 0** |

**The design consequence** of the moment being independent of section:

> **Design proceeds in one direction: compute M from statics, then choose a section with adequate Z.** For a determinate beam there is no iteration — which is exactly why determinate structures are simpler to design as well as to analyse.

> **For an indeterminate structure the analysis and the design are coupled**, and an initial assumption about member sizes must be made and then checked — which is why preliminary sizing matters there and not here.

examTip.trick: **Bending moment comes from EQUILIBRIUM alone** — the section never enters the statics equations. What the section changes is the **STRESS: σ = M/Z**.
examTip.trap: **For an INDETERMINATE beam the section DOES matter indirectly**, through relative **EI** — moments redistribute toward stiffer members. The question's answer holds for the determinate case a bare "beam" implies.
examTip.mnemonic: **Making a member stiffer ATTRACTS more moment to it** — strengthening can increase the load it must carry. That surprises people, and it is the basis of moment distribution.

questions.stem: A ……… is a structure used to provide for the controlled release of flows from a dam or levee.
questions.solution:
**A spillway.**

**What a spillway does:**

> It provides the **controlled release of surplus water from a reservoir**, passing flood flows safely downstream without damaging the dam.

> **It is the dam's SAFETY VALVE**, and it is the most important single appurtenant structure — because **overtopping is the commonest cause of embankment dam failure**.

**Controlled versus uncontrolled:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **UNCONTROLLED (ungated)** | **Crest at full reservoir level**; spills automatically once the level rises above it. Simple, needs no operator, cannot fail to open |
| **CONTROLLED (gated)** | **Gates raised or lowered**, so the crest can be set **below** FRL and **more storage retained** |

> **The source's own note captures the key point: with a controlled spillway, when the reservoir is full its water level is the same as the crest level.** The gates allow the reservoir to be held above the crest, storing extra water that an ungated spillway would have released.

> **The advantage of gates is EXTRA STORAGE; the cost is dependence on operation.** A gate that fails to open in a flood is far more dangerous than having no gate at all — which is why gated spillways need reliable power, backup, and trained operators.

**Spillway types:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **OGEE (overflow)** | **The most efficient**; profile follows the **lower nappe** of a free jet. Standard for concrete dams |
| **Chute (trough)** | Water conveyed down an open channel |
| **Side channel** | Where the crest must be long but the valley narrow |
| **SHAFT (morning glory)** | Compact, but **CHOKES once the shaft runs full**, giving a flat rating curve |
| **SIPHON** | Runs **full bore once primed** — high capacity per unit width, but sudden onset and debris-prone |
| Emergency / fuse plug | Operates only in extreme events |

> **The shaft spillway's choking behaviour is a genuine hazard**: once the shaft primes, further rise in reservoir level produces **almost no increase in discharge**. A spillway that cannot pass more when more is needed is exactly the wrong property in an extreme flood.

**The ogee's design point** matters:

| Head | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Below** design head | Water **presses on the crest** — safe, slightly less efficient |
| **AT** design head | **Atmospheric pressure — maximum efficiency** |
| **ABOVE** design head | Flow tends to **LIFT OFF**, creating **sub-atmospheric pressure and CAVITATION risk** |

> **That asymmetry is why crest profiles are built to tight tolerances** — a few millimetres of irregularity in a 30 m/s flow can initiate cavitation damage.

**Energy dissipation below the spillway:**

> The water arrives with enormous kinetic energy, and a **STILLING BASIN** dissipates it in a **HYDRAULIC JUMP**.

| Fr₁ | Jump | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **2.5 – 4.5** | **Oscillating** | **AVOID — throws waves far downstream** |
| **4.5 – 9.0** | **STEADY** | **Best for a stilling basin** |
| > 9.0 | Strong | Effective but rough |

> **The TAILWATER must actually supply the conjugate depth y₂.** If it does not, the jump **SWEEPS OUT** of the paved basin and undermines it — the failure that destroys spillway aprons, and it typically occurs at an **intermediate discharge**, not the design flood.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Weir** | A **DIVERSION** structure raising the level so a canal can draw — not a reservoir release structure |
| **Sluice** | A **gated opening**, usually low-level, for **drawing water off or flushing silt** — a component, not the flood release structure |
| **Approach** | The channel **leading to** a structure, not a structure itself |

> **A sluice is the closest near-miss** and does release water in a controlled way — but a **low-level outlet or under-sluice serves drawdown and flushing**, while a **spillway passes the FLOOD**. The two have different capacities and different purposes.

**Sizing the spillway** is governed by the design flood: for a **large dam** the consequences of failure are so severe that no annual probability is acceptable, so the design flood becomes the **PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD (PMF)** — derived from the **Probable Maximum Precipitation**, not from a return period.

examTip.trick: A spillway is the dam's **SAFETY VALVE** — and **overtopping is the commonest cause of embankment dam failure**, which is why it is the most important appurtenant structure.
examTip.trap: **A SLUICE also releases water in a controlled way** — but low-level outlets serve **drawdown and silt flushing**, while a spillway passes the **FLOOD**. Different capacity, different purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gates buy extra STORAGE at the cost of depending on operation** — a gate that fails to open is worse than no gate. And a **SHAFT spillway CHOKES** once primed: no more discharge just when more is needed.

questions.stem: The purpose of constructing a 'groyne' is to:
options: Expand a river channel to improve its depth
Train the flow along a certain course
Reduce the silting in the river bed
questions.solution:
**To train the flow along a desired course.**

**What a groyne is:**

> A structure built **transverse to the river flow, extending from the bank into the river**. Also called a **spur** or **spur dike**, it is the **most widely used river training work**.

**Its functions:**

| Function | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **TRAIN the river along a desired course** | By **attracting, deflecting or repelling** the flow |
| **Protect the bank** | Keeps the high-velocity current away from it |
| **Create SLACK water and induce SILTING** | In the pocket behind the groyne |
| **CONTRACT a wide channel** | Improving depth for navigation |

> **Note the flat contradiction with options (a) and (d)**: a groyne **CONTRACTS** a wide channel rather than expanding it, and it **PROMOTES silting** in its lee rather than reducing it. Both distractors state the reverse of what it does.

> **Option (b) is wrong for the same reason** — training a river means **controlling** its course, which is the opposite of encouraging it to meander freely.

**Types of groyne, by orientation:**

| Type | Points | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **ATTRACTING** | **DOWNSTREAM** | Draws the current **toward** the bank |
| **DEFLECTING** | **Perpendicular** to the bank | Local change of direction |
| **REPELLING** | **UPSTREAM** | **Pushes the current AWAY** — the usual choice for bank protection |
| **Sedimenting** | — | Designed to induce deposition |

> **A REPELLING groyne points UPSTREAM**, which is genuinely counter-intuitive — the instinct is that pointing downstream would deflect flow away. **In fact an upstream-pointing groyne throws the current off the bank, while a downstream-pointing one draws it in.**

> **Getting that backwards would put the groyne to work attacking the bank it was built to protect.**

**The critical detail — the NOSE:**

> **The nose of the groyne is subjected to a tremendous action of water** and must be **heavily protected by pitching**, usually with a **launching apron**.

> The nose projects furthest into the flow, so it experiences the **highest velocity and the deepest scour**. **Groynes fail at the nose far more often than anywhere else**, and the protection there is what determines whether the structure survives.

**Denehy's T-headed groyne** carries a head across the nose precisely to spread that attack.

**The other river training works:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **GUIDE BANK (Bell's bund)** | Confines the river to a bridge or barrage waterway; **prevents OUTFLANKING** |
| **Marginal bund** | Embankment along the bank confining floodwater |
| **LAUNCHING APRON** | Loose stone that **"launches" itself down the developing scour hole**, armouring the new slope |
| Revetment / pitching | Armours the bank face directly |
| Cut-off | Shortens an excessive meander |

> **The launching apron is designed to be destroyed in a controlled way** — it consumes itself to protect the structure. Its stone quantity is calculated to cover the **anticipated scour slope (usually 2:1)** down to the deepest expected scour.

> That scour depth comes from **Lacey: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, times a location factor — **2.0 at a bridge pier nose, 2.75 at a severe bend**.

**Why river training matters:**

> **A river left alone migrates.** It erodes its outer banks, deposits on the inner, and its meanders move downstream over time — **taking land, threatening structures, and outflanking bridges and headworks.**

> **Outflanking is the specific danger for a barrage or bridge**: the river simply goes round the end of the structure, which is why guide banks exist and why they extend well upstream and downstream of the works.

examTip.trap: Options (a) and (d) state the **reverse** of what a groyne does — it **CONTRACTS** a wide channel and **PROMOTES** silting in its lee. Recognising the reversal eliminates both at once.
examTip.trick: **A REPELLING groyne points UPSTREAM** — counter-intuitive but correct. Pointing downstream **attracts** the current to the bank, which is the opposite of bank protection.
examTip.mnemonic: **Groynes fail at the NOSE** — highest velocity, deepest scour. Protect it with pitching and a **launching apron**, sized from **Lacey's scour depth × a location factor** (2.0 at a pier nose, 2.75 at a severe bend).

questions.stem: The water which can be utilized by the crops from the soil is called:
questions.solution:
**Capillary water.**

**The three categories of soil water, by how tightly it is held:**

| Type | Held in | Held by | Available to plants? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GRAVITATIONAL (superfluous)** | **Large pores (macropores)** | Nothing — **drains away under gravity** | **NO — it leaves** |
| **CAPILLARY** | **Capillary pores (micropores)** | **Surface forces** — held against gravity but **not too tightly** | **YES — this is the plant's water** |
| **HYGROSCOPIC** | **On the surface of colloidal particles** | **Held SO TENACIOUSLY that roots cannot extract it** | **NO — it stays** |

> **Capillary water is the middle case, and it is the only useful one**: held firmly enough not to drain away, loosely enough for roots to take it.

> **Gravitational water leaves before the plant can use it; hygroscopic water never leaves at all.** Only the middle band is available — which is why the answer is capillary water and not either extreme.

**Why field capacity is the near-miss:**

> **FIELD CAPACITY is a MOISTURE CONTENT (a state), not a TYPE of water.**

> It is the moisture the soil retains **after free drainage has ceased** — that is, **after the gravitational water has gone**. So field capacity marks the **upper limit** of the capillary water, not the water itself.

> **Option (a) names a level; the question asks for a type.** That category difference is what makes it wrong.

**The moisture constants:**

| Constant | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Saturation** | All voids full — the excess drains away |
| **FIELD CAPACITY (FC)** | After free drainage — **upper limit of available water** |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT (PWP)** | Water held too tightly to extract — **lower limit** |
| **AVAILABLE WATER = FC − PWP** | **What the crop can actually use** |
| Readily available water | About **50%** of available, before stress begins |

> **Available water is bounded above by field capacity and below by the wilting point** — and it consists precisely of the capillary water between those two states.

**Available water by soil type:**

| Soil | Available water | Irrigation practice |
|---|---|---|
| **Sandy** | **LOW (~60 mm/m)** | **Frequent, small applications** |
| Loam | ~140 mm/m | Intermediate |
| **Clayey** | **HIGH (~180 mm/m)** | Infrequent, large applications |

> **A sandy soil does not need MORE water in total — it needs the same water MORE OFTEN**, because it cannot hold a large reserve. **Confusing frequency with quantity is a standard error.**

**The irrigation schedule follows directly:**

> **Interval = readily available water in the root zone ÷ daily consumptive use**

> And the **depth applied** is what brings the root zone **back up to field capacity** — no more, since anything beyond drains away and **carries dissolved nutrients with it**.

**Why over-irrigation is actively harmful, not merely wasteful:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water above FC drains away** | Wasted, and it **leaches nutrients** |
| **While present, it EXCLUDES AIR** from the root zone | **Roots suffocate** |
| Raises the water table | **Waterlogging**, then **salinity** by capillary rise and evaporation |

> **Roots need oxygen as well as water.** A saturated root zone drowns the crop — which is why drainage is as much a part of irrigation as supply is.

**And the capillary mechanism itself:** **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**, so **h ∝ 1/d** — fine pores hold water more strongly, which is exactly why a **clay holds more available water than a sand** but also why the tightest-held fraction (hygroscopic) is unavailable.

examTip.trick: Three bands by how tightly water is held: **gravitational LEAVES, hygroscopic NEVER LEAVES, capillary is the useful middle.** Only the middle band is available to roots.
examTip.trap: **Field capacity is a moisture LEVEL, not a TYPE of water** — it marks the upper limit of the capillary water. The question asks for a type, which is the category difference that rules it out.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sandy soil needs the same water MORE OFTEN, not more water.** And **over-irrigation excludes AIR from the root zone** — roots need oxygen, so a saturated soil drowns the crop.

questions.stem: The minimum cover for a slab is:
questions.solution:
**15 mm** (or the bar diameter, whichever is greater).

**Minimum cover by member (IS 456):**

| Member | Minimum cover |
|---|---|
| **SLAB** | **15 mm** — or the bar diameter |
| **BEAM** | **20 mm** |
| **COLUMN** | **25 mm** (bars < 12 mm) or **40 mm** (bars ≥ 12 mm) |
| **FOOTING** | **50 mm** |
| Structural member in contact with earth | 75 mm |

> **The absolute floor in every case is the BAR DIAMETER** — cover can never be less than the diameter of the bar it protects, regardless of the tabulated minimum.

> **The progression 15 / 20 / 25–40 / 50 tracks EXPOSURE and consequence**: a slab is protected inside a building, a footing sits in the ground.

**But the tabulated minimum is only half the story — DURABILITY cover usually governs:**

| Exposure | Nominal cover | Min grade | Max w/c |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **20 mm** | M20 | 0.55 |
| **Moderate** | **30 mm** | M25 | 0.50 |
| **Severe** | **45 mm** | M30 | 0.45 |
| **Very severe** | **50 mm** | M35 | 0.45 |
| **Extreme** | **75 mm** | M40 | 0.40 |

> **The exposure-based cover is usually LARGER than the member-based minimum**, and the greater of the two governs. **A slab in severe exposure needs 45 mm, not 15 mm.**

> **So "minimum cover for a slab" is a structural minimum, not a design value** — a distinction worth holding, because quoting 15 mm on a coastal or aggressive site would be seriously wrong.

**Why cover matters — the three functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **DURABILITY** | **Protects steel from CORROSION** — the dominant reason |
| **BOND** | Enough concrete around the bar to develop its force |
| **FIRE resistance** | Delays the steel reaching critical temperature |

**The corrosion mechanism the cover defends against:**

> Fresh concrete is **strongly alkaline (pH ~13)**, which forms a **passive oxide film** on the steel. **Steel in sound concrete does not rust.**

| Attack | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CARBONATION** | Atmospheric CO₂ penetrates the cover and **drops the pH to ~9**, depassivating the steel |
| **CHLORIDES** | Break the film locally, causing **pitting** — far more aggressive |

> Once corrosion starts, **rust occupies 2–4 times the volume of the original steel**, and the expansion **SPALLS the cover off** — exposing more steel and accelerating the process.

> **The failure is self-accelerating**, which is why prevention through adequate cover and low-permeability concrete matters so much more than repair.

**And why cover and grade are specified TOGETHER:**

> **A thick cover of permeable concrete protects nothing.** Carbonation and chloride ingress depend on **permeability as much as thickness** — which is why IS 456 pairs each exposure class with a **minimum grade and maximum w/c ratio** alongside the cover.

> **Permeability is the master durability property**, since every deterioration mechanism requires something to get **in**.

**The practical failure on site:**

> **Cover is lost when cover blocks are omitted, too few, or of poor quality** — and bars pushed against the formwork have effectively **zero cover**, however carefully the drawing specified it.

> **Cover blocks should be of the same grade as the concrete**, not weak mortar, or they become the entry point themselves.

examTip.trick: **Slab 15, beam 20, column 25–40, footing 50 mm** — the progression tracks exposure and consequence. And the absolute floor is always **the bar diameter**.
examTip.trap: **Durability cover usually GOVERNS over the member minimum.** A slab in severe exposure needs **45 mm**, not 15 mm — so 15 mm is a structural floor, not a design value.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rust occupies 2–4× the steel's volume and SPALLS the cover off** — self-accelerating. And a thick cover of **permeable** concrete protects nothing, which is why cover, grade and w/c are specified together.

questions.stem: The rules of ethics are also called:
questions.solution:
**Law** — the rules of ethics are also called **law, laws and moral law**.

> The distinguishing feature the source draws out is **obligation**: **"morality is not obligatory or binding"**, whereas rules of ethics expressed as a professional code **are** binding on those subject to them.

**The distinction worth holding:**

| | **MORALITY** | **ETHICS (as a professional code)** |
|---|---|---|
| Source | Personal or societal belief | **A body or profession** |
| Binding? | **Not obligatory** | **Obligatory on members** |
| Enforcement | Conscience, social pressure | **Disciplinary action — suspension, removal from the register** |
| Scope | Everyone | Members of the profession |

> **A professional code turns ethical principles into enforceable rules** — which is precisely why it functions as a kind of law for those it governs.

**The ethical skills the source lists**, which are worth reading as the substance of professional conduct:

> **Code of conduct, courage, dependability, duty, efficiency, ingenuity, initiative, perseverance, punctuality, resourcefulness, respect for all, and responsibility.**

> **Note that COURAGE appears in that list.** It is not decorative: **the obligation to refuse unsafe work, or to report a defect that will embarrass a client or employer, requires courage** — and a code that did not name it would be incomplete.

**The fundamental principles of ethical behaviour:**

| Principle | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **INTEGRITY** | Straightforward and honest in all professional relationships |
| **OBJECTIVITY** | No bias, conflict of interest, or undue influence |
| **PROFESSIONAL COMPETENCE AND DUE CARE** | Maintain knowledge and skill; act diligently |
| **CONFIDENTIALITY** | Respect information acquired professionally |
| **PROFESSIONAL BEHAVIOUR** | Comply with law; avoid discrediting the profession |

> **These five recur, near-identically worded, in professional codes worldwide** — engineering, accountancy, medicine — which suggests they capture something genuine about what professional standing requires.

**The obligation that overrides the rest, for engineers specifically:**

> **Hold the safety, health and welfare of the PUBLIC paramount** — above the client's instructions and above the engineer's own interest.

> **That is what distinguishes a profession from a trade.** A tradesman does what the customer asks; **a professional owes a duty to people who are not party to the contract and cannot protect themselves.**

> It is also a **protection for the engineer**: the code gives standing to refuse, which an employee without professional status would lack.

**Enforcement in Nepal:**

| Sanction | Effect |
|---|---|
| Warning or reprimand | Minor breaches |
| **Suspension** | For a period |
| **REMOVAL from the register** | **Ends the right to practise** |

> **Because NEC registration is a legal requirement to practise, removal ends the career** — which is what gives the code real force rather than merely moral weight.

**The commonest actual breach:**

> **Signing drawings one did not prepare or supervise.** It is treated seriously because **the signature is the public's only assurance that a competent person took responsibility** — and it is exactly the situation where the code's obligations become concrete rather than abstract.

examTip.trick: The discriminator is **obligation**: **morality is not binding; a professional code IS** — enforceable by suspension or removal from the register. That is why the rules of ethics function as law.
examTip.trap: "Responsibility" and "rules" are both genuine parts of ethical practice, but neither is the **name** given to the rules of ethics as a body.
examTip.mnemonic: **Integrity, Objectivity, Competence and Due Care, Confidentiality, Professional Behaviour** — five principles, near-identical across professions worldwide. And for engineers, **public safety is paramount** — above client and self.

questions.stem: For a given discharge, the efficiency of a sedimentation tank can be increased by:
options: Increasing the depth of the tank
Increasing the surface area of the tank
Decreasing the depth of the tank
Decreasing the surface area of the tank
questions.solution:
**Increasing the surface area of the tank.**

**The governing relation.** A particle is removed if its **settling velocity exceeds the OVERFLOW RATE** (surface loading rate):

> **V_s = Q/(B × L) = Q/A_surface**

> **A larger surface area gives a LOWER overflow rate**, so **slower-settling particles are also captured** and efficiency rises.

**The result that surprises everyone — HAZEN'S LAW:**

> **Removal efficiency depends on the SURFACE AREA ALONE — not on the depth, and not on the detention time.**

> Two tanks of equal plan area remove the same particles whether one is 2 m deep or 4 m deep, even though the deeper one holds twice the water and gives twice the detention time.

**Why depth cancels out:**

> A particle entering at the surface must fall the **full depth** to be captured — but it also has **proportionally longer** to do it. **The two effects cancel exactly.**

> The particle's fate depends only on the **ratio of its settling velocity to the overflow rate**, and depth does not appear in that ratio.

> **That is why increasing depth (option a) does nothing, and decreasing it (option c) does nothing either** — both distractors assume depth matters, and it does not.

**Where depth DOES matter, in practice:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sludge storage** | Room for settled solids between removals |
| **Avoiding SCOUR** | Sufficient depth keeps the horizontal velocity low enough not to re-suspend settled material |
| Inlet and outlet zones | Space for the flow to distribute and collect |

> **So depth is a practical requirement, not an efficiency variable** — a distinction worth stating precisely.

**The design consequence — TUBE and PLATE SETTLERS:**

> **If efficiency depends only on surface area, then stacking inclined plates or tubes inside a tank MULTIPLIES its effective settling area** without enlarging its footprint.

> A tank fitted with plate settlers can achieve **several times** the throughput of the same empty tank. **It is Hazen's law paying for itself directly**, and it is the standard way of upgrading an overloaded works on a constrained site.

**The other efficiency factors**, from the source's own list:

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Flow velocity** | Efficiency **rises as velocity falls** |
| **Viscosity** | Efficiency **rises as viscosity falls** — so **warm water settles faster**; a real seasonal effect |
| **PARTICLE SIZE** | **Efficiency rises as particle size increases** — which is exactly what **COAGULATION** achieves |

> **Coagulation is the most powerful of these levers**, because settling velocity goes as the **square of the diameter** (Stokes' law, **v_s = gd²(G−1)/18ν**).

> **Aggregating colloids into flocs increases the effective diameter enormously**, and a tenfold increase in diameter is a **hundredfold** increase in settling velocity. **That is why coagulation precedes sedimentation and why it transforms what the tank can remove.**

**Typical design values:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Overflow rate** | **20 – 40 m³/m²/day** (plain sedimentation) |
| Detention time | 2 – 4 hours |
| **Horizontal velocity** | **≤ 0.3 m/min** — above it, scour |
| Weir loading | ≤ 300 m³/m/day |

**And the departures from ideal theory** worth knowing: **short-circuiting**, **dead zones**, **wind-induced currents** and **density currents** all reduce real performance below the ideal-basin prediction — which is why baffles, good inlet distribution and adequate weir length matter as much as the tank's dimensions.

examTip.trick: **V_s = Q/A_surface** — efficiency is set by the overflow rate, which contains **surface area and nothing else**. Bigger area, lower overflow rate, more particles captured.
examTip.trap: **Two of the four options are about DEPTH, and depth cancels out entirely.** A deeper tank gives longer detention but the particle must also fall further — the effects cancel exactly.
examTip.mnemonic: **Because only AREA counts, inclined PLATE or TUBE settlers multiply capacity in the same footprint.** And **v_s ∝ d²** (Stokes), so coagulating colloids into flocs raises settling velocity a hundredfold.

questions.stem: In which stage of a river are sediments deposited?
questions.solution:
**The delta stage.**

**The stages of a river, from source to mouth:**

| Stage | Character | River training |
|---|---|---|
| **ROCKY (hilly) stage** | Steep, confined in rock; **erosion dominates** | **Not required** — the river cannot move |
| **BOULDER stage** | Bed of **boulders, gravels, shingles and alluvial sand** created by the river itself | Some |
| **TROUGH (alluvial) stage** | **Flood plain**; the river **forms new land by depositing excess load during floods** | Considerable |
| **DELTA stage** | **The FINAL stage, where the river meets a sea, ocean or lake** | **Significant — substantial changes from deposition** |

> **Deposition dominates at the delta because the river meets a standing water body and its velocity collapses.** With no velocity there is no transport capacity, and everything the river is carrying is dropped.

> **That is the whole mechanism: transport capacity depends on velocity, and at the delta the velocity goes to nearly zero.**

**Why the trough stage is the meaningful near-miss:**

> **Deposition genuinely occurs in the trough stage too** — the source says so explicitly, describing how the river "forms new land by depositing its excess load during the flood season."

> **But that deposition is EPISODIC (during floods) and PARTIAL**, whereas at the delta it is **continuous and complete**. The delta is where the river ends and deposits everything remaining.

> **The question asks where sediments are deposited, and the delta is the definitive answer** — but knowing that the trough stage also deposits is what makes the distinction meaningful rather than arbitrary.

**How velocity governs the whole sequence:**

| Stage | Velocity | Dominant process |
|---|---|---|
| **Rocky** | **Highest** | **EROSION** |
| Boulder | High | Erosion and coarse transport |
| Trough | Moderate | **Transport, with episodic deposition** |
| **Delta** | **Lowest** | **DEPOSITION** |

> **Erosion at the top, transport in the middle, deposition at the bottom** — a single gradient of velocity explains the entire longitudinal profile of a river.

**The engineering consequences by stage:**

| Stage | Concern |
|---|---|
| **Rocky** | Bridge foundations on rock; **no training needed** |
| **Boulder** | **Heavy bed load damages structures and turbines**; gravel traps essential |
| **Trough** | **MEANDERING and bank erosion**; guide banks, groynes, marginal bunds |
| **Delta** | **Aggradation raises the bed**; channels shift; drainage and flood problems |

> **Aggradation at the delta is a serious long-term problem**: as the bed rises, the river's capacity falls, flooding worsens, and embankments must be raised — which raises the bed further. **The process is self-reinforcing**, which is why deltaic flood defence is so difficult.

**The meandering river** in the trough stage deserves a note, since it is where most river training happens:

> A meander **erodes the OUTER bank** (where velocity and depth are greatest) and **deposits on the INNER bank** (a point bar). **The meander therefore migrates laterally and downstream over time**, taking land and threatening structures.

> **The secondary (helical) current is what drives it**: surface water moves outward, bed water inward, carrying bed load toward the inside of the bend.

> **That same helical current is why a river INTAKE is best placed on the OUTSIDE of a bend** — the bed load is swept to the inside, leaving cleaner water at the outer bank. **One siting decision removes more sediment than any structure downstream, and it costs nothing.**

examTip.trick: **Velocity governs everything**: highest at the rocky stage (erosion), lowest at the delta (deposition). At a delta the river meets standing water, velocity collapses, and transport capacity goes with it.
examTip.trap: **The TROUGH stage also deposits** — episodically, during floods, forming the flood plain. The delta is where deposition is **continuous and complete**, which is why it is the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **A meander erodes the OUTER bank and deposits on the INNER**, driven by the helical secondary current. Which is why a river **INTAKE belongs on the OUTSIDE of a bend** — the bed load goes to the inside.

questions.stem: ……… is a method of surface drainage which makes use of dead furrows.
questions.solution:
**Bedding.**

**What the bedding system is:**

> Essentially a **LAND-FORMING process**. The land is **ploughed into beds, separated by DEAD FURROWS** which run **parallel to the prevailing land slope**.

> **A "bed" is the area between two adjacent dead furrows**, and the beds are shaped slightly convex so that water sheds sideways into the furrows and drains away along them.

**Its characteristics:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ploughing** | Done **parallel to the furrow** |
| Other farming operations | Either across the beds or parallel to the furrow |
| **Most practicable on** | **FLAT slopes of less than 1.5%** |
| **Suits** | **Slowly permeable soils where PIPE drainage is not economical** |

> **The last point is the key to why it exists**: on a slowly permeable soil, subsurface drains would need to be very closely spaced (spacing is proportional to permeability) and would therefore be uneconomic. **Bedding achieves surface removal cheaply instead.**

**Why a FRENCH DRAIN is the meaningful near-miss:**

> A **French drain is a SUBSURFACE drain** — a trench filled with coarse aggregate, with or without a perforated pipe, that intercepts and conducts water below ground.

> **The question specifies SURFACE drainage**, and a French drain is not that. **The two work on different water entirely.**

**SURFACE versus SUBSURFACE drainage — the distinction that matters:**

| | **SURFACE** | **SUBSURFACE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Removes** | **PONDED water from the surface** | **Lowers the WATER TABLE** |
| Methods | **Bedding**, land grading, open ditches, field drains | **Tile drains**, mole drains, French drains |
| Suits | **Flat, slowly permeable land** | **Waterlogging and SALINITY** |

> **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems, so they require SUBSURFACE drainage.** Surface drainage removes standing water and **does nothing whatever to the water table beneath.**

> **That is why the two are not alternatives** — a field can need both, and using the wrong one solves nothing.

**Why waterlogging and salinity travel together:**

| Step | Effect |
|---|---|
| Water table rises into the root zone | **WATERLOGGING** — roots suffocate |
| **Capillary rise** brings water to the surface | Carrying dissolved salts with it |
| **Evaporation** removes the water | **Salts CONCENTRATE at the surface** |

> **The remedy for both is drainage** — and **LEACHING WITHOUT DRAINAGE IS FUTILE**, because the dissolved salts must have somewhere to go or they simply return by capillary action.

> Worse than futile: **applying extra leaching water without drainage RAISES the water table and accelerates the salinisation it was meant to cure.** That combination has destroyed large areas of irrigated land worldwide.

**For a SODIC (alkali) soil the order is critical:**

> **Apply GYPSUM first, THEN leach.** Gypsum supplies **calcium to displace the sodium** from the clay's exchange sites.

> **Leaching a sodic soil without gypsum makes it worse** — it removes the remaining soluble calcium, further **dispersing the clay** and destroying what permeability remains, after which the soil cannot be reclaimed at all.

**Tile drain placement rules**, since subsurface drainage is the other half of the subject:

> **Within a PERVIOUS stratum, BELOW the root zone (1–2 m), and ABOVE any impervious layer** — never below one, or the waterlogged water cannot reach the drain.

> **Spacing is proportional to permeability** (Hooghoudt), and a **graded filter or gravel envelope** is essential to stop soil piping into the drain.

examTip.trap: **A FRENCH DRAIN is SUBSURFACE** — a gravel-filled trench below ground. The question says **surface** drainage, and the two work on entirely different water.
examTip.trick: Bedding exists because on **slowly permeable soil, pipe drains would need impractically close spacing** (spacing ∝ permeability) and be uneconomic. Land forming is the cheap alternative.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging and salinity are WATER TABLE problems — they need SUBSURFACE drainage.** And **leaching without drainage is worse than futile**: it raises the water table and accelerates the salinisation.

questions.stem: The canal normally used for diversion of flood water of a river is:
questions.solution:
**An inundation canal.**

**What it is:**

> A **long canal taking off DIRECTLY from a river WITHOUT any headworks** — no weir, no barrage, no regulator.

> **It receives water only when the river level is high enough — especially in flood.** When the river falls, the canal simply runs dry.

**Its characteristics:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **No headworks** | **Very cheap to construct** |
| **Supply is UNCONTROLLED** | Depends entirely on the river stage |
| **Runs only in the flood season** | Dry for much of the year |
| **Unreliable** | Cannot be depended on for a crop |
| **Carries heavy silt** | No excluder; silting is a constant problem |

> **Its cheapness is its only virtue, and its unreliability is a serious one.** A crop planted on an inundation canal's supply may fail entirely if the river does not rise as expected.

> **That is why inundation canals are historic rather than modern practice** — they were superseded by **PERENNIAL canals** taking off from a barrage, which supply water throughout the year under control.

**The canal classifications, which the distractors draw on:**

**By source of supply:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **PERENNIAL** | Fed from a **dam or barrage**; supplies water **throughout the year**; irrigates a vast area |
| **INUNDATION** | **Direct from the river, no headworks**; flood season only |

**By function:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **CARRIER canal** | **Both direct irrigation AND feeding another canal** |
| **FEEDER canal** | **ONLY feeds another canal** — no direct irrigation |
| **Field canal / watercourse** | The farmer's responsibility |

**By ALIGNMENT — the group most often examined:**

| Alignment | Runs along | Cross-drainage works |
|---|---|---|
| **RIDGE (watershed) canal** | The **ridge line separating two catchments** | **NONE** — streams flow away both sides; **commands land on BOTH sides** |
| **SIDE SLOPE canal** | **Perpendicular to the contours, PARALLEL to the natural drainage** | **NONE** — it does not intercept the drains |
| **CONTOUR canal** | Along a contour, **across the fall of the land** | **MANY** — used in hilly regions |

> **Both the ridge and the side slope canal avoid cross-drainage works, for different geometric reasons** — the ridge because streams flow away on both sides, the side slope because it runs **with** the drainage rather than across it.

> **The ridge alignment is preferred wherever topography allows**: no cross-drainage works (the largest single saving in canal design) **and** command on both sides. Its cost is a **long lead** from the headworks to the ridge, commanding nothing.

**The four cross-drainage works**, named by **which one goes over**:

| Structure | Arrangement |
|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** | **Canal over drain**; drain flows free |
| **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** | Canal over drain; **drain under PRESSURE** |
| **SUPER PASSAGE** | **Drain over canal**; canal free |
| **CANAL SYPHON** | Drain over canal; **canal under PRESSURE** |

> **"Aqueduct" always means the CANAL is on top. Add "syphon" when the thing underneath runs under pressure.** One rule generates all four.

**Why the alignment decision matters so much:** it is one of the first decisions in canal design, and **it sets the cost of the whole scheme** — because cross-drainage works are expensive and numerous on a contour alignment.

examTip.trick: **Inundation = no headworks, so no control** — it takes water only when the river is high. Cheap to build, unreliable to depend on, and historic rather than modern practice.
examTip.trap: **FEEDER and CARRIER differ**: a feeder canal **only** feeds another canal; a **carrier** does both irrigation and feeding. The pair is examined together.
examTip.mnemonic: **RIDGE and SIDE SLOPE canals both avoid cross-drainage works** — the ridge because streams flow away both sides, the side slope because it runs **with** the drainage. Only a **CONTOUR** canal crosses them.

questions.stem: Dowel bars are provided at:
options: Both expansion and contraction joints, and longitudinal joint
questions.solution:
**Both expansion and contraction joints** — the **TRANSVERSE** joints.

> The source states it precisely: **"Dowel bars are provided at expansion joints and sometimes at contraction joints also."**

> **Option (d) adds the LONGITUDINAL joint, and that is where TIE BARS go, not dowels** — which is exactly the discrimination being tested.

**The two bar types, which are constantly confused:**

| | **DOWEL BAR** | **TIE BAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Purpose** | **TRANSFER LOAD across the joint** | **HOLD the slabs together** |
| **Joint** | **TRANSVERSE** (expansion, contraction) | **LONGITUDINAL** (parallel to traffic) |
| **Bar type** | **PLAIN, SMOOTH — greased or capped at one end** | **DEFORMED — must grip the concrete** |
| **Movement** | **Free to SLIDE along its axis** | **None intended** |
| Designed for | **Shear, bending and bearing** | **Tension** |
| Diameter | **> 25 mm** | Smaller |

> **One sentence covers every question on this pair: TIE bars TIE (hold together, deformed, longitudinal); DOWEL bars carry the LOAD across (smooth, transverse).**

**Why a dowel MUST be smooth:**

> The slab has to **slide freely along the dowel** as the concrete expands and contracts with temperature. **Using a DEFORMED bar as a dowel LOCKS the joint** — the slab can then no longer move, and it **cracks elsewhere**, producing exactly the uncontrolled cracking the joint was built to prevent.

> **That is a real and damaging construction error**, not a technicality, and it is why the distinction is examined so often. **A locked contraction joint is worse than no joint at all.**

**The dowel's functions**, from the source's own list:

> **1. To transfer wheel loads from one slab to another. 2. To reduce the differential deflection between slabs.**

> **Stresses developed in a dowel: SHEAR, BENDING and BEARING** — it acts as a short cantilever transferring load across the gap, and the **bearing stress on the surrounding concrete** usually governs its diameter.

**The joints in a rigid pavement:**

| Joint | Direction | Purpose | Bars |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EXPANSION** | Transverse | Allow **thermal expansion**; has a **compressible filler**. Normally where a structure **exceeds 45 m** | **Dowels** (one end capped) |
| **CONTRACTION** | Transverse | Allow **shrinkage**; **control WHERE cracks form** | **Dowels** |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | Parallel to traffic | Control **warping** cracking; separate lanes | **TIE BARS** |
| Construction | Either | End of a day's work | As appropriate |

**The logic of "controlled cracking":**

> **Concrete WILL crack as it shrinks — that is unavoidable. A contraction joint decides WHERE.**

> By sawing a groove to about **a quarter of the slab depth**, a plane of weakness is created and the crack forms there — **straight, sealed and maintainable** — instead of wandering randomly across the slab.

> **The timing of the saw cut is critical**: too early and the concrete ravels at the cut; too late and the slab has already cracked somewhere of its own choosing.

**Why longitudinal joints are TIED rather than dowelled:**

> Adjacent lanes must **stay together** — if they separate, water enters, the subgrade softens, and a step forms at the joint.

> **But there is no significant thermal movement ACROSS the width** to accommodate, unlike along the length. **So the joint is tied shut, not allowed to open.**

**Stresses in a rigid pavement (Westergaard):** load at the **INTERIOR**, **EDGE** (usually most critical for load stress) and **CORNER** (critical when **warping** combines).

> **The corner is the weakest point**, supported on only two sides — which is precisely why dowels matter: they let the adjacent slab share the load rather than leaving the corner alone.

> And **WARPING stresses — from a temperature GRADIENT through the slab depth — often EXCEED the traffic stresses**, which is why slab length is capped at about **4.5 m** between contraction joints.

examTip.trick: **TIE bars TIE slabs together — deformed, LONGITUDINAL. DOWEL bars carry LOAD across — smooth, TRANSVERSE.** Option (d) adds the longitudinal joint, which is tie-bar territory.
examTip.trap: **Using a deformed bar as a dowel LOCKS the joint**, preventing the thermal movement it exists to allow — and the slab then cracks elsewhere. A real construction error, not a technicality.
examTip.mnemonic: **A contraction joint does not prevent cracking — it decides WHERE.** Saw to a quarter depth, and time the cut carefully. And the **CORNER is the slab's weakest point**, which is why dowels matter.

questions.stem: What is the minimum pitch distance for bolts?
questions.solution:
**2.5 times the nominal diameter of the fastener.**

> **PITCH is the centre-to-centre spacing of bolts IN A ROW, measured ALONG the direction of the load.** The distance between centres shall **not be less than 2.5 times** the nominal diameter.

**The bolt spacing rules (IS 800):**

| Dimension | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Minimum PITCH** | **2.5 d** |
| **Maximum pitch** | **16t or 200 mm** (t = thinner plate), whichever is less |
| **Minimum EDGE distance** | **1.5 d** (sheared edge) or **1.7 d** (rolled/machine flame cut) |
| Maximum edge distance | 12tε, or 40 mm + 4t in corrosive environments |
| **Gauge** | Spacing **PERPENDICULAR** to the load direction |

> **Pitch is ALONG the load; gauge is ACROSS it.** The pair is easy to swap.

**Why there is a MINIMUM pitch:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent bearing failure between holes** | Too close and the material between them shears out |
| **Allow room for the spanner or riveting tool** | A practical constraint |
| **Avoid excessive stress concentration** | Overlapping stress fields |
| **Prevent the plate tearing between holes** | — |

**And why there is a MAXIMUM pitch, which is less obvious:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent BUCKLING of the plate between fasteners** | The plate acts as a strut between bolts |
| **Keep the plates in contact** | So moisture cannot enter the gap |
| **Prevent corrosion between plies** | The reason for the tighter limit in corrosive conditions |

> **The maximum pitch exists to stop the plate buckling between bolts and to keep water out of the joint** — both structural and durability reasons, which is why the limit tightens in corrosive environments.

**Why the MINIMUM EDGE distance matters most in practice:**

> **A bolt too close to the edge tears out** — the material between the hole and the edge shears away in a straight line. **It is the commonest failure mode of a badly detailed bolted connection**, and it is entirely avoidable.

> **1.5 d for a sheared edge, 1.7 d for a rolled or flame-cut one** — the difference reflecting the greater damage a sheared edge suffers.

**The failure modes of a bolted connection**, all of which must be checked:

| Failure | Where |
|---|---|
| **SHEAR of the bolt** | Through the shank |
| **BEARING** on the plate | The hole elongates |
| **TENSION failure of the plate** | Through the **net section** at the holes |
| **TEAR-OUT / end splitting** | Insufficient **edge distance** |
| Bolt tension failure | In a tension connection |

> **The connection's capacity is the LEAST of these**, and a designer who checks only bolt shear has checked the easiest one.

**Bolt types:**

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **BEARING type (black bolts)** | Load transferred by **shear and bearing**; some slip occurs |
| **HSFG (high strength friction grip)** | **Pre-tensioned; load transferred by FRICTION between plies** — **NO SLIP** |

> **HSFG bolts are used where slip cannot be tolerated** — under fatigue loading, in bridges, and where deflection must be tightly controlled. **The bolts are tightened to a specified tension, and the joint works by clamping, not by the bolts bearing at all.**

**Welds versus bolts:** welds give **no reduction for holes** and a **neater joint**, but need skilled labour and inspection; **bolts suit site work and are easily inspected** — which is why the common practice is **shop welding and site bolting**.

examTip.trick: **PITCH is ALONG the load, GAUGE is ACROSS it.** Minimum pitch **2.5 d**, minimum edge distance **1.5 d (sheared) or 1.7 d (rolled)**.
examTip.trap: There is a **MAXIMUM pitch too (16t or 200 mm)** — to stop the plate **buckling between bolts** and to keep water out of the joint. The limit tightens in corrosive environments.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tear-out from inadequate EDGE distance is the commonest bolted-connection failure** — and entirely avoidable. Check all modes: bolt shear, bearing, **net section tension**, and tear-out; capacity is the least of them.

questions.stem: The time of concentration is:
options: time of maximum possible precipitation that may concentrate and fall over a given basin
time taken by the rain water to flow to an existing defined drain in a basin
time for which the rain water remains concentrated on the basin
maximum time taken by the rain water to reach the outlet of the basin
questions.solution:
**The maximum time taken by rainwater to reach the outlet of the basin.**

**The definition:**

> The **time required for the ENTIRE drainage area to contribute to the runoff** — equivalently, **the time taken by water from the most remote point in the basin to reach the point of interest**.

> **t_c = overland flow time + channel flow time**

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **OVERLAND (sheet) flow time** | The phase where water flows **as a sheet over the land surface** |
| **CHANNEL flow time** | Time in the **open channel up to the gauging site** |

> **It depends on the slope, the catchment characteristics and the flow path length.**

**Why it is the MAXIMUM time, and why that matters:**

> **It is at t_c that the WHOLE catchment is contributing simultaneously.** Before that moment, only part of the basin is delivering water to the outlet; after it, the earlier contributions have passed.

> **Therefore the peak discharge occurs when the storm duration equals the time of concentration** — and that is the single most important consequence of the concept.

**The design rule that follows:**

> **The DESIGN STORM DURATION is taken EQUAL to the time of concentration.**

| Storm duration | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Shorter than t_c** | **Only part of the basin contributes** at any instant — smaller peak |
| **Equal to t_c** | **The whole basin contributes — MAXIMUM PEAK** |
| **Longer than t_c** | Whole basin contributes, but at a **lower intensity** (intensity falls with duration) — smaller peak |

> **Both a shorter and a longer storm give a smaller peak**, for different reasons. **The maximum sits exactly at t_c**, which is why the design duration is chosen that way rather than arbitrarily.

**Where it is used — the RATIONAL METHOD:**

> **Q = CIA/360** (Q in m³/s, I in mm/hr, A in hectares)

| Term | Note |
|---|---|
| **C** | Runoff coefficient — **0.05 (forest) to 0.95 (paved)** |
| **I** | **Rainfall intensity for a duration equal to t_c**, at the design return period |
| **A** | Catchment area |

> **The intensity I is read at duration = t_c** from the intensity–duration–frequency curves. **That is where t_c actually enters the calculation.**

> **The rational method assumes the whole catchment contributes**, which is exactly the assumption t_c makes valid. It is limited to **small catchments (under about 50 ha)**, because uniform rainfall over a large area is unrealistic.

**How urbanisation changes it — and this is the practically important consequence:**

| Change | Effect on t_c | Effect on peak |
|---|---|---|
| **Paving** | **Reduces overland flow time sharply** | **Increases** |
| **Storm drains replacing natural channels** | **Reduces channel flow time** | **Increases** |
| Loss of depression storage | Less water retained | Increases |

> **Urbanisation shortens t_c dramatically**, so the same rainfall produces **a higher, earlier peak** — and simultaneously **raises C** because the surface is impervious.

> **Both effects push the peak discharge up together**, which is why urban flooding worsens even without any change in rainfall. **A catchment's hydrology is changed by development as surely as by climate.**

**Estimating t_c:** **Kirpich's formula** is the common empirical relation, from the flow path length and slope; for larger catchments a **unit hydrograph** approach replaces the rational method entirely.

examTip.trick: At **t_c the WHOLE catchment contributes at once** — which is why the peak occurs when the **storm duration equals t_c**, and why that is taken as the design duration.
examTip.trap: **Both a SHORTER and a LONGER storm give a smaller peak** — shorter because only part of the basin contributes, longer because intensity falls with duration. The maximum sits exactly at t_c.
examTip.mnemonic: **Urbanisation SHORTENS t_c and RAISES C together** — a higher, earlier peak from the same rainfall. Development changes a catchment's hydrology as surely as climate does.

questions.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are incorrect?

**(i)** Earliest start of an activity is the early event time of the node it leaves.
**(ii)** Latest finish of an activity is the late event time of the node it enters.
**(iii)** Latest start of an activity is its latest finish minus its duration.
questions.solution:
**None — all three statements are correct.**

**Checking each:**

| Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **(i)** EST = early event time of the **tail** node (the node it **leaves**) | ✓ **Correct** — an activity can start as soon as its tail event is reached |
| **(ii)** LFT = late event time of the **head** node (the node it **enters**) | ✓ **Correct** — it must finish by the time its head event must occur |
| **(iii)** **LST = LFT − duration** | ✓ **Correct** — this is the definition |

> **All three are standard network definitions**, so the answer is "None".

**The four activity times:**

| Time | Definition |
|---|---|
| **EST** — earliest start | Earliest the activity **can** start |
| **EFT** — earliest finish | **EFT = EST + D** |
| **LST** — latest start | Latest it **can** start without delaying the project |
| **LFT** — latest finish | **LFT = LST + D** |

> **The two relations are symmetric: EFT = EST + D and LFT = LST + D.** Both simply add the duration to a start to get a finish.

**The forward and backward pass:**

| Pass | Direction | Rule at a node |
|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD** | First to last event | **Take the MAXIMUM** — an activity cannot start until **all** predecessors finish |
| **BACKWARD** | Last to first event | **Take the MINIMUM** — it must not delay the **earliest** successor |

> **Forward takes the maximum, backward the minimum.** That single asymmetry is where most computational errors arise, and remembering the reason for each makes it hard to get wrong.

**FLOAT, which the passes exist to produce:**

| Float | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **LST − EST** (= LFT − EFT) — delay possible **without affecting project completion** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the NEXT activity** |
| **Independent float** | Without affecting either neighbour |
| Interfering float | Total − free |

> **A CRITICAL activity has ZERO total float** — which is precisely how the critical path is identified.

> **Free float ≤ total float always**, since the free-float condition is stricter.

**Why float matters practically:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **RESOURCE SMOOTHING** | Non-critical activities are **shifted within their float** to even the resource histogram — **without changing the completion date** |
| Prioritising attention | Manage the critical path first |
| Assessing a delay's significance | A delay within float costs nothing |
| Contractual claims | Whether a delay is **excusable and compensable** often turns on whether it consumed float |

> **"Who owns the float" is a genuine contractual question** — if a contractor uses up the float and the employer then causes a delay, the employer's delay becomes critical. **Modern contracts often address it explicitly.**

**Critical path characteristics:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Longest path** through the network | It determines the project duration |
| **Zero total float** throughout | The identifying test |
| **Any delay on it delays the project** | Directly |
| **There may be MORE THAN ONE** critical path | And **crashing one can make another critical** |

> **That last point is the practical warning about CRASHING**: shortening the critical path only helps until another path becomes critical. **The critical path must be re-identified after every crashing step**, or money is spent shortening a path that no longer governs.

examTip.trick: All three are **standard definitions**, so "None" is correct. When every statement in such a question looks textbook-correct, check whether "none" is offered before hunting for a subtle error.
examTip.trap: **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM; backward pass takes the MINIMUM.** That asymmetry is where most computational errors come from — and each has a clear reason, so it need not be memorised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total float = LST − EST, and a CRITICAL activity has ZERO.** Float is what **resource smoothing** consumes. And after each **crashing** step, re-identify the critical path — another may have become critical.

questions.stem: In Bernoulli's equation, used in pipe flow, each term represents:
questions.solution:
**Work done (energy) per unit WEIGHT** — which is why every term has the dimensions of a **length**.

> **p/γ + V²/2g + z = constant**

| Term | Name | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **p/γ** | **Pressure head** | metres |
| **V²/2g** | **Velocity (kinetic) head** | metres |
| **z** | **Elevation (potential) head** | metres |

**Check the dimensions:** **p/γ = (N/m²)/(N/m³) = m** ✓ and **V²/2g = (m²/s²)/(m/s²) = m** ✓

**The three forms of the same equation:**

| Divided by | Form | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **WEIGHT** | **p/γ + V²/2g + z** | **metres — HEAD** |
| Mass | p/ρ + V²/2 + gz | J/kg |
| Volume | p + ρV²/2 + ρgz | Pa |

> **All three are valid statements of Bernoulli's equation** — which is why options (b) and (c) are not nonsense. The source's own note puts it well: **unless the actual equation is specified, the answer is work done or energy per unit WEIGHT**, because that is the form universally used in hydraulics.

**Why the head form dominates civil engineering:**

> **Every term becomes a LENGTH that can be DRAWN.** That gives the **hydraulic grade line (HGL)** and the **energy grade line (EGL)** — a picture of the flow's energy along the pipe.

> **A form you can draw is worth more than one you can only compute**, which is the whole reason for the convention.

**HGL and EGL properties:**

| Property | Statement |
|---|---|
| **EGL is always ABOVE the HGL** by **V²/2g** | The gap **is** the velocity head |
| **EGL always FALLS** in the flow direction | Friction — unless a **pump** adds energy |
| **HGL may RISE** where the pipe expands | Velocity head converts back to pressure |
| **HGL coincides with the water surface** in an open channel | Since p = 0 there |
| **HGL BELOW the pipe** | **NEGATIVE pressure — risk of air ingress and CONTAMINATION** |

> **The last row is a genuine public health matter**: where the HGL falls below the pipe, the pressure inside is sub-atmospheric, and **any leak draws contaminated groundwater IN rather than letting clean water out.**

> **That is why a water main must be kept under positive pressure at all times**, and why intermittent supply — common in South Asia — is a serious contamination risk.

**Bernoulli's assumptions:**

> **Steady, incompressible, frictionless (inviscid) flow along a streamline**, with no energy added or removed.

**The extended form**, which is what is actually used:

> **p₁/γ + V₁²/2g + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L**

**And the essential caution about where it fails:**

> **Bernoulli must NOT be applied across a region of large, unknown loss** — a sudden expansion, or a **HYDRAULIC JUMP**.

> **There the MOMENTUM equation is used instead**, precisely because it does not require the losses to be quantified: the forces are small and measurable even when the energy loss is not.

> **That is the recurring theme wherever a flow changes abruptly** — energy for smooth transitions, momentum for abrupt ones.

examTip.trick: **Every term is a LENGTH**, so it must be energy per unit **weight** (energy ÷ force = length). Checking the units of **p/γ = (N/m²)/(N/m³) = m** settles it in one step.
examTip.trap: **Per mass (J/kg) and per volume (Pa) are BOTH valid forms** — they are not nonsense. But unless the equation is specified, hydraulics means the **head** form.
examTip.mnemonic: **HGL below the pipe means NEGATIVE pressure** — a leak then draws contamination **IN**. Which is why mains must stay under positive pressure, and why intermittent supply is a real health risk.

questions.stem: Pick up the incorrect statement from the following:
options: The activity is the time-consuming part of a project
The beginning and end of a job are called events
The activity which consumes maximum time is called a node
Logically and sequentially connected activities and events form a network
questions.solution:
**"The activity which consumes maximum time is called a node" — this is incorrect.**

**Why.** A **NODE is a POINT in the network — an EVENT** — not an activity, and certainly not the longest one.

> A node represents a **specific task, activity, event or milestone** as a **point** in the diagram. **It has position, not duration.**

> **The statement confuses two different things**: it takes a term for a **point** (node) and attaches it to a **duration property** (maximum time). **Nothing in network analysis is named for consuming the most time.**

**What the longest-duration items actually are called:**

| Concept | Correct name |
|---|---|
| The **longest PATH** through the network | **CRITICAL PATH** |
| An activity **on** that path | **Critical activity** (zero total float) |
| A point in the network | **EVENT** or **NODE** |

> **The critical path is the longest path — not the longest single activity.** A very long activity can sit on a non-critical path and have plenty of float, while a series of short activities can form the critical path.

> **That distinction matters practically**: managers instinctively watch the biggest activities, but **the activities that control the project are the ones with zero float**, whatever their individual durations.

**Why the other three statements are correct:**

| Statement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Activity is the time-consuming part** | ✓ An activity consumes **time and usually resources** |
| **Beginning and end of a job are events** | ✓ The **tail event** and **head event** |
| **Connected activities and events form a network** | ✓ The definition of a network diagram |

**The core terminology:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVITY** | A **task consuming time and resources** — an **arrow** in AOA |
| **EVENT (node)** | A **point in time** — the start or completion of activities. **Consumes nothing** |
| **DUMMY** | **Consumes NEITHER time NOR resources** — dashed arrow; shows a dependency or separates parallel activities |
| **PATH** | A continuous chain from start to finish |
| **CRITICAL PATH** | The **longest** path; determines the project duration |

> **The essential contrast: an ACTIVITY consumes time; an EVENT does not.** An event is an instant, marking that something has finished or may begin.

**AOA versus AON:**

| | **Activity on ARROW** | **Activity on NODE** |
|---|---|---|
| Activity is | The **arrow** | The **node (box)** |
| **Dummies** | **REQUIRED** | **Not needed** |
| Modern software | Rare | **Standard** |

> **In AON the word "node" means the ACTIVITY itself**, which is a genuine source of confusion between the two conventions — and worth noting, since the statement in this question would still be wrong in AON, but for a different reason.

**The rules a valid network must satisfy:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **No LOOPS** | A loop would mean an activity precedes itself |
| **No dangling activities** | Every activity must connect at both ends |
| **Only ONE start and ONE end event** | — |
| **No two activities share the same tail AND head** | Use a **dummy** to separate them |
| **Arrow LENGTH has no meaning** | **A network is a LOGIC diagram, not a scaled drawing** |

> **That last rule is worth carrying**: a one-day activity and a hundred-day one may be drawn as identical arrows. **Only the direction and the connections carry meaning** — which is exactly what distinguishes a network from a **bar chart**, where length **is** duration.

> **A bar chart shows WHEN; a network shows WHY.** A bar chart cannot trace the effect of a delay, because it holds no dependency information.

examTip.trick: A **NODE is a POINT (an event)** — it has position, not duration. The statement attaches a **duration property** to a term for a point, which is the category error.
examTip.trap: **The CRITICAL PATH is the longest PATH, not the longest ACTIVITY.** A long activity can sit on a non-critical path with plenty of float; short activities can form the critical path.
examTip.mnemonic: **An ACTIVITY consumes time; an EVENT does not** — an event is an instant. And a **DUMMY** consumes neither, existing only to show a dependency or separate parallel activities.

questions.stem: "Risk management" is a process that includes:
options: Interactive exchange of information and opinions
questions.solution:
**Evaluation of policy alternatives.**

**The distinction this question tests — three separate processes:**

| Process | What it does |
|---|---|
| **RISK ASSESSMENT** | A **scientifically based** process: **hazard identification → hazard characterization → exposure assessment → risk characterization** |
| **RISK MANAGEMENT** | **WEIGHING POLICY ALTERNATIVES** in consultation with interested parties, considering the risk assessment and other relevant factors, and **selecting prevention and control options** |
| **RISK COMMUNICATION** | The **interactive exchange of information and opinions** about risk among assessors, managers and the public |

> **Options (a) and (c) — hazard identification and hazard characterization — are steps of RISK ASSESSMENT, not management.**
> **Option (b) — interactive exchange of information and opinions — is RISK COMMUNICATION.**

> **Each distractor belongs to a genuine neighbouring process**, which is what makes this a real test rather than a recognition exercise.

**The essential difference:**

> **ASSESSMENT is SCIENTIFIC — it asks "how bad is it?"**
> **MANAGEMENT is a DECISION — it asks "what shall we do about it?"**
> **COMMUNICATION is a DIALOGUE — it asks "how do we discuss it?"**

> **Management is where VALUES enter.** Assessment can tell you the probability and consequence; **it cannot tell you how much risk is acceptable, or whose interests should prevail.** That is a policy judgement, made in consultation — which is exactly why the definition mentions **"in consultation with all interested parties"** and **"other factors relevant"** beyond the assessment.

**The four risk responses**, which are the options a manager evaluates:

| Response | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **AVOID** | **Eliminate** the risk by changing the plan or scope | Reroute away from an unstable slope |
| **TRANSFER** | Shift the **impact and ownership** to a third party | **Insurance**, bonds, fixed-price subcontract |
| **MITIGATE** | **REDUCE** the probability or impact | Ground improvement, extra investigation |
| **ACCEPT** | Absorb the consequence | **Contingency reserve** (active) or monitoring (passive) |

> For a **positive** risk (an opportunity) the mirror responses are **exploit, share, enhance and accept**.

**The risk management process:**

| Step | Activity |
|---|---|
| **1. Identify** | Brainstorming, checklists, expert judgement, lessons learned |
| **2. Analyse — qualitative** | **Probability × Impact matrix**; rank and prioritise |
| **3. Analyse — quantitative** | Expected monetary value, sensitivity, **Monte Carlo** |
| **4. Plan responses** | Avoid / transfer / mitigate / accept |
| **5. Monitor and control** | Track the register; watch for new risks |

> **The risk register is a LIVING document.** One written at tender and never revisited has no value — and that is the commonest failure of risk management in practice.

**When risk management pays:**

> Risks are **cheapest to address EARLY**, in **feasibility and design**, where the **ability to influence is high and the cost of change is low**. **By the time a risk materialises in construction, the response options have narrowed to the expensive ones.**

> **That is why risk analysis belongs at feasibility** — the phase that spends the least and decides the most.

**And the note on TRANSFER worth carrying:**

> **Transfer does not reduce the risk** — insurance does not stop the flood, it pays for it. **And the RESIDUAL risk always remains with the project**: an insurer who disputes the claim, or a subcontractor who becomes insolvent, hands the risk straight back.

examTip.trick: Three neighbouring processes: **ASSESSMENT is scientific ("how bad?"), MANAGEMENT is a decision ("what shall we do?"), COMMUNICATION is dialogue ("how do we discuss it?").** Each distractor belongs to one of the others.
examTip.trap: **Hazard identification and characterization are ASSESSMENT steps**; interactive exchange of information is **COMMUNICATION**. All three distractors are genuine — just from the wrong process.
examTip.mnemonic: **Management is where VALUES enter** — assessment gives probability and consequence, but only policy decides what is acceptable. Hence "in consultation with all interested parties".

questions.stem: The permissible error (E) for precise levelling, with distance (D) in kilometres, is given by:
questions.solution:
**E = ±0.006 √D** metres, with D in kilometres.

**The permissible error by class of levelling:**

| Class | Permissible error |
|---|---|
| **ROUGH** | **±0.100 √D** |
| **ORDINARY** | **±0.025 √D** |
| **ACCURATE** | **±0.012 √D** |
| **PRECISE** | **±0.006 √D** |

> **The sequence halves at each step from ordinary onward: 0.100 → 0.025 → 0.012 → 0.006.** Learning it as a descending progression is far easier than four isolated numbers, and **the smallest value belongs to the most precise class** — which alone identifies the answer.

**Why the error goes as √D and not D:**

> Levelling errors are **RANDOM and independent** between setups. Random errors **accumulate as the square root of the number of observations**, not linearly.

> **Four times the distance gives only twice the error**, which is why the permissible error is expressed with a square root.

> **That is a general principle of random error propagation**, not a convention peculiar to levelling — the same √n appears in traverse closure, in repeated angle measurement, and in the standard error of a mean.

> **A SYSTEMATIC error would accumulate linearly** — which is exactly why systematic errors are so much more dangerous than random ones, and why they must be eliminated by procedure rather than averaged away.

**Eliminating the systematic errors — BALANCING THE SIGHTS:**

> Setting the instrument **midway** between the staff stations makes the backsight and foresight distances equal, so three errors that are **proportional to distance** become identical in both readings and **cancel in the difference**:

| Error | Cause |
|---|---|
| **CURVATURE** | The earth curves away from the horizontal line of sight — **+0.0785 d²** m |
| **REFRACTION** | The line of sight bends **downward** — **−0.0112 d²** m, about **1/7 of curvature, opposite sign** |
| **COLLIMATION** | The line of sight is not truly horizontal |

> **Combined curvature and refraction correction = −0.0673 d²** metres (d in km).

> **Balancing the sights is the single most effective precaution in levelling**, and it costs nothing but care in positioning the instrument.

**What balancing does NOT remove:** staff not vertical (use a staff bubble or **wave the staff and take the minimum**), staff graduation errors, **settlement** of the instrument or change point, bubble not centred, and parallax.

**RECIPROCAL LEVELLING** is the technique for when balancing is impossible:
