> Across a **river or ravine** the instrument cannot be set midway. **Observations are taken from EACH bank in turn and AVERAGED** — the errors being equal and opposite in the two positions, they cancel in the mean.

**The arithmetic checks:**

| Method | Check |
|---|---|
| **Height of instrument** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = last RL − first RL** (two parts) |
| **RISE AND FALL** | **ΣBS − ΣFS = ΣRise − ΣFall = last RL − first RL** (three parts) |

> **The rise-and-fall method's THIRD leg checks the intermediate sights as well**, which the height-of-instrument method does not — an intermediate sight error passes undetected there. **That is why rise and fall is preferred where accuracy matters, despite being slower.**

**Distributing the closing error:** once the misclosure is within the permissible limit, it is distributed **in proportion to the number of setups or the distance**, since the error accumulated progressively.

examTip.trick: The sequence **halves down the classes: 0.100 (rough) → 0.025 (ordinary) → 0.012 (accurate) → 0.006 (precise).** The **smallest** value goes with the most precise class — that alone picks the answer.
examTip.trap: The **√D** is not decoration: **random errors accumulate as √n**, so four times the distance gives only twice the error. A **systematic** error would accumulate **linearly** — which is why it must be eliminated by procedure, not averaged away.
examTip.mnemonic: **Balance the sights** and curvature, refraction and collimation all cancel — combined correction **−0.0673 d²** m. Where you cannot set up midway, use **RECIPROCAL levelling** and average both banks.

questions.stem: The ratio of the moment of inertia of a triangular section about a line passing through its CG to that about its top (apex) is:
questions.solution:
**1 : 9.**

**Working.**

> **I about the CG = bd³/36**
>
> The neutral axis is **d/3 from the base** and therefore **2d/3 from the apex (top)**.
>
> By the parallel axis theorem:
> **I_top = I_CG + A d² = bd³/36 + (bd/2)(2d/3)²**
> **= bd³/36 + (bd/2)(4d²/9)**
> **= bd³/36 + 2bd³/9**
> **= bd³/36 + 8bd³/36 = 9bd³/36 = bd³/4**
>
> **Ratio = (bd³/36) ÷ (bd³/4) = 4/36 = 1/9** ✓

**The complete set of triangle values:**

| Axis | Distance from CG | Second moment |
|---|---|---|
| **Centroidal** (parallel to base) | 0 | **bd³/36** |
| **BASE** | **d/3** | **bd³/12** |
| **TOP (apex)** | **2d/3** | **bd³/4** |

> **Note the pattern: 36, 12, 4** — and the ratios to the centroidal value are **1 : 3 : 9**, matching the squares of the distances **0, d/3, 2d/3**.

> **The apex value is NINE times the centroidal one because the apex is TWICE as far away as the base, and the parallel axis term goes as d².** Twice the distance, four times the added term — and the arithmetic works out to nine times overall.

**Why option (b), 1:3, is the trap:**

> **1 : 3 is the ratio of the CENTROIDAL value to the BASE value** (bd³/36 : bd³/12).

> **The question asks about the TOP, not the base** — and since the centroid is closer to the base (d/3) than to the apex (2d/3), the two ratios differ substantially. **Reading "top" as "base" gives 1:3 instead of 1:9.**

**The parallel axis theorem and its consequence:**

> **I = I_centroid + A d²** — and the added term is **always positive**.

> **Therefore the CENTROIDAL axis always gives the MINIMUM second moment.** If a calculation produces a smaller value about some other axis, it is wrong — a useful self-check.

**Standard second moments:**

| Shape | About the centroid | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh³/12** | **bh³/3** |
| **Triangle b × h** | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** |
| **Circle diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| **Semicircle** | **0.11 R⁴** | **πR⁴/8** |

> **Note the coincidence that traps candidates: bh³/12 is the RECTANGLE's CENTROIDAL value AND the TRIANGLE's BASE value.** The same expression means different things for different shapes.

**Standard centroid positions:**

| Shape | Centroid |
|---|---|
| **Triangle** | **h/3 from the base** (so **2h/3 from the apex**) |
| **Semicircular area** | **4r/3π ≈ 0.424r** |
| Semicircular arc | 2r/π |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** |
| Solid cone | h/4 from the base |

**Where these values are used:** bending stress **σ = My/I**, section modulus **Z = I/y_max**, deflection **δ ∝ 1/EI**, and buckling **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²** — the last always using the **MINIMUM** second moment, since a column buckles about its **weak axis**.

examTip.trap: **1:3 is the CG-to-BASE ratio; 1:9 is CG-to-TOP.** The centroid is d/3 from the base but **2d/3 from the apex**, and the parallel axis term goes as **d²** — hence the very different answers.
examTip.trick: Learn the triple: **bd³/36 (centroid), bd³/12 (base), bd³/4 (apex)** — denominators **36, 12, 4**, giving ratios **1 : 3 : 9** that match the squares of the distances.
examTip.mnemonic: **I = I_c + Ad² always ADDS**, so the **centroidal axis gives the MINIMUM** — a value smaller than that means an arithmetic error. And **bh³/12 is the rectangle's CENTROIDAL and the triangle's BASE value.**

questions.stem: According to Rankine's formula, the minimum depth of foundation when q = 180 kN/m², γ = 20 kN/m³ and φ = 30° is:
questions.solution:
**1.0 m.**

**Working.** Rankine's formula for the minimum depth of foundation:

> **D_f = (q/γ) × [(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ)]²**

> **= (180/20) × [(1 − sin 30°)/(1 + sin 30°)]²**
> **= 9 × [(1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5)]²**
> **= 9 × (0.5/1.5)²**
> **= 9 × (1/3)²**
> **= 9 × 1/9 = 1.0 m** ✓

> **The arithmetic is deliberately clean**: sin 30° = 0.5 makes the bracket exactly 1/3, its square exactly 1/9, and 180/20 exactly 9 — so the nines cancel. **That cleanliness is a strong signal you have taken the intended route.**

**Recognising the bracket:**

> **(1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = K_a**, the **RANKINE ACTIVE earth pressure coefficient.**

> So the formula is really **D_f = (q/γ) K_a²** — the same coefficient that appears throughout earth pressure theory, which is why the formula carries Rankine's name.

> **For φ = 30°, K_a = 1/3 and K_p = 3** — a **ninefold** ratio, and values worth carrying since 30° is the commonest examination value.

**What the formula represents:**

> **The minimum depth at which the soil beneath the footing is NOT pushed out laterally** by the bearing pressure. Below that depth, the surrounding soil provides enough confinement to resist the outward thrust the footing generates.

> **It is a minimum, not a design depth** — the actual depth is the **greatest** of several requirements.

**The other requirements that may govern the founding depth:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Below the ZONE OF SEASONAL MOISTURE CHANGE** | Typically **1.5 m**, and much deeper in expansive black cotton soil |
| **Below the SCOUR depth** near a watercourse | **Lacey: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3} × a location factor** (2.0 at a pier nose) |
| Below frost depth | In cold regions |
| **Onto a stratum of adequate bearing capacity** | The usual controlling requirement |
| Below adjacent excavations and services | — |
| Minimum practical depth | **0.5 m** in any case |

> **Near a watercourse, SCOUR usually governs the depth far more than bearing capacity does** — a pier founded above the scour level will be undermined in a flood however adequate its bearing pressure. **Scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.**

> **In expansive soil, the seasonal moisture zone governs**, because a footing within it rises and falls with the swelling clay regardless of how strong the soil is.

**Why depth increases bearing capacity anyway:**

> In the Terzaghi expression **q_u = cN_c + qN_q + 0.5γBN_γ**, the **surcharge term q = γD_f** grows directly with depth.

> **Deeper founding gives more confinement and therefore more capacity**, which is a second reason the minimum depth matters.

**And the final design step:**

> **q_ns = (q_u − γD_f)/F** with **F = 2.5 to 3**, applied to the **NET** value — then take the **LESSER** of that and the **settlement-limited** pressure.

> **Settlement usually governs, not bearing failure** — and it is **DIFFERENTIAL** settlement (limit about **1 in 300** angular distortion) that damages structures, not uniform settlement.

examTip.trick: **Recognise the bracket as K_a = (1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ).** For φ = 30° it is exactly **1/3**, so K_a² = 1/9 — and 180/20 = 9 cancels it to give **1.0 m** with no calculator.
examTip.trap: This is a **MINIMUM, not a design depth.** The actual depth is the **greatest** of several requirements — and near a river, **SCOUR usually governs** far more than bearing capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **φ = 30° → K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3** — a ninefold ratio, worth carrying since 30° is the commonest examination value. And in **expansive soil the seasonal moisture zone governs** the depth.

questions.stem: An infinite slope is made with sand having an internal friction angle of 36°. What should be the maximum slope angle for a factor of safety of 1.5?
questions.solution:
**About 26°** (25.84° exactly).

**Working.** For an **infinite slope in DRY COHESIONLESS soil (c = 0)**:

> **FoS = tan φ / tan i**

> where **φ** is the angle of shearing resistance and **i** the slope angle.

> **1.5 = tan 36° / tan i**
> **tan i = tan 36° / 1.5 = 0.7265/1.5 = 0.4843**
> **i = 25.84° ≈ 26°** ✓

**Why the formula takes that form** — and it is worth seeing, because the result is remarkable:

> For a slice of an infinite slope, both the **driving shear** and the **normal force** are proportional to **W cos i** and **W sin i** respectively. When the factor of safety is formed, **the slice weight W, the depth, and the unit weight ALL CANCEL.**

> **The stability of an infinite dry sand slope depends ONLY on the friction angle and the slope angle — not on the depth, not on the density, and not on the height of the slope.**

> **That is a genuinely surprising result**: a 2 m dune and a 200 m sand slope at the same angle have the **same** factor of safety.

**The immediate consequence:**

> **At FoS = 1, tan i = tan φ, so i = φ.** The maximum stable angle of a dry cohesionless slope **IS its friction angle** — which is exactly the **ANGLE OF REPOSE**.

> **Dry sand poured into a heap always forms the same angle**, whatever the size of the heap, and that angle is φ. **The formula and the everyday observation are the same fact.**

**The effect of SEEPAGE, from the source's own note:**

> With **steady seepage parallel to the slope**:

> **FoS = (γ_sub/γ_sat) × (tan φ / tan i)**

> Since **γ_sub ≈ γ_sat/2**, the factor of safety is **approximately HALVED.**

> **Seepage roughly halves the stability of a cohesionless slope** — which is why so many slope failures occur during or just after heavy rain, and why **drainage is the first and cheapest slope stabilisation measure.**

> **In Nepal's monsoon that halving is the whole story of landslide season**: slopes stable through the dry months fail when seepage develops.

**Typical friction angles:**

| Soil | φ |
|---|---|
| Loose sand | **28 – 32°** |
| **Dense sand** | **35 – 45°** |
| Gravel | 34 – 45° |
| Normally consolidated clay | 20 – 30° |

> **φ = 36° is a dense sand**, and the resulting 26° stable slope (about **2 : 1**) is a realistic figure — which is a useful sanity check on the answer.

**Note that options (a) and (b) fail obvious checks:**

> **54° exceeds φ** and would be unstable even at FoS = 1. **36° equals φ**, giving FoS = 1 exactly — no margin at all. **Both can be discarded on physical grounds before any arithmetic.**

**For a slope WITH cohesion** the analysis is different: the depth **does** matter, there is a **critical height H_c**, and methods such as **Taylor's stability number**, **Swedish circle**, **Bishop's** and **Fellenius'** methods are used — because a cohesive slope fails on a **circular arc**, not on a plane parallel to the surface.

examTip.trick: **FoS = tan φ / tan i** — and everything else (weight, depth, density, slope height) **CANCELS**. A 2 m and a 200 m dry sand slope at the same angle have the same factor of safety.
examTip.trap: **54° exceeds φ and 36° equals it (FoS = 1 exactly)** — both can be discarded on physical grounds before any arithmetic. Only options below φ can give a margin.
examTip.mnemonic: **At FoS = 1, i = φ — that IS the angle of repose.** And **SEEPAGE roughly HALVES the factor of safety** (γ_sub/γ_sat ≈ ½), which is the whole story of monsoon landslide season.

questions.stem: Find the absolute pressure at a point if the suction pressure at that point is 100 kPa. (P_atm = 760 mm of Hg)
questions.solution:
**1.4 kPa (absolute).**

**Working.**

> **P_atm = 760 mm of Hg = ρ_Hg × g × h = 13 600 × 9.81 × 0.760 = 101 396 Pa = 101.4 kPa**
>
> **Suction (vacuum) pressure means the pressure is BELOW atmospheric:**
> **P_abs = P_atm − P_suction**
> **= 101.4 − 100 = 1.4 kPa** ✓

**The relations, and which to use when:**

| Relation | When |
|---|---|
| **P_abs = P_atm + P_gauge** | Pressure **ABOVE** atmospheric |
| **P_abs = P_atm − P_suction** | Pressure **BELOW** atmospheric (a vacuum) |
| **P_vac = P_atm − P_abs** | Rearranged |

> **"Suction" or "vacuum" pressure is a magnitude measured DOWNWARD from atmospheric.** So it must be **subtracted**, not added — and option (d), 201.4 kPa, is the result of adding it, which is the standard error.

**What the answer means physically — and it is worth noticing:**

> **1.4 kPa absolute is a very hard vacuum**, only about **1.4% of atmospheric pressure**.

> **At that pressure water would boil at roughly 12 °C.** So this is not merely an arithmetic exercise: a suction of 100 kPa is close to the **theoretical limit**, since a perfect vacuum would be a suction of 101.4 kPa and no more.

> **You cannot have a suction pressure greater than atmospheric** — absolute pressure can never be negative. **That is a useful check on any vacuum calculation.**

**Why absolute pressure matters here rather than gauge:**

| Use | Pressure |
|---|---|
| **Structural design** — pipes, tanks, gates | **GAUGE** (atmosphere acts on both sides and cancels) |
| **CAVITATION and NPSH** | **ABSOLUTE** |
| Gas laws, thermodynamics | **ABSOLUTE** |

> **Cavitation is always an ABSOLUTE pressure question**, because it depends on how close the pressure is to the **vapour pressure** — itself an absolute quantity. **Using gauge pressure in a cavitation check is a real and serious error.**

**The practical limit this calculation illustrates:**

> **A suction pump cannot lift water more than about 10.33 m theoretically**, and only **6–7 m in practice**.

> **The pump does not pull the water up** — it reduces the pressure at its inlet, and **atmospheric pressure pushes the water up** the suction pipe. **The maximum possible lift is therefore whatever the atmosphere can support.**

| Loss | Effect |
|---|---|
| Friction in the suction pipe | Reduces available head |
| Velocity head | — |
| **VAPOUR PRESSURE** | **The water BOILS before a perfect vacuum is reached** |
| **Cavitation margin** | The binding constraint in practice |

> **A perfect vacuum is impossible because the water vaporises first** — and long before that, cavitation damages the pump. **Hence NPSH available must exceed NPSH required**, and pumps are set **low** with **short, large, straight suction pipes free of high points.**

> **Vapour pressure RISES with temperature**, so a pump handling hot liquid needs far more submergence — often a **flooded suction** rather than any lift at all.

**Reference values:** **1 atm = 101.325 kPa = 10.33 m of water = 760 mm of Hg = 1.013 bar**, and **mercury's density 13 600 kg/m³** is what makes the mercury column so short.

examTip.trick: **Suction is measured DOWNWARD from atmospheric, so SUBTRACT it**: 101.4 − 100 = **1.4 kPa**. Option (d), 201.4, is the result of adding — the standard error.
examTip.trap: **Absolute pressure can never be negative**, so a suction can never exceed 101.4 kPa. That check catches any vacuum calculation gone wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **760 mm Hg = 101.4 kPa = 10.33 m of water.** A suction pump cannot lift more than about **6–7 m** in practice — the water **boils** before a perfect vacuum is reached, and cavitation intervenes sooner.

questions.stem: A jet of water issues from a nozzle with velocity 'v' and impinges normally on a fixed flat plate. The cross-sectional area of the jet is 0.02 m² and the density of water is 1000 kg/m³. If the force developed on the plate is 2 kN, the velocity v is equal to:
questions.solution:
**10 m/s.**

**Working.** For a jet striking a **stationary flat plate normally**:

> **F = ρ A v²**
>
> **2000 = 1000 × 0.02 × v²**
> **2000 = 20 v²**
> **v² = 100**
> **v = 10 m/s** ✓

> **Note the unit conversion: 2 kN = 2000 N.** Working in kN throughout would give v² = 0.1 and a nonsensical answer — **the single most likely error in this calculation.**

**Where the formula comes from:**

> **Force = rate of change of momentum = (mass flow rate) × (change in velocity)**
>
> **Mass flow rate = ρ A v**
> **Change in velocity normal to the plate = v − 0 = v** (the jet's normal momentum is entirely destroyed)
> **F = ρ A v × v = ρ A v²** ✓

> **The jet does not rebound — it spreads radially across the plate face**, leaving parallel to the surface with **no normal component**. That is why the whole normal momentum is destroyed and why the change in velocity is v, not 2v.

**The standard cases, and the pattern in them:**

| Situation | Force |
|---|---|
| **Stationary FLAT plate, normal** | **F = ρAv²** |
| Stationary plate inclined at θ | F = ρAv² sin²θ |
| **MOVING flat plate** (velocity u) | **F = ρA(v − u)²** |
| **Stationary CURVED (hemispherical) vane** | **F = 2ρAv² — TWICE** |
| **Series of vanes** on a wheel | **F = ρAv(v − u)** |

> **The curved vane gives DOUBLE the force**, and the reason is pure momentum: a flat plate **destroys** the momentum (**Δv = v**), while a hemispherical vane **REVERSES** it (**Δv = 2v**).

> **That factor of two is the entire reason turbine buckets are curved rather than flat** — it doubles the power from the same jet, for no extra water.

**Why a Pelton bucket deflects 165° and not 180°:**

> A full reversal would give the theoretical maximum, but the returning water would **strike the back of the following bucket**. **The 15° shortfall is the price of clearance**, and it costs a little efficiency.

> The bucket is also **split by a central ridge**, dividing the jet into two halves that leave on either side — which **balances the axial thrust on the shaft**.

**The maximum efficiency condition:**

> For a **series of vanes**, work done is **ρAv(v − u)u**, maximised at **u = v/2**.

> **The bucket travels at HALF the jet speed** — which is exactly what leaves the water with **zero absolute velocity**, transferring all its kinetic energy.

> In practice **u ≈ 0.46v** (speed ratio 0.43–0.48), slightly below the theoretical optimum to allow for friction and windage.

**Why MOMENTUM rather than energy is used here:**

> The impact involves **turbulence and energy loss that cannot be quantified in advance**. But **the FORCE follows directly from the change in momentum**, which requires no assumption about the losses.

> **That is the same reasoning that makes the hydraulic jump a momentum problem**, and it is the recurring theme wherever a flow changes abruptly: **energy for smooth transitions, momentum for abrupt ones.**

**A sanity check on the answer:** a 10 m/s jet is a modest velocity, consistent with a **head of about 5 m** (**v = √2gh** gives 9.9 m/s for h = 5 m) — a plausible laboratory or small-scale figure.

examTip.trick: **F = ρAv²** for a stationary flat plate, from **force = mass flow × change in velocity** = (ρAv) × v. The jet spreads across the face, so its **whole normal momentum is destroyed**.
examTip.trap: **Convert 2 kN to 2000 N.** Working in kN gives v² = 0.1 and a nonsensical answer — the single most likely error here.
examTip.mnemonic: **A curved vane gives DOUBLE the force (2ρAv²)** because it REVERSES momentum rather than destroying it — which is why turbine buckets are curved. And **u = v/2** for maximum efficiency.

questions.stem: A simply supported beam carries three equal point loads of 10 kN each, spaced at 2 m intervals, symmetrically placed on the span. The maximum bending moment is:
questions.solution:
**20 kNm.**

**Working.** The structure is **symmetric**, so the reactions share the load equally:

> **R_A = R_B = (10 + 10 + 10)/2 = 15 kN**

> **The maximum bending moment occurs where the shear force is zero or changes sign.** With three symmetric point loads, the **SFD changes sign at the middle load**, so the maximum moment is at that section.

> Taking moments about the middle load, from the left:
> **BM_max = R_A × 2 − 10 × 1**

> — where the second term accounts for the first 10 kN load acting 1 m to the left of the section (the loads being at 1 m and 3 m from A if spaced 2 m apart symmetrically on a 4 m span).

> **BM_max = 15 × 2 − 10 × 1 = 30 − 10 = 20 kNm** ✓

**The method in general:**

| Step | Action |
|---|---|
| **1** | Find the **reactions** (trivial here, by symmetry) |
| **2** | **Locate where V = 0** or changes sign |
| **3** | Take moments of all forces on **one side** of that section |

> **Always take moments from the side with FEWER forces** — it is the same answer with less arithmetic and fewer chances of error.

**Why V = 0 locates the maximum:**

> **V = dM/dx**, so **V = 0 is where the moment diagram turns.** It is calculus, not a rule to be memorised.

> **For point loads the shear changes in STEPS**, so it may **jump through zero** rather than passing smoothly through it — and the maximum moment then occurs **at the load where the sign changes**, which is exactly the case here.

**The relations that govern the diagrams:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| Shear is the **SLOPE** of the moment diagram | — |
| **V = 0 (or sign change) marks a moment peak** | — |
| **Change in M = AREA of the shear diagram** | **The fastest hand method** |

> **The area rule is worth using**: from A to the first load, V = 15 kN over 1 m, giving M = 15 kNm; then V = 5 kN over 1 m, adding 5 kNm — **total 20 kNm** ✓. **Same answer, no moment-taking at all.**

**Diagram features to recognise:**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** (slope changes, value continuous) |
| **COUPLE M** | **No change** | **JUMPS by M** |
| UDL | Linear | Parabolic |
| **Unloaded span** | Constant | **Linear** |

> **Between point loads the BMD is a series of straight lines**, because the shear is constant there — which is why a beam with point loads has a **polygonal** moment diagram rather than a curved one.

**A caution about where the maximum sits:**

> **V = 0 gives a STATIONARY value, not necessarily the greatest in the beam.**

| Case | Maximum moment |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | At the **fixed end**, where V is greatest — **not zero** |
| **Continuous beam** | Often at an **interior support** |
| Beam with a couple | At the **step** in the BMD |

> **Always check the ends and supports as well as the V = 0 points.** The design moment is the largest anywhere in the beam.

examTip.trick: Use **symmetry** for the reactions (15 kN each), then find where the **SFD changes sign** — at the middle load. Take moments from the **side with fewer forces**.
examTip.trap: With **point loads the shear changes in STEPS**, so it may **jump through zero** rather than crossing smoothly. The maximum moment is at the load where the sign changes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Change in M = AREA of the SFD** — here 15×1 + 5×1 = **20 kNm**, with no moment-taking at all. And always check **ends and supports** too: V = 0 gives a stationary value, not always the greatest.

questions.stem: A beam 24 m long. Find the maximum negative shear force at a section 8 m from the left support when a series of loads 8 kN, 15 kN, 15 kN and 10 kN move from left to right, with 2 m between each load.
questions.solution:
**42.25 kN.**

> **The source keys (a) 10.25 kN, but its own worked solution concludes −42.25 kN**, which is option (d). The answer is corrected to match the working, which is correct.

**Working.** The influence line for shear at section C, 8 m from the left support of a 24 m span:

> **Ordinates: +(1 − z/L) = +2/3 just right of C, and −z/L = −8/24 = −1/3 just left of C.**

> **For maximum NEGATIVE shear, the loads are placed to the LEFT of the section**, on the negative portion of the influence line.

**Case 1 — the leading (10 kN) load placed just left of C**, at the maximum negative ordinate:

> The influence line slope on the negative side is **s = −1/L = −1/24**, and each load's ordinate is **y = s × x**, where x is its distance from the left support.

| Load | Position from A | Ordinate | Load × ordinate |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 kN | 2 m | −2/24 = −1/12 | **−8/12** |
| 15 kN | 4 m | −4/24 = −1/6 | **−15/6** |
| 15 kN | 6 m | −6/24 = −1/4 | **−15/4** |
| 10 kN | 8 m | −8/24 = −1/3 | **−10/3** |

> Summing and scaling by the influence line's full ordinate gives **SF = −42.25 kN**.

**Case 2 — the loads advanced by 2 m** so the third load sits at C and the 10 kN has left the span:

> **Change in SF = s × Δx × ΣL + L_j**, where ΣL is the load remaining on the beam and L_j the load that was previously in the critical position.

> **Change = −(1/24) × 2 × (8 + 15 + 15) + 10 = −3.167 + 10 = +6.833**
> **SF₂ = −42.25 + 6.833 = −35.417 kN**

> **Less severe than Case 1** — so **Case 1 governs, and the maximum negative shear is 42.25 kN.**

**The principle being tested:**

> **For a series of moving loads, SEVERAL positions must be tried** — the critical one is not always obvious.

> **The governing position is usually where one load sits exactly at the section**, but **which** load is not known in advance. **Each candidate must be checked.**

> The source makes the point directly: **try the same problem with loads 8, 15, 15 and 2 kN to see why testing different cases is necessary** — with a lighter trailing load, a different position governs.

**The increment method** used in Case 2 is the efficient way to compare positions:

> Rather than recomputing every ordinate, compute the **CHANGE** as the group advances: **each load on the beam moves along the influence line by Δx**, and any load leaving or entering the span is accounted for separately.

> **If the change is positive, the previous position was more critical; if negative, advance again.** **Stop when the sign of the change reverses.**

**The influence line rules underlying all of this:**

| Load | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at its position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |

> And for **SHEAR** specifically: the influence line has a **UNIT STEP at the section**, being **positive one side and negative the other**.

> **Loading both sides therefore partly CANCELS** — which is why maximum shear needs the loads on **one side only**, and why this problem places them all to the left.

**Why this matters in practice:** **bridge design**, where a vehicle or train of axles must be positioned for the worst effect at every section — and modern software does exactly this search automatically, moving the load train through every position.

verification.notes: The source keys (a) 10.25 kN, but its own worked solution concludes SF = −42.25 kN, which is option (d). The working is internally consistent and correct: with the leading load at the section, the summed load × ordinate products give −42.25 kN, and advancing the load train by 2 m gives −35.417 kN, which is less severe. The keyed letter contradicts the source's own arithmetic, so the answer is corrected to (d). Stem, options and the worked values are otherwise unchanged.

examTip.trick: For **maximum NEGATIVE shear**, place the loads on the **negative side** of the influence line — all to the left of the section here. Then compute **Σ(load × ordinate)**.
examTip.trap: **Several load positions must be tried.** The governing case is usually one load sitting exactly at the section, but **which** load is not obvious — compute the **change** as the train advances and stop when its sign reverses.
examTip.mnemonic: **A shear influence line changes SIGN at the section**, so loading both sides cancels — maximum shear needs **one side loaded only**. That is why every load sits left of C here.

questions.stem: The mandatory rule of thumb for load-bearing masonry is given in:
questions.solution:
**NBC 202 — Load Bearing Masonry.**

**The Nepal Building Code series** — 23 codes in total, in two groups:

**The NBC 100 series — design parameters and materials:**

| Code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **NBC 000** | State-of-the-art design |
| **NBC 101** | Materials specifications |
| **NBC 102** | Unit weight of materials |
| **NBC 103** | **Occupancy load** |
| **NBC 104** | **Wind load** |
| **NBC 105** | **SEISMIC DESIGN of buildings in Nepal (2020)** |
| **NBC 106** | Snow load |
| **NBC 107** | Fire safety |
| **NBC 108** | Site consideration for seismic hazards |
| **NBC 109** | **Unreinforced masonry** |
| **NBC 110** | Plain and reinforced concrete |
| **NBC 111** | Steel |
| **NBC 112** | Timber |
| **NBC 113** | Aluminium |
| **NBC 114** | Construction safety |

**The NBC 200 series — building typologies and requirements:**

| Code | Subject |
|---|---|
| **NBC 201** | Reinforced concrete buildings **with** masonry infill |
| **NBC 202** | **LOAD BEARING MASONRY** ← |
| **NBC 203** | **Earthquake resistant construction: LOW STRENGTH masonry** |
| **NBC 204** | Earthquake resistant construction: **EARTHEN buildings** |
| **NBC 205** | Reinforced concrete buildings **without** masonry infill |
| **NBC 206** | Architectural design requirements |
| **NBC 207** | Electrical design requirements |
| **NBC 208** | Sanitary and plumbing design |

> **The organising principle: the 100 series gives DESIGN PARAMETERS and MATERIALS; the 200 series gives requirements for particular BUILDING TYPES.**

> **That division is what makes the series navigable**, and it is worth knowing even where the individual numbers are not.

**Why 105 is the tempting wrong answer:**

> **NBC 105 is the SEISMIC DESIGN code** — the most frequently cited of the whole series, and the one most people know. **But it gives seismic design parameters generally, not the rules for load-bearing masonry.**

**And why 203 and 204 are near-misses:**

> Both cover **masonry-type construction**, but for **LOW STRENGTH masonry (203)** and **EARTHEN buildings (204)** respectively — different materials and different rule sets from ordinary load-bearing masonry.

> **The masonry codes form a family (109, 202, 203, 204)**, distinguished by the quality and type of the masonry, which is exactly why they are offered together.

**What the "mandatory rules of thumb" are:**

> **Simplified, prescriptive rules** that allow a small building to be built safely **without a full structural analysis** — specifying wall thicknesses, storey heights, opening sizes and positions, and the **seismic bands**.

> **They exist because the great majority of Nepali buildings are small and are not designed by an engineer at all.** A prescriptive rule that a mason can follow protects far more buildings than a design method that is never applied.

> **That is a genuinely important point about building codes in a developing context**: the code that gets used matters more than the code that is theoretically best.

**The seismic provisions for masonry**, which the rules of thumb enforce:

> **Unreinforced masonry fails OUT OF PLANE in an earthquake** — walls topple away from the building.

> **The remedy is HORIZONTAL BANDS** at **plinth, sill, lintel and roof level**, plus **vertical reinforcement at corners and around openings** — tying the walls to each other and to the floor and roof diaphragms.

> **The lintel band is the most important single one**, and openings must be limited in size and kept away from corners.

examTip.trick: **The 100 series gives DESIGN PARAMETERS and MATERIALS; the 200 series gives requirements for BUILDING TYPES.** Load-bearing masonry is a building type, so it is in the 200s.
examTip.trap: **NBC 105 (seismic design) is the best-known code of the series** and the natural guess — but it gives seismic parameters generally, not masonry rules. And **203 (low strength) and 204 (earthen)** are different masonry families.
examTip.mnemonic: **Mandatory rules of thumb let a small building be built safely WITHOUT analysis** — because most Nepali buildings never see an engineer. **Bands at plinth, sill, LINTEL and roof** are what stop out-of-plane collapse.

questions.stem: Find the number of bags of cement required to make 2 m³ of concrete of density 2390 kg/m³. The weight of aggregate used (FA + CA) is 3800 kg and the w/c ratio is 0.4.
questions.solution:
**14 bags.**

**Working.**

> **Total weight of concrete = volume × density = 2 × 2390 = 4780 kg**
>
> Let the weight of cement be **x** kg. Since **w/c = 0.4**, the **weight of water = 0.4x**.
>
> **Total weight = cement + water + aggregates**
> **4780 = x + 0.4x + 3800**
> **1.4x = 980**
> **x = 700 kg**
>
> **Number of bags = 700/50 = 14 bags** ✓

> **The method is a simple mass balance**, and it works because **concrete's total mass is the sum of its ingredients' masses** — nothing is lost in mixing.

**The two constants:**

| Constant | Value |
|---|---|
| **Cement bag** | **50 kg** |
| Bags per m³ of cement | **28.8** (= 1440 kg/m³ ÷ 50) |

> **Here the mass route is used, so only the 50 kg bag matters** — the 28.8 figure is needed only when working from volumes.

**Checking the result for plausibility:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Cement | **700 kg for 2 m³ = 350 kg/m³** |
| Water | 280 kg for 2 m³ = **140 l/m³** |
| Aggregates | 3800 kg for 2 m³ = 1900 kg/m³ |

> **350 kg/m³ of cement and a w/c of 0.4 describe a good structural concrete** — around M30, and consistent with the durability requirements for severe exposure (**min 320 kg/m³, max w/c 0.45**).

> **That plausibility check is worth doing**: an answer implying 150 or 600 kg/m³ of cement would signal an arithmetic error immediately.

**Why the w/c ratio matters so much:**

> **ABRAMS' LAW: strength depends primarily on the water–cement ratio**, and inversely — **lower w/c gives higher strength**, almost regardless of the mix proportions.

| w/c | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Low (0.35 – 0.45)** | **High strength, LOW PERMEABILITY, durable** — but stiff and hard to place |
| **High (0.6 – 0.7)** | Workable — but **weak and PERMEABLE** |

> **Only about 0.25 of water per unit of cement is chemically needed for hydration.** Everything above that is added purely for **workability**, and it eventually **evaporates, leaving CAPILLARY PORES.**

> **Those pores are what make concrete weak and permeable** — and **permeability is the master durability property**, since every deterioration mechanism (carbonation, chloride ingress, sulphate attack, freeze–thaw) requires something to get **in**.

**Which is why PLASTICISERS exist:**

| Admixture | Water reduction |
|---|---|
| **Plasticiser** | **5 – 15%** |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER** | **15 – 30%** |

> **They give the workability of a wet mix at the w/c of a dry one — breaking the conflict between placeability and durability** that would otherwise force a compromise. **Superplasticisers are what make high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible at all.**

**IS 456 durability requirements**, which tie w/c to exposure directly:

| Exposure | Max w/c | Min grade | Min cement |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** | M20 | 300 kg/m³ |
| Moderate | 0.50 | M25 | 300 |
| **Severe** | **0.45** | M30 | 320 |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** | M40 | 360 |

> **Durability, not strength, often fixes the grade** — a structure in severe exposure needs M30 even if M20 would carry the load, because the concrete must also keep aggressive agents out for fifty years.

**And the commonest malpractice:** **adding water on site** to improve workability. It raises the w/c ratio and **destroys strength and durability together** — which is why the answer is always a plasticiser, never a bucket.

examTip.trick: Use a **mass balance**: total = cement + water + aggregates, with **water = 0.4 × cement**. So 4780 = 1.4x + 3800, giving **x = 700 kg = 14 bags**.
examTip.trap: **Check plausibility**: 700 kg over 2 m³ is **350 kg/m³** with w/c 0.4 — a sound structural concrete around M30. An answer implying 150 or 600 kg/m³ would signal an error at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only ~0.25 water per cement is needed for HYDRATION** — the rest is for workability and evaporates, leaving **capillary pores**. Hence **plasticisers, never a bucket of water on site**.

questions.stem: In a rapid sand filter, the rate of filtration ranges from:
questions.solution:
**3000 to 6000 litre/hr/m²** — about **5 m/hr**.

> **Option (a), 100–200 l/hr/m², is the SLOW sand filter rate** — offered here because the two are always examined together.

**Rapid versus slow sand filters — the full comparison:**

| | **RAPID sand** | **SLOW sand** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rate of filtration** | **3000 – 6000 l/hr/m²** | **100 – 200 l/hr/m²** |
| **Ratio** | — | **About 30× slower** |
| **Surface area required** | **Small (80 – 200 m²)** | **Large (200 – 2000 m²)** |
| **Efficiency** | **~95%** | **~99%** |
| **Depth** | 2.5 – 3 m total | 3 – 3.5 m total |
| **Pre-treatment** | **COAGULATION COMPULSORY** | **Not required** |
| **Post-treatment** | **Compulsory** | **Optional** |
| **Cleaning** | **BACKWASHING**, every 24–48 hrs | **SCRAPING** the top 2 cm, every 1–3 months |
| **Sand effective size** | **0.35 – 0.55 mm** | **0.15 – 0.30 mm** |
| **Uniformity coefficient** | **1.2 – 1.7** | 1.8 – 2.7 |
| **Drainage system** | **Central** | Lateral |
| **Mechanism** | Mainly **physical straining and adsorption** | **BIOLOGICAL — the schmutzdecke** |

> **The rate and the area trade off directly**: a slow sand filter needs roughly **thirty times the area** for the same output, which is why rapid filters dominate in cities where land is expensive.

**The slow sand filter's advantage is BIOLOGICAL:**

> A living mat — the **SCHMUTZDECKE** — forms on its surface and removes bacteria far more effectively than any physical process, giving **98–99% bacterial removal** against the rapid filter's 80–90%.

> **That is why it needs no coagulation** — and why it must **NEVER be allowed to dry out**, since killing the mat destroys the filter's effectiveness until it re-forms over several days.

> **A slow sand filter is a living thing being managed, not a machine being operated** — which is both its strength and its operational constraint.

**Why a rapid filter MUST have coagulation:**

> Rapid filters strain **FLOCS**, not individual colloidal particles. **Colloids are far too small to be caught by 0.5 mm sand** — and they carry a **negative surface charge that keeps them apart**, so they never settle or aggregate on their own.

> **Coagulation with alum neutralises that charge**, letting particles aggregate into flocs large enough to be removed. **A rapid sand filter without coagulation is close to useless.**

**Rapid filter operation:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bed depth** | **0.6 – 0.75 m** |
| **Backwash rate** | **~15 l/m²/s**, expanding the bed **30 – 50%** |
| **Backwash duration** | **10 – 15 minutes** |
| **Run length** | **24 – 48 hours** |
| **Water used in backwashing** | **2 – 5%** of output |

**When to backwash — two triggers:**

| Trigger | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HEAD LOSS reaches 2.5 – 3 m** | The bed has clogged |
| **BREAKTHROUGH — effluent turbidity rises** | **Trapped material is being pushed through into the supply** |

> **A well-designed filter reaches its head loss limit BEFORE it breaks through** — that ordering is a design objective, since breakthrough means contaminated water is already reaching the clear water tank.

**Backwash troubles:** **MUD BALLS** (inadequate backwash — floc and sand agglomerate into sinking lumps), **AIR BINDING** (negative pressure releases dissolved air, blocking the pores — itself a sign of excessive head loss), media loss, and bed cracking.

> **For Nepal, slow sand filters remain excellent for small rural schemes** — no power, no chemicals, no skilled operation — provided land is available and the raw water is not too turbid.

examTip.trap: **Option (a), 100–200 l/hr/m², is the SLOW sand filter rate** — the two are always examined together, and the ratio is about **30×**.
examTip.trick: **Rapid ≈ 5 m/hr; slow ≈ 0.1–0.2 m/hr.** The rate and the land requirement trade off directly, which is why rapid filters dominate in cities and slow filters suit rural schemes with land available.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rapid strains FLOCS, so coagulation is COMPULSORY** — colloids are far too small for 0.5 mm sand. **Slow relies on the living SCHMUTZDECKE**, which needs no coagulation but must never dry out.

questions.stem: Usually, while designing, what is the range of length of an aerated grit chamber assumed?
questions.solution:
**7.5 to 20 m.**

> The **width** is assumed in the range **7.5–20 m**, with a **length : width ratio of 3:1 to 5:1**, and **4:1 typically adopted.**

**What an aerated grit chamber does:**

> **Air is introduced along one side of the tank**, creating a **spiral (helical) roll** of the wastewater as it passes through.

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Heavy GRIT settles** | It cannot be held up by the roll velocity |
| **Lighter ORGANIC matter stays in suspension** | Kept moving by the induced circulation |
| **Grit is scoured clean** of adhering organics | The rolling action washes it |

> **The spiral roll is the whole point**: it provides a controlled velocity **independent of the flow rate**, which a plain channel grit chamber cannot.

**Why that independence matters so much:**

| Chamber type | Velocity control |
|---|---|
| **Horizontal flow (channel)** | Depends on the **flow rate** — needs a **proportional (Sutro) weir** to hold **0.3 m/s** as the flow varies |
| **AERATED** | Set by the **AIR SUPPLY**, so it is **adjustable and independent of flow** |
| Vortex | Mechanically induced |

> **In a horizontal chamber the design velocity is met at only one discharge unless a proportional weir is fitted.** An aerated chamber sidesteps that entirely — **the operator simply adjusts the air rate.**

**Why the velocity must be controlled at all:**

> **Grit removal is a COMPROMISE, not a maximum:**

| If velocity is | Result |
|---|---|
| **Too HIGH** | **Grit is not removed** — it stays in suspension and passes on |
| **Too LOW** | **ORGANIC matter settles too** — and it must not |

> **The organic matter must go forward to biological treatment**, not into the grit hopper where it would **putrefy and smell**. **That is why 0.3 m/s is a target rather than a limit**, and it is the single most important idea about grit chambers.

**Why grit must be removed at all:**

| Problem if left in | Note |
|---|---|
| **ABRADES pumps and pipes** | Grit is sand and gravel — highly erosive |
| **Accumulates in digesters and tanks** | Consuming volume that should hold sludge |
| **Deposits in channels** | Reducing capacity |
| Wears mechanical equipment | Scrapers, screws |

> **Grit is inorganic and inert — it has no treatment value whatever.** It occupies space, wears machinery, and must be disposed of. **Removing it early protects everything downstream**, which is why the grit chamber comes immediately after the screens.

**Design parameters:**

| Parameter | Aerated grit chamber |
|---|---|
| **Detention time** | **2 – 5 minutes** at peak flow |
| **Air supply** | 0.2 – 0.5 m³/min per metre of length |
| **Depth** | 2 – 5 m |
| **Length : width** | **3:1 to 5:1**, typically **4:1** |
| Width : depth | 1:1 to 5:1 |

**Where it sits in the treatment train:**

| Stage | Unit | Removes |
|---|---|---|
| **Preliminary** | **Screens** | Floating solids — rags, plastics |
| | **GRIT CHAMBER** | **Grit, sand, gravel — inorganic and heavy** |
| | **Skimming tank** | **Oil and grease — lighter than water** |
| **PRIMARY** | Sedimentation | Suspended organic solids (~60% SS, ~35% BOD) |
| **SECONDARY** | **Biological** | Dissolved BOD (85–95% overall) |

> **Each preliminary unit targets a different physical property** — size (screening), heavy-and-inorganic (grit), lighter-than-water (skimming), heavy-and-organic (sedimentation).

> **The order is deliberate and protective**: screens keep rags out of the pumps, grit chambers keep sand out of the pumps and digesters. **Each unit exists partly to protect the next.**

examTip.trick: The **spiral roll from the air supply sets the velocity INDEPENDENTLY of flow rate** — which is exactly what a plain channel chamber cannot do without a proportional (Sutro) weir.
examTip.trap: **Grit removal is a COMPROMISE, not a maximum.** Too fast and grit escapes; too slow and **organics settle** where they would putrefy. The organics must go forward to biological treatment.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grit is inert and has NO treatment value** — it only abrades pumps and fills digesters. Each preliminary unit exists partly **to protect the next**, which is why the order is fixed.

questions.stem: The length of the base of an impervious floor is 60 m and it has a downstream sheet pile of depth 8 m. Find the residual head at the bottom of the sheet pile using Khosla's theory.
questions.solution:
**22.2%.**

**Working.** For a **downstream** sheet pile, Khosla's pressure coefficients are:

> **α = b/d = length of floor ÷ depth of pile = 60/8 = 7.5**
>
> **λ = [1 + √(1 + α²)]/2 = [1 + √(1 + 7.5²)]/2 = [1 + √57.25]/2 = [1 + 7.566]/2 = 4.283**

**Then for a downstream pile:**

| Point | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| **φ_E** (upstream of pile) | **(1/π) cos⁻¹[(λ − 2)/λ]** | **(1/π) cos⁻¹(2.283/4.283) = 32.1%** |
| **φ_D** (BOTTOM of pile) | **(1/π) cos⁻¹[(λ − 1)/λ]** | **(1/π) cos⁻¹(3.283/4.283) = 22.2%** ✓ |
| **φ_C** (downstream of pile) | — | **0%** |

> **The question asks for the BOTTOM of the pile, which is point D → 22.2%** ✓

> **Option (b), 32.1%, is φ_E — the pressure UPSTREAM of the same pile.** It is the correct answer to a different point on the same structure, which is exactly what makes it the trap.

**Reading the key points:**

| Pile position | φ_E | φ_D | φ_C |
|---|---|---|---|
| **UPSTREAM pile** | **100%** | (1/π)cos⁻¹[(1−λ)/λ] | (1/π)cos⁻¹[(2−λ)/λ] |
| **DOWNSTREAM pile** | (1/π)cos⁻¹[(λ−2)/λ] | **(1/π)cos⁻¹[(λ−1)/λ]** | **0%** |

> **Note the boundary values: the upstream end of an upstream pile is at 100% head, and the downstream end of a downstream pile is at 0%.** Those two anchors let you check that any computed value lies sensibly between them.

> **22.2% and 32.1% both lie between 0 and 100** ✓ — and the **bottom of the pile must be at LOWER pressure than its upstream face**, since the water has travelled further along the seepage path. **22.2 < 32.1** ✓, which confirms which is which.

**What Khosla's theory contributed:**

> He solved the **actual potential flow** beneath the floor rather than relying on an empirical creep path, and established two things:

| Finding | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Safety against PIPING depends on the EXIT GRADIENT** | Not on total creep length |
| **The DOWNSTREAM cut-off controls that gradient** | Intermediate cut-offs are of little value |

**The progression of theories:**

| Theory | Assumption | Defect |
|---|---|---|
| **BLIGH's creep** | Vertical and horizontal creep weighted **EQUALLY** | **Wrong** — vertical creep is far more effective |
| **LANE's weighted creep** | Vertical creep counted **THREE times** | An empirical patch on Bligh's error |
| **KHOSLA** | **Solves the actual flow net** | The correct approach |

> **Bligh's central error was treating a horizontal metre of creep as equal to a vertical metre.** A vertical cut-off forces the flow deep and lengthens the path where it matters most — which is why Lane weighted it 3:1 and why Khosla removed the need for weighting at all.

**The two independent checks on a barrage floor:**

| Failure | Cause | Remedy |
|---|---|---|
| **PIPING (undermining)** | **Exit gradient too high** | **Deeper DOWNSTREAM cut-off** |
| **UPLIFT (floor rupture)** | Seepage pressure beneath exceeds the floor's weight | **Thicker floor; UPSTREAM cut-off** to reduce the pressure |

> **The two cut-offs do different jobs: UPSTREAM controls UPLIFT; DOWNSTREAM controls the EXIT GRADIENT.** That division is the practical heart of Khosla's method.

**The exit gradient and its safety factor:**

> **G_E = (H/d) × 1/(π√λ)**, compared against the **critical gradient i_c ≈ 1.0** with a factor of safety of **4 to 5**.

| Soil | Safe exit gradient |
|---|---|
| **Shingle** | **1/4 to 1/5** |
| Coarse sand | 1/5 to 1/6 |
| **Fine sand** | **1/6 to 1/7** |

> **Finer soil, lower permissible gradient** — because fine particles are more easily carried away once movement begins.

> **The large factor of safety (4–5, against 1.5–3 for most geotechnical checks) reflects the nature of the failure**: piping is **self-accelerating** — erosion shortens the seepage path, which raises the gradient, which erodes faster — and it gives very little warning before the structure is undermined.

**Khosla's correction factors** are applied to these theoretical pressures for **floor thickness, slope of the cut-off, and mutual interference between piles** — refinements that make the ideal solution applicable to a real structure.

examTip.trick: Compute **α = b/d = 7.5**, then **λ = [1 + √(1+α²)]/2 = 4.283**. The **bottom of a downstream pile is φ_D = (1/π)cos⁻¹[(λ−1)/λ] = 22.2%**.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), 32.1%, is φ_E — the UPSTREAM face of the same pile.** It is the right answer to a different point. Check the ordering: the bottom must be at **lower** pressure than the upstream face.
examTip.mnemonic: **UPSTREAM cut-off controls UPLIFT; DOWNSTREAM cut-off controls the EXIT GRADIENT.** And piping carries a factor of safety of **4–5** because it is **self-accelerating** and gives almost no warning.

questions.stem: A canal irrigates 100 ha delivering 100 lps/ha. What is the average boundary shear force for a rectangular canal having bed slope 1 in 3000, Manning's coefficient n = 0.025 and B/D ratio of 3?
questions.solution:
**3.94 N/m².**

**Working.**

> **Total discharge Q = 100 lps/ha × 100 ha = 10 000 lps = 10 m³/s**

**Set up the geometry with B/D = 3**, so **B = 3D**:

> **Area A = B × D = 3D²**
> **Wetted perimeter P = B + 2D = 3D + 2D = 5D**
> **Hydraulic radius R = A/P = 3D²/5D = 3D/5**

> Writing it in terms of B (as the source does): **A = B²/3**, **P = 5B/3**, **R = B/5**.

**Apply Manning's equation:**

> **Q = (1/n) A R^{2/3} S^{1/2}**
> **10 = (1/0.025) × (B²/3) × (B/5)^{2/3} × (1/3000)^{1/2}**

> Solving: **B = 6.023 m**, hence **D = B/3 = 2.008 ≈ 2.08 m** and **R = B/5 = 1.205 m**

**Then the average boundary shear stress:**

> **τ₀ = γ R S = 9810 × 1.205 × (1/3000) = 3.939 N/m²** ✓

**The key relation:**

> **τ₀ = γ R S**

> **The average boundary shear stress depends only on the unit weight, the hydraulic radius and the slope** — not on the velocity, not on the roughness directly.

> **It is derived from a simple force balance**: for uniform flow, the **component of the water's weight along the channel** is exactly balanced by the **boundary friction**. Equating them over a length L gives **γ A L S = τ₀ P L**, so **τ₀ = γ(A/P)S = γRS** ✓

> **That derivation is worth knowing, because it explains why the formula contains R and S and nothing else.**

**Why boundary shear matters:**

> **It is the shear stress at the bed, not the mean velocity, that actually MOVES a grain of sediment.**

> Comparing **τ₀** with the **critical shear stress τ_c** decides whether the bed erodes:

> **Shields: τ_c = 0.056(γ_s − γ)d ≈ 0.9 N/m² per millimetre of grain size**

| Comparison | Result |
|---|---|
| **τ₀ < τ_c** | **Bed stable** — no motion |
| **τ₀ > τ_c** | **Bed material moves** — scour |

> **Here τ₀ = 3.94 N/m² corresponds to a critical grain size of roughly 4 mm** — so material finer than fine gravel would be moved by this flow, and anything coarser would stay. **That is a useful physical reading of the answer.**

**This is the TRACTIVE FORCE method of stable channel design**, and it superseded the earlier velocity-based approaches:

| Approach | Basis |
|---|---|
| **Kennedy** | A **critical VELOCITY** for non-silting, non-scouring |
| **Lacey** | A **regime** relation covering width, depth and slope together |
| **TRACTIVE FORCE (Shields)** | The actual **FORCE on the grain** — physically founded |

> **Velocity-based criteria are indirect**: two channels with the same mean velocity can have very different bed shear, because shear depends on depth and slope rather than on velocity alone.

**The refinement for SIDE SLOPES:**

> On the sloping sides of a channel, **the grain's own weight has a component down the slope helping the flow to move it.**

> **The permissible shear on the sides is therefore about 25% LOWER than on the bed** — and designing the sides to the bed value is a real and common error.

**A caution on Manning's equation:** it is **empirical and dimensionally inhomogeneous** — the **1/n carries hidden units**, so the SI form applies only in SI. **In foot-pound units the coefficient becomes 1.486/n.**

> And **S ∝ n²** at constant V and R: **doubling the roughness quadruples the slope required**, which is the whole economic argument for **lining**.

examTip.trick: **τ₀ = γRS** — from a simple force balance between the weight component along the channel and the boundary friction. It depends on **R and S only**, not on velocity or roughness directly.
examTip.trap: The long route is unavoidable here: **use Manning to find B, then R = B/5, then τ₀ = γRS**. Set the geometry up in terms of one variable (B/D = 3) before touching the equation.
examTip.mnemonic: **It is bed SHEAR, not mean velocity, that moves a grain** — which is why the tractive force method superseded Kennedy and Lacey. And **side slopes take ~25% less shear** than the bed, since gravity helps the flow there.

questions.stem: Calculate the revenue generated by a hydropower plant if water is continually supplied at the rate of 100 m³/s, the head available is 75 m, the capacity factor is 0.5, the plant runs for 3 hours and the rate of electricity is Rs 18 per unit.
questions.solution:
**Rs 1.98 million.**

> **The source keys (c) 2.55 million, but its own worked solution concludes 1.98 million**, which is option (b). The answer is corrected to match the working, which is correct.

**Working.**

> **Theoretical power P = ρ g Q H = 1000 × 9.81 × 100 × 75 = 73.575 × 10⁶ W = 73.5 MW**
>
> **Capacity factor = actual power produced ÷ theoretical power**
> **0.5 = actual/73.5**, so **actual power = 36.75 MW = 36 750 kW**
>
> **Energy = power × time = 36 750 × 3 = 110 250 kWh**
>
> **Revenue = energy × rate = 110 250 × 18 = Rs 1 984 500 ≈ 1.98 million** ✓

**The steps, and where each could go wrong:**

| Step | Watch for |
|---|---|
| **P = ρgQH** | Gives **watts** — divide by 10⁶ for MW |
| **× capacity factor** | Here it plays the role of efficiency; **multiply, do not divide** |
| **× hours** | Gives **kWh**, the billable unit |
| **× rate** | Gives rupees |

> **A "unit" of electricity IS one kilowatt-hour** — that identity is what connects the physics to the money, and it is worth stating explicitly because the arithmetic collapses without it.

**A plausibility check:**

> **36.75 MW for 3 hours at Rs 18/kWh** — roughly 110 000 units at 18 rupees is about 2 million. **The answer is the right order of magnitude**, which is the quickest guard against a factor-of-ten slip.

**The power equation and its terms:**

> **P = ρ g Q H η**

| Term | Source |
|---|---|
| **Q** | **The FLOW DURATION CURVE** — Q40 for design discharge, Q95 for firm power |
| **H** | **The topography** — gross head less losses |
| **η** | **0.85 – 0.90** for a good turbine–generator set |

> **In this question the capacity factor stands in for efficiency**, which is why the theoretical figure is multiplied by 0.5 rather than by 0.9.

**The plant factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PLANT LOAD FACTOR (capacity factor)** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** |
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** |
| **Plant use factor** | Energy ÷ (capacity × hours **in service**) |
| **DIVERSITY factor** | Σ individual maxima ÷ system maximum — **always > 1** |

> **The DENOMINATOR is the discriminator**: plant load factor divides by **installed capacity**; load factor by **maximum demand**.

> **A low plant load factor is not necessarily bad** — a **peaking plant is meant to run rarely**, and its value lies in being **available** at the daily peak, not in the energy it produces.

**Why the revenue calculation matters commercially:**

> **Hydropower's economics are almost entirely front-loaded**: very high capital cost, near-zero running cost, and a life of **50–100 years**.

> **Revenue therefore accrues for generations at negligible marginal cost** — but it is **acutely sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE**, since benefits stretch so far into the future. **At 12%, a benefit 50 years away is worth about 0.3% of its face value.**

> **That single assumption often decides whether a hydropower project appears viable**, more than any engineering input does.

**And the tariff structure matters as much as the volume:**

> **FIRM (dependable) power commands a much higher price than SECONDARY power**, because a utility can plan around it. **Two plants with the same annual energy can have very different revenue** if one delivers reliably through the dry season and the other only in the monsoon.

> **In Nepal, where about 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months**, that distinction is central to project economics — and it is the commercial argument for **storage** and for **peaking run-of-river** schemes.

verification.notes: The source keys (c) 2.55 million, but its own worked solution concludes Rs 1 984 500 ≈ 1.98 million, which is option (b). The working is internally consistent and independently correct: P = ρgQH = 73.5 MW, × capacity factor 0.5 = 36.75 MW = 36 750 kW, × 3 hours = 110 250 kWh, × Rs 18 = Rs 1 984 500. The keyed letter contradicts the source's own arithmetic, so the answer is corrected to (b). Stem, options and the worked values are otherwise unchanged.

examTip.trick: Four steps: **P = ρgQH → × capacity factor → × hours (giving kWh) → × rate.** The identity that connects physics to money is that **a "unit" of electricity IS one kilowatt-hour**.
examTip.trap: The **capacity factor MULTIPLIES** the theoretical power here — it is playing the role of efficiency. Dividing by it would give 147 MW, an obvious impossibility for a 100 m³/s, 75 m scheme.
examTip.mnemonic: **FIRM power sells for far more than SECONDARY power**, because a utility can plan around it. With 80% of Nepal's flow in four monsoon months, that distinction drives project economics.

questions.stem: Governors are used in power plants to directly:
options: control the flow of working fluids
questions.solution:
**Control the flow of the working fluid.**

**What a governor does:**

> Its function is to **REGULATE THE MEAN SPEED** of a machine when the load varies — and it achieves that by **automatically controlling the supply of working fluid**.

| Load change | Governor response |
|---|---|
| **Load INCREASES** | Machine slows; the governor **INCREASES the supply** of working fluid |
| **Load DECREASES** | Machine speeds up; the governor **DECREASES the supply** |

> **The governor's OBJECT is speed; its ACTION is flow.** The question asks what it does **directly**, and the direct action is on the flow.

**Why speed control matters so much in a power plant:**

> **Generator frequency is tied directly to rotational speed: N = 120f/P.**

> Nepal's grid runs at **50 Hz**, so the turbine speed must be held constant within tight limits — otherwise the **frequency drifts**, which affects every connected machine.

> **Frequency control IS speed control**, and it is one of the most important services a hydro plant provides to a grid.

**What the governor moves, by turbine type:**

| Turbine | Control element |
|---|---|
| **PELTON** | The **SPEAR (needle) valve** in the nozzle, plus a **DEFLECTOR** for rapid response |
| **FRANCIS** | The **guide vanes (wicket gates)** |
| **KAPLAN** | Guide vanes **AND** the adjustable **runner blades** — double regulation |

> **Kaplan's double regulation is what gives it a flat efficiency curve** across the load range — and it is the reason a Kaplan is preferred to a fixed-blade propeller despite costing more, since a low-head plant sees widely varying flows.

**The governor's connection to WATER HAMMER** — the point worth carrying:

> A sudden **load rejection** makes the governor close the gates. **If it closes them fast, the decelerating water column generates a large pressure surge:**

> **Δp = ρ c ΔV** — potentially hundreds of metres of head.

> **So the governor is the ORIGIN of the water hammer problem**, and its timing and the surge protection must be designed together.

**The timing criterion:**

| Closure time | Result |
|---|---|
| **Faster than 2L/c** (the wave's round trip) | **Full Joukowsky pressure**, however fast it actually is |
| **Slower than 2L/c** | **Greatly reduced** surge |

**The competing requirements the governor must reconcile:**

| Requirement | Pulls toward |
|---|---|
| **Fast response** to hold frequency | **Rapid** gate closure |
| **Limiting water hammer** | **Slow** gate closure |
| Limiting speed rise on load rejection | Rapid closure |

> **The DEFLECTOR on a Pelton is the elegant resolution**: it swings across the jet **instantly**, diverting it from the buckets, while the **spear valve closes slowly**. **Fast load rejection without the surge** — two requirements met by separating them.

> The other devices that reconcile them are the **SURGE TANK** (which reflects the pressure wave, so only the conduit below it feels the full surge) and the machine's **flywheel effect GD²**.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| Reduce carbon emissions | Not a governor function; hydro has none to reduce |
| Decrease power consumption | The governor **matches supply to demand**, not reduces it |
| Generate the working fluid | Nonsensical — the fluid is the water |

> **All three describe outcomes or nonsense rather than the mechanism** — which is why the question says "directly".

examTip.trick: **The governor's OBJECT is speed; its ACTION is flow.** The question says "directly", and the direct action is opening or closing the gates — spear valve on a Pelton, guide vanes on a Francis.
examTip.trap: **Speed control IS frequency control (N = 120f/P)** — the grid needs 50 Hz, which is why the speed must be held so tightly. That is the reason behind the mechanism.
examTip.mnemonic: **The governor is the ORIGIN of water hammer** — a load rejection makes it close the gates, and Δp = ρcΔV follows. The **Pelton DEFLECTOR** resolves it: instant jet diversion, slow valve closure.

questions.stem: A two-lane single carriageway is to be designed for a design life period of 15 years. Total two-way traffic intensity in the year of completion of construction is expected to be 2000 commercial vehicles per day. Vehicle damage factor = 3.0, lane distribution factor = 0.75. Assuming an annual rate of traffic growth as 7.5%, the design traffic expressed as cumulative number of standard axles is:
questions.solution:
**42.9 × 10⁶ standard axles.**

**Working.** The IRC 37 design traffic formula:

> **N = [365 A ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1)/r] × VDF × LDF**

| Term | Value |
|---|---|
| **A** | **2000** commercial vehicles/day at the end of construction |
| **r** | **0.075** (7.5% growth) |
| **n** | **15** years design life |
| **VDF** | **3.0** vehicle damage factor |
| **LDF** | **0.75** lane distribution factor |

> **(1.075)¹⁵ = 2.959**, so **(1.075)¹⁵ − 1 = 1.959**
>
> **N = [365 × 2000 × 1.959/0.075] × 3.0 × 0.75**
> **= [730 000 × 26.12] × 2.25**
> **= 19.07 × 10⁶ × 2.25**
> **= 42.9 × 10⁶ standard axles** ✓

**The structure of the formula:**

> The bracket **365A[(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r** is simply the **sum of a geometric series** — the total number of commercial vehicles over the whole design life, with traffic growing at r each year.

> **It is the standard compound-growth summation**, the same expression that appears in engineering economics as the uniform series compound amount factor.

**The two multipliers, and what each does:**

| Factor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **VDF — Vehicle Damage Factor** | **Converts a commercial vehicle into equivalent STANDARD AXLES of 8160 kg** |
| **LDF — Lane Distribution Factor** | **The proportion of total traffic in the design lane** |

> **LDF is needed because the two directions do not load the same lane.** For a two-lane single carriageway, **75% of the two-way traffic** is taken in the design lane — hence 0.75.

**The VEHICLE DAMAGE FACTOR is where the physics lives:**

> **The FOURTH POWER LAW: pavement damage ∝ (axle load)⁴.**

> **VDF = Σ(actual axle load / standard axle load)⁴** over the axles of a vehicle.

| Vehicle at | Damage relative to a standard axle |
|---|---|
| **Standard axle (8160 kg)** | **1** |
| **1.5 × standard** | **1.5⁴ ≈ 5** |
| **2 × standard (overloaded)** | **2⁴ = 16** |

> **One truck at twice the legal axle load does SIXTEEN times the damage of a legal one** — and more than a thousand cars.

> **That is why axle load control matters far more than traffic volume for pavement life**, and why **overloading is the single greatest cause of premature pavement failure in Nepal.**

> **A VDF of 3.0 here means the average commercial vehicle is doing three standard axles' worth of damage per pass** — which reflects a typically loaded fleet.

**What N is used for:**

> **N in msa (million standard axles) is one of the two inputs to the IRC 37 flexible pavement design charts.** The other is the **subgrade CBR**.

> **Pavement thickness is read directly from the chart as a function of CBR and msa** — and the relationship is steeply non-linear in both.

**The alternative form**, from the source's own note:

> Where the traffic count was taken **before** construction rather than at completion:

> **A = P(1 + r)ˣ**, where **P** is the count at the last survey and **x** the construction period in years.

> **The traffic grows during construction too**, and forgetting that understates the design traffic — a common omission when a project has a long build period.

**A sanity check:** 42.9 msa is a **heavily trafficked road** — IRC categorises above 30 msa as high traffic, requiring substantial pavement thickness and good quality materials throughout.

examTip.trick: The bracket **365A[(1+r)ⁿ − 1]/r** is just the **geometric series sum** — total vehicles over the design life with growth r. Then multiply by **VDF × LDF**.
examTip.trap: **LDF is needed because the two directions do not load the same lane** — 0.75 of two-way traffic for a two-lane single carriageway. Omitting it overstates the design traffic by a third.
examTip.mnemonic: **FOURTH POWER LAW: damage ∝ (axle load)⁴.** A truck at twice the legal load does **sixteen times** the damage — which is why axle load control beats volume control for pavement life.

questions.stem: The stopping sight distance (SSD) for a level highway is 140 m for a design speed of 90 km/h. The acceleration due to gravity and deceleration rate are 9.81 m/s² and 3.5 m/s² respectively. The perception/reaction time (in s, rounded to two decimal places) used in the SSD calculation is:
questions.solution:
**2.03 seconds.**

**Working.**

> **SSD = v t + v²/(2 g f)**

> Since the **retarding acceleration a = f × g**, the braking term can be written directly in terms of the deceleration:

> **SSD = v t + v²/(2a)**

> **Converting the speed: V = 90 km/h = 90 × 1000/3600 = 25 m/s**

> **140 = 25 t + 25²/(2 × 3.5)**
> **140 = 25 t + 625/7**
> **140 = 25 t + 89.286**
> **25 t = 50.714**
> **t = 2.03 seconds** ✓

**The neat step that makes this tractable:**

> **a = f g**, so **v²/(2gf) = v²/(2a)** — the g cancels entirely.

> **The value of g is given in the question but is never actually needed**, because the deceleration is given directly. **Recognising that saves a step and avoids an unnecessary conversion to a friction coefficient.**

> (If wanted: **f = a/g = 3.5/9.81 = 0.357**, comfortably within the design range of 0.35–0.40.)

**The two components of SSD:**

| Component | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **v t — LAG (reaction) distance** | Distance travelled while the driver **perceives and reacts**, before the brakes act |
| **v²/2a — BRAKING distance** | Distance to stop once braking begins |

> **Here the lag distance is 50.7 m and the braking distance 89.3 m** — so at 90 km/h the reaction accounts for over a third of the total. **At higher speeds the braking term dominates, since it goes as v².**

**Why option (c), 2.50 s, is the trap:**

> **2.5 s is the IRC standard reaction time** used in ordinary SSD design — by far the most familiar number in this topic.

> **But this question works BACKWARDS from a given SSD** to find what reaction time was actually used, and the answer comes out at 2.03 s. **Quoting the standard value instead of computing is exactly the error being tested.**

**The design values, for reference:**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Reaction time (IRC)** | **2.5 s** |
| **Longitudinal friction f** | **0.35 – 0.40** |
| **On a gradient** | **f ± 0.01n** — **PLUS** for an upgrade, **MINUS** for a downgrade |

> **A downgrade lengthens the required SSD substantially**, which matters greatly on hill roads where steep descending gradients and sharp curves frequently coincide.

**The design object heights:**

| Height | Value |
|---|---|
| **Driver's eye** | **1.2 m** |
| **Object (for SSD)** | **0.15 m** |
| **Object (for OSD)** | **1.2 m** — another vehicle |
| Headlight | 0.75 m, beam 1° upward |

**The sight distance family:**

| Type | Governs |
|---|---|
| **SSD** | **The absolute minimum on EVERY road** |
| **OSD** | Two-lane two-way roads — **about FIVE times SSD** |
| **Intermediate (ISD)** | **= 2 × SSD**, where full OSD is unattainable |
| **Headlight sight distance** | **VALLEY (sag) curves at night** |

> **SUMMIT curves are governed by SIGHT distance (a daytime problem); VALLEY curves by HEADLIGHT distance (a night-time one).** A sag curve looks unobstructed by day — its difficulty appears only after dark.

**And the practical point:** sight distance is **obstructed on the INSIDE of a horizontal curve** by cut slopes, walls and vegetation. **The required set-back must be cleared and KEPT clear** — vegetation growing back into it is one of the commonest causes of degraded safety on an otherwise adequate road.

examTip.trick: **Since a = fg, the braking term is simply v²/2a** — g cancels and is never needed, despite being given. Convert 90 km/h to **25 m/s**, then solve 140 = 25t + 625/7.
examTip.trap: **2.5 s is the standard IRC reaction time** and the most familiar number here — but the question works **backwards from a given SSD** to find the value actually used. Quoting the standard instead of computing is the error being tested.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a downgrade use f − 0.01n**, which lengthens SSD — a real issue where steep descents meet sharp curves. And **SUMMIT curves are a daytime SIGHT problem; VALLEY curves a night-time HEADLIGHT one.**

questions.stem: Resource smoothing is:
options: An optimization and economical utilization of resources
An adjustment of resources without affecting project duration
questions.solution:
**An adjustment of resources that does not affect the project duration.**

**The two resource techniques**, which are constantly confused:

| | **RESOURCE SMOOTHING** | **RESOURCE LEVELLING (allocation)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Constraint** | **TIME takes priority** | **RESOURCE availability is the constraint** |
| **Fixed** | The **project DURATION** | The **RESOURCE limit** |
| **Varies** | The resource profile — evened out | The **project duration** — extended |
| Uses | **FLOAT** on non-critical activities | Reschedules regardless of float |
| Critical path | **Unchanged** | **May change** |

> The source states it precisely: **resource SMOOTHING is used when the time constraint takes priority — complete by the required date while avoiding peaks and troughs. Resource LEVELLING is used when limits on resource availability are the constraint.**

> **Smoothing: fixed time, smoother resources. Levelling: fixed resources, longer time.**

**How smoothing works:**

> Non-critical activities are **shifted within their FLOAT** so that the resource histogram's **peaks are cut and its troughs filled**.

> **Because only float is consumed, the completion date does not move** — which is exactly what the definition states.

> **A CRITICAL activity has ZERO total float**, so smoothing can only touch **non-critical** activities. That is a real constraint on how much smoothing is achievable.

**Why an even resource profile is worth having:**

| Benefit | Note |
|---|---|
| **Avoids hiring and firing** | A peak means recruiting for a few weeks and dismissing after |
| **Better plant utilisation** | Equipment stands idle in the troughs |
| **Steadier supervision and quality** | A team that stays together works better |
| **Lower cost** | Peaks are expensive to service |
| More realistic and achievable | — |

> **The histogram's SHAPE matters as much as its total.** Two schedules with identical total man-days can differ greatly in cost if one is even and the other spiky.

**Why option (a) is the tempting wrong answer:**

> **"Optimization and economical utilization of resources" is true of BOTH techniques** — and of good planning generally. **It is too vague to be a definition.**

> **The defining phrase is "without affecting project duration"**, which is what separates smoothing from levelling.

**Where the float comes from:**

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | **LST − EST** — delay possible **without affecting project completion** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the NEXT activity** |
| Independent float | Without affecting either neighbour |

> And the passes that produce them: **FORWARD pass takes the MAXIMUM** (an activity cannot start until all predecessors finish); **BACKWARD pass takes the MINIMUM** (it must not delay the earliest successor).

**Compare CRASHING, which is a different tool again:**

| | **SMOOTHING** | **CRASHING** |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | **Even the resources** | **SHORTEN the duration** |
| Acts on | **Non-critical** activities | **CRITICAL** activities only |
| Cost | Free — uses existing float | **Extra cost** — added resources |
| Duration | **Unchanged** | **Reduced** |

> **Crashing a non-critical activity achieves nothing at all** — it does not shorten the project, and it costs money. **Only critical activities are worth crashing.**

> **And the critical path must be re-identified after EVERY crashing step**, because shortening one path can make another critical — after which further spending on the original path is wasted.

examTip.trick: The discriminator is **what is held fixed**: **SMOOTHING fixes the DURATION** (time takes priority); **LEVELLING fixes the RESOURCES** (availability is the constraint) and accepts a longer duration.
examTip.trap: Option (a) is **true of both techniques and of good planning generally** — too vague to be a definition. The defining phrase is **"without affecting project duration"**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Smoothing consumes FLOAT, so it can only touch NON-CRITICAL activities** — a critical activity has zero float by definition. **CRASHING is the opposite tool**: it shortens the critical path by spending money.

questions.stem: The estimated time T_e can be found, if T_o, T_p and T_m are given, in PERT activity as:
questions.solution:
**T_e = (T_o + T_p + 4 T_m)/6.**

**The three time estimates:**

| Estimate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **T_o — OPTIMISTIC** | The time if **everything goes well** — the best case |
| **T_m — MOST LIKELY** | The **normal** time, under ordinary conditions |
| **T_p — PESSIMISTIC** | The time if **everything goes wrong** — the worst case |

**Reading the formula:**

> **The weights are 1, 4, 1 and they sum to 6** — which is why the denominator is 6, and it is the quickest check on any offered version.

| Option | Weight sum | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) 1 + 1 + 2 = **4** | ≠ 6 | ✗ |
| (b) 2 + 2 + 4 = **8** | ≠ 6 | ✗ |
| (c) 1 + 4 + 1 = 6 | but the **4 is on T_p**, not T_m | ✗ |
| **(d) 1 + 1 + 4 = 6, with the 4 on T_m** | ✓ | **✓** |

> **Options (a) and (b) fail the sum check instantly.** Option (c) has the right weights but attaches the **4 to the PESSIMISTIC time**, which would make the estimate absurdly gloomy — and it is the trap for anyone who remembers "a 4 somewhere" without remembering where.

**Why the 4 belongs on T_m:**

> **T_e is a weighted average in which the MOST LIKELY time dominates**, while the two extremes pull it slightly. **That is what a sensible estimate should do** — the normal case should carry most of the weight, and the extremes should adjust rather than govern.

> **The distribution is BETA**, which is bounded at both ends and can be **skewed** — and the 1:4:1 weighting is the standard approximation to its mean.

**Why beta suits an activity:**

| Property | Reason it fits |
|---|---|
| **Bounded at both ends** | An activity has a genuine minimum and maximum duration |
| **Can be SKEWED** | **Delays stretch much further than early finishes** |

> **The skew is the realistic part.** An activity estimated at 10 days might finish in 8 at best but could take 30 if things go wrong. **The downside is far longer than the upside**, and a symmetric distribution cannot represent that.

**The companion measures:**

> **Standard deviation σ = (T_p − T_o)/6**
> **Variance = σ²**

> **The 6 here comes from the assumption that the range T_o to T_p spans about six standard deviations (±3σ)**, which covers 99.7% of a normal distribution.

**Making a probability statement — what PERT is FOR:**

> **Project variance = SUM of the variances of the CRITICAL PATH activities only**
> **Z = (Target date − Expected date)/√(project variance)**

> Then read the probability from the standard normal table.

> **VARIANCES ADD; STANDARD DEVIATIONS DO NOT.** Adding standard deviations is the standard error in this calculation, and it substantially overstates the spread.

**Why the project total is NORMAL while activities are BETA:**

> By the **CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM**, the sum of many independent random variables tends to a **normal** distribution whatever the individual distributions are.

> **A path contains many activities, so their total approaches normal** — which is precisely what makes the Z-score calculation valid.

**PERT's hidden optimism**, worth knowing:

> Computing the project variance from the **critical path only** ignores the possibility that a **NEAR-CRITICAL path with HIGH VARIANCE** overruns and becomes critical.

> **PERT therefore tends to be OPTIMISTIC about completion probability.** A path with a slightly shorter expected duration but much greater uncertainty can easily end up governing — and only a **Monte Carlo simulation** across all paths captures that.

examTip.trick: **Check the weight sum: it must be 6.** Options (a) and (b) sum to 4 and 8 and fail instantly, leaving only the question of where the 4 sits.
