examTip.trap: **Option (c) puts the 4 on T_p (pessimistic)** — right weights, wrong place, and absurdly gloomy. The 4 belongs on **T_m**, because the most likely time should dominate.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = (T_p − T_o)/6**, and **VARIANCES ADD — standard deviations do NOT.** Activities follow **BETA** (bounded, skewed); the project total follows **NORMAL** by the central limit theorem.

questions.stem: Efflorescence in brickwork is caused by:
options: Soluble salts in the bricks or mortar crystallising at the surface as water evaporates
Excessive compressive stress in the wall
Rapid drying of the mortar joints
questions.solution:
**Soluble salts crystallising at the surface as water evaporates.**

**The mechanism, in three steps:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Water enters the masonry** — rain, rising damp, or residual construction water |
| **2** | It **DISSOLVES soluble salts** present in the bricks, the mortar, the sand or the ground |
| **3** | The water **migrates to the surface and EVAPORATES**, leaving the salts behind as a **white crystalline deposit** |

> **Efflorescence therefore requires THREE things together: soluble salts, water to dissolve and carry them, and a surface where evaporation occurs.** Remove any one and it stops — which is what makes the remedies obvious once the mechanism is understood.

**Where the salts come from:**

| Source | Salts |
|---|---|
| **Bricks** | Sulphates of sodium, potassium, magnesium and calcium from the clay |
| **Mortar sand** | If unwashed, especially sea sand — **chlorides** |
| **Cement** | Alkalis |
| **Ground water** | Sulphates rising through the foundation |
| Mixing water | If saline |

**Why it matters — and it is more than cosmetic:**

| Effect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Unsightly white staining** | The obvious symptom |
| **CRYPTOFLORESCENCE** | Salts crystallising **WITHIN the pores, below the surface** |
| **SPALLING and disintegration** | **The crystals EXPAND in the pores and break up the brick and plaster** |
| Paint and plaster failure | Repeatedly, however often redecorated |

> **Cryptoflorescence is the damaging form.** Surface efflorescence merely looks bad and can be brushed off; **salts crystallising inside the pores generate expansive pressure that destroys the material from within.**

> **The visible deposit is therefore the less serious symptom of the two** — a wall showing no efflorescence may still be suffering internal salt damage if the evaporation is happening below the surface.

**The remedies, each removing one of the three requirements:**

| Remedy | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Use bricks with LOW soluble salt content** | **The salts** — the first-class brick requirement is "nil to slight" efflorescence |
| **Use washed sand and clean water** | The salts |
| **DPC, and keep the external ground 150 mm below it** | **The water** — stops rising damp |
| **Good rainwater disposal; adequate eaves overhang** | The water |
| **Do not allow saturation during construction** | The water |
| Brush off dry deposits; **do NOT wash** | — |

> **Washing efflorescence off is counter-productive**: the water redissolves the salts and carries them **back into the wall**, where they will re-emerge. **Brushing the dry deposit off removes them permanently.**

> **Efflorescence usually diminishes over the first year or two** as the available salts are exhausted — provided no new water is being supplied. **Persistent efflorescence indicates a continuing water source**, and that source is what must be found and cut off.

**The connection to rising damp:**

> Ground water carries dissolved salts up through the masonry by **capillary action** (**h ∝ 1/pore radius**), and the classic band of efflorescence at the base of a wall is the visible record of it.

> **That is precisely why a DPC is provided**, and why **BRIDGING it** — by raising the external ground or carrying render down across it — reintroduces the problem in a wall that was built correctly.

**Why the other options fail:** compressive stress causes **crushing or buckling**, not salt deposits; rapid drying causes **shrinkage cracking**; and over-burnt bricks are **distorted and brittle**, but their higher firing generally makes them **less** prone to efflorescence, not more.

examTip.trick: Efflorescence needs **three things at once: SALTS, WATER to carry them, and EVAPORATION at a surface.** Remove any one and it stops — which is what makes the remedies obvious.
examTip.trap: **CRYPTOFLORESCENCE — salts crystallising WITHIN the pores — is the damaging form.** The visible white deposit is the less serious symptom; internal crystallisation spalls the brick from inside.
examTip.mnemonic: **Brush the dry deposit off; never WASH it** — washing redissolves the salts and carries them back into the wall. And **persistent efflorescence means a continuing water source** that must be found and cut off.

questions.stem: In the compressive strength test of bricks, the frog is filled with 1:1 cement mortar and cured before testing because:
options: It increases the measured strength of the brick
Otherwise the load would bear on a rim rather than a flat plane, giving a meaningless result
It prevents the brick from absorbing water during the test
It is required to identify the manufacturer
questions.solution:
**Because without it the load would bear on a rim rather than a flat plane, and the result would be meaningless.**

**The problem the procedure solves:**

> **The FROG is the indentation on the surface of a brick** — provided so that mortar keys into it, improving the bond between courses.

> **But in a compression test that indentation is a void.** If the brick were tested as it comes, the platen would bear only on the **narrow rim** around the frog.

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Load concentrated on a small rim area** | Very high local stress |
| **Stress distribution completely non-uniform** | The brick fails prematurely by local crushing |
| **Measured "strength" reflects the rim, not the brick** | **The number means nothing** |

> **Filling the frog restores a flat, full-area bearing surface**, so the load is uniformly distributed and the result actually measures the brick's compressive strength.

**The procedure:**

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Fill the frog with 1:1 cement mortar** |
| **2** | **Cure for 3 days** (some codes: store in damp jute, then immerse 24 hours) |
| **3** | **Immerse in water** before testing |
| **4** | Place between plywood sheets and load at a specified rate |
| **5** | **Strength = failure load ÷ gross area** |

> **The 1:1 mortar is deliberately rich** so that it is **stronger than the brick** — the filling must not become the weak point, or it would be the mortar's strength being measured.

**Why option (a) is wrong in an important way:**

> **The purpose is not to increase the measured strength but to make it MEANINGFUL.**

> A test that gives a falsely low number is as useless as one that gives a falsely high one. **The frog filling removes an artefact of the specimen's shape, so that the property being measured is the material's and not the geometry's.**

> **That principle — eliminating specimen effects so the measured value belongs to the material — runs through all materials testing**, and it is why concrete cubes are capped, why steel specimens have a defined gauge length, and why soil samples are trimmed to a standard size.

**The brick class ladder that this test establishes:**

| Class | Minimum compressive strength | Water absorption |
|---|---|---|
| **First class** | **10.5 N/mm²** | **≤ 20%** |
| **Second class** | **7.0 N/mm²** | ≤ 22% |
| **Third class** | **3.5 N/mm²** | ≤ 25% |

> **Strength falls and absorption rises together down the ladder**, because both measure the same underlying quality: **the degree of VITRIFICATION achieved in firing.**

**The other first-class brick requirements:**

| Test | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Sound** | A **clear metallic RING** when two are struck together |
| **Scratch** | No impression from a fingernail |
| **Drop test** | Does not break when dropped flat from about **1 m** |
| **Fracture** | Uniform, compact, homogeneous |
| **Efflorescence** | **Nil to slight** |
| Shape and colour | Sharp edges, true right angles, uniform deep red |

> **The ring test is a genuine field test, not folklore**: a well-fired brick is dense and rings; an under-fired one is porous and gives a dull thud. **It costs nothing and can be done on site by anyone.**

**Why bricks are soaked before laying** — a related procedure with a different reason:

> A dry brick would **absorb water from the mortar**, leaving it too dry to hydrate properly and producing a weak joint. **Soaking prevents that**, and also washes off dust so the bond can form.

> **But over-soaking is also wrong** — a saturated brick will not absorb any water and the mortar cannot key into it. **The brick should be damp, not dripping.**

examTip.trick: **The frog is a VOID.** Without filling, the platen bears on a narrow rim, the stress is wildly non-uniform, and the brick fails early — measuring the geometry, not the material.
examTip.trap: The purpose is **not to raise the number but to make it MEANINGFUL.** A falsely low result is as useless as a falsely high one — the procedure removes a specimen-shape artefact.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strength falls and absorption rises together down the class ladder (10.5/7/3.5 and 20/22/25%)** — both measure the same thing: how well the brick was **vitrified** in firing.

questions.stem: In a thin cylindrical shell under internal pressure, the ratio of hoop stress to longitudinal stress is:
questions.solution:
**2 : 1 — the hoop stress is TWICE the longitudinal stress.**

**The two stresses:**

> **Hoop (circumferential) stress: σ_h = pd/(2t)**
> **Longitudinal (axial) stress: σ_l = pd/(4t)**

> **Ratio σ_h : σ_l = 2 : 1** ✓

**Where each comes from:**

| Stress | Derivation |
|---|---|
| **HOOP** | Cut the cylinder **along its length**. Bursting force **p × d × L** is resisted by **two** wall thicknesses: **σ_h × 2tL**. Hence **σ_h = pd/2t** |
| **LONGITUDINAL** | Cut **across** the cylinder. End force **p × πd²/4** is resisted by the **annular area πdt**. Hence **σ_l = pd/4t** |

> **The hoop stress is larger because the longitudinal cut has less resisting material relative to the force it must carry** — a cut along the length exposes only **2tL**, while the circumferential cut exposes the whole perimeter **πdt**.

**The consequence that makes this worth knowing:**

> **A thin cylinder under internal pressure FAILS BY SPLITTING ALONG ITS LENGTH**, not by tearing across — because the hoop stress reaches the limit first.

> **That is why a burst pipe splits lengthwise**, why a pressure vessel's **longitudinal weld is the critical one**, and why **circumferential reinforcement matters more than longitudinal** in a pressurised pipe.

> **It is also why a sausage splits along its length when cooked** — the same mechanics, and a memorable check on which stress is larger.

**Design consequences:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Penstock wall thickness** | **t = pD/(2σ_permissible)** — from the **hoop** stress, plus a corrosion allowance |
| **Pressure vessel welds** | The **longitudinal seam** carries the hoop stress and is designed for the full value; **circumferential seams carry only half** |
| **Water main design** | Hoop stress governs |
| Boiler shells | Longitudinal joint efficiency is the critical parameter |

> **In a welded pressure vessel the longitudinal joint is often given a higher joint efficiency requirement than the circumferential one**, precisely because it carries twice the stress.

**The related strains:**

> **Hoop strain ε_h = (pd/2tE)(1 − μ/2)**
> **Longitudinal strain ε_l = (pd/2tE)(1/2 − μ)**
> **Volumetric strain ε_v = (pd/2tE)(5/2 − 2μ)**

**Compare a thin SPHERE:**

> **σ = pd/(4t) in ALL directions** — a sphere has no preferred direction, so both principal stresses are equal and each is **half** the cylinder's hoop stress.

> **That is why a sphere is the most efficient pressure vessel shape**, and why high-pressure gas storage uses spheres despite their higher fabrication cost. **For the same pressure and diameter, a sphere needs half the wall thickness of a cylinder.**

**The "thin" assumption:**

> Valid when **d/t > about 20** (equivalently t < d/20). The stress is then taken as **uniform through the thickness**.

> **For a THICK cylinder the stress varies radially** and **LAMÉ's equations** are required — the hoop stress is then **greatest at the inner surface**, which is where a thick cylinder starts to fail.

**And the practical note on penstocks:** the wall thickness is often governed **not by the static head but by WATER HAMMER** — **Δp = ρcΔV** on sudden gate closure can multiply the design pressure — which is why the **governor closure timing and the penstock design are settled together**, against the **2L/c** criterion.

examTip.trick: **σ_h = pd/2t, σ_l = pd/4t** — the hoop stress is twice, because a **longitudinal cut exposes only 2tL** of material while a circumferential cut exposes the whole perimeter **πdt**.
examTip.trap: The consequence is physical, not just numerical: **a pressurised cylinder SPLITS ALONG ITS LENGTH**, because the hoop stress reaches the limit first. A burst pipe never tears across.
examTip.mnemonic: **A SPHERE has pd/4t in all directions — half the cylinder's hoop stress**, so it needs half the wall thickness. That is why high-pressure gas storage is spherical despite the fabrication cost.

questions.stem: In the analysis of a plane truss, a member carrying zero force can often be identified when:
options: The member is the longest in the truss
Two non-collinear members meet at an unloaded joint
The member lies on the centre line of the truss
questions.solution:
**When two non-collinear members meet at an unloaded joint — both carry zero force.**

**The zero-force member rules**, which are worth knowing because they can eliminate a large fraction of a truss's members before any calculation:

| Rule | Condition | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **TWO non-collinear members** at a joint, **no external load or reaction** | **BOTH are zero-force** |
| **2** | **THREE members** at a joint, **two COLLINEAR**, no external load | **The THIRD (non-collinear) member is zero-force** |
| **3** | Two members at a joint with a load **along one of them** | The other is zero-force |

**Why rule 1 works:**

> At the joint, **ΣF must be zero in every direction.** With only two non-collinear members and no applied load, resolve **perpendicular to one member**: only the other member has a component in that direction, so **its force must be zero**. Then resolve again and the first member is zero too.

> **The argument is pure equilibrium at a single joint** — no analysis of the whole truss is needed.

**Why rule 2 works:**

> The two collinear members lie along one line. **Resolving PERPENDICULAR to that line, only the third member contributes** — so its force must be zero.

> The two collinear members then simply pass the same force through the joint.

**Why zero-force members exist at all — they are not useless:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent BUCKLING of long compression members** | By reducing the unbraced length |
| **Provide stability** under a **different load case** | A member idle under one loading may be vital under another |
| **Carry load during erection** | — |
| Maintain the truss's geometry | — |

> **A member with zero force under ONE load case is not redundant.** Removing it can leave the truss unstable, or leave a compression member unbraced over twice the length — **and buckling capacity falls as the SQUARE of the length.**

> **That is the essential caution**: zero force is a property of the loading, not of the member.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

> **Length, orientation and position have NOTHING to do with the force in a member.** Force depends on **equilibrium at the joints**, and a vertical member can be the most heavily loaded in the truss.

> **All three wrong options appeal to geometry rather than to equilibrium**, which is the category error being tested.

**The truss assumptions** these rules rest on:

| Assumption | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Members joined by frictionless PINS** | No moments transmitted |
| **Loads applied ONLY at the joints** | **Members carry only AXIAL force** |
| Members are straight and weightless | — |

> **A load applied BETWEEN joints causes BENDING in the member**, which the truss idealisation does not account for — which is why purlins are placed at panel points and why a load hung mid-member is a detailing error.

**Determinacy:**

> **D_s = m + r − 2j** for a plane truss.

| D_s | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **= 0** | **Determinate** |
| **> 0** | Indeterminate |
| **< 0** | **A MECHANISM — unstable** |

> **A SIMPLE truss (m = 2j − 3) is built from a base triangle by adding two members and one joint at a time** — and it can always be solved by the **method of joints** working outward from a support.

> **But the count checks DEGREE, not STABILITY**: a truss can satisfy m = 2j − 3 and still be a mechanism if its geometry is wrong — for instance if three members meeting a body are **parallel or concurrent**.

examTip.trick: Resolve **perpendicular to one member** at the joint: only the other has a component in that direction, so it must be zero. **Pure joint equilibrium — no whole-truss analysis needed.**
examTip.trap: **All three wrong options appeal to GEOMETRY (length, orientation, position)**, which has nothing to do with member force. Force comes from **equilibrium**, and a vertical member can be the most heavily loaded.
examTip.mnemonic: **A zero-force member is NOT useless** — it braces compression members against buckling (capacity falls as the **square** of unbraced length) and may be vital under a different load case. Zero force is a property of the **loading**.

questions.stem: In limit state design, the partial safety factor for concrete (1.5) is greater than that for steel (1.15) because:
options: Concrete strength is far more variable, being site-made and dependent on workmanship
Steel is used in smaller quantities
questions.solution:
**Because concrete's strength is far more variable** than steel's.

**The principle behind partial safety factors:**

> **Each quantity is factored ACCORDING TO HOW WELL IT IS KNOWN.** Loads are factored **UP**, strengths **DOWN**, and the size of each factor reflects the **uncertainty** in that particular quantity.

> **That is the whole idea of limit state design, and it is more rational than working stress design's single global factor**, which treated every uncertainty alike.

**Why concrete is more variable:**

| Steel | Concrete |
|---|---|
| **Made in a FACTORY** under controlled conditions | **Made ON SITE**, often in variable conditions |
| Composition and rolling controlled | **Depends on aggregate grading, moisture, batching accuracy** |
| **Tested and certified at the mill** | **Depends on mixing, placing, compaction and CURING** |
| Properties consistent batch to batch | **Strength varies with workmanship** |
| No curing required | **Curing is essential and frequently neglected** |

> **Concrete is the only major structural material manufactured at the point of use, by whoever happens to be there.** Steel arrives with a mill certificate; concrete's strength is created by the care taken on the day.

> **That difference in controllability is exactly what the two factors encode.**

**The design strengths that result:**

| Material | γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Concrete** | **1.5** | **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.447 f_ck** |
| **Steel** | **1.15** | **0.87 f_y** |

> **The additional 0.67 applied to concrete** accounts for the difference between the **cube strength** and the strength of concrete in a real flexural member under **sustained** load — a separate effect from variability, and worth keeping distinct.

**The statistical expression of the same idea:**

> **Characteristic strength = the value below which not more than 5% of results fall** — the **5th percentile**.

> **f_target = f_ck + 1.65 s**, where **s** is the standard deviation and 1.65 the standard normal deviate for 5%.

| Producer | s | Target for M25 |
|---|---|---|
| **Well-controlled plant** | **3 MPa** | **30 MPa** |
| **Poor site control** | **6 MPa** | **35 MPa** |

> **The poorly-controlled producer must aim nearly 5 MPa higher — and pay for the extra cement — to achieve the same characteristic strength.**

> **Consistency is worth money, literally.** That is the argument for quality control: it is not merely a guard against failure but a **direct saving in materials**.

**The load factors, for completeness:**

| Combination | Factors |
|---|---|
| **DL + LL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL** |
| **DL + WL/EL** | **1.5 DL + 1.5 WL**, or **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** when DL **stabilises** |
| **DL + LL + WL** | **1.2 (DL + LL + WL)** |

> The **1.2** in the three-load case reflects the **improbability** of full live load and full wind occurring together at their design values — again, a factor sized to the uncertainty.

> **And the 0.9 DL case is the one most often forgotten**: where dead load **RESISTS** overturning, sliding or uplift, it is factored **DOWN**, because relying on a load that might be smaller than estimated is unsafe. **Applying 1.5 there conceals the failure entirely.**

**Serviceability uses UNFACTORED loads** (1.0 DL + 1.0 LL), because deflection and cracking are checked against **what the structure will actually experience**, not against a hypothetical overload.

examTip.trick: **Each quantity is factored by how well it is KNOWN.** Concrete is the only major structural material **made at the point of use by whoever is there**; steel arrives with a mill certificate.
examTip.trap: The extra **0.67 on concrete is a SEPARATE effect** — the difference between cube strength and strength in a real member under sustained load. Keep it distinct from the 1.5 variability factor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Consistency is worth money**: a well-controlled plant (s = 3) targets 30 MPa for M25; a poor site (s = 6) must target 35 and buy the extra cement. Quality control is a **material saving**, not just a safeguard.

questions.stem: Shear reinforcement in a reinforced concrete beam is provided mainly to:
options: Carry the diagonal tension that concrete cannot resist
questions.solution:
**To carry the diagonal tension that concrete cannot resist.**

**Why shear failure is really a TENSION failure:**

> Pure shear at a point is equivalent to **equal tension and compression on planes at 45°**. In a beam, the shear combines with the flexural stress to produce **principal tensile stress on inclined planes**.

> **Concrete's tensile strength is only 10–15% of its compressive strength**, so it cracks along those planes — producing the characteristic **DIAGONAL cracks near the supports**, inclined at roughly **45°**.

> **The reinforcement's job is to cross those cracks and carry the tension across them.** It is not resisting "shear" as such; it is resisting the diagonal tension that shear produces.

> **That is why cracks open PERPENDICULAR to the maximum principal tension**, and why **vertical stirrups work** — they cross a 45° crack effectively.

**The forms shear reinforcement takes:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Vertical STIRRUPS** | **The standard** — simple to fix, effective, and they also hold the main bars in position |
| **Bent-up bars** | Main bars bent up at 45° near the supports — historically common |
| Inclined stirrups | More efficient in principle, awkward in practice |

> **IS 456 requires that bent-up bars alone must not carry more than half the shear** — the rest must come from stirrups, because bent-up bars are effective only over a limited region.

**The design procedure:**

| Step | Check |
|---|---|
| **1** | **τ_v = V_u/(bd)** — nominal shear stress |
| **2** | Compare with **τ_c**, the concrete's capacity (depends on **grade and percentage of tension steel**) |
| **3** | If **τ_v < τ_c**: provide **MINIMUM** stirrups only |
| **4** | If **τ_v > τ_c**: design stirrups for the **excess (V_u − τ_c b d)** |
| **5** | If **τ_v > τ_c,max**: **the SECTION IS INADEQUATE — enlarge it** |

> **Step 5 is the critical one.** Above **τ_c,max** the concrete itself would fail by **crushing of the diagonal compression strut**, and **no amount of stirrup steel can prevent that.**

> **More shear reinforcement cannot fix an undersized section** — the depth must increase. That is a genuine and important limit, and it is the shear equivalent of the over-reinforced beam problem in flexure.

**Why τ_c depends on the TENSION steel percentage** — a detail worth understanding:

> More tension steel means a **deeper neutral axis and a larger uncracked compression zone**, plus better **aggregate interlock** across cracks and more **dowel action** from the bars themselves. **All three raise the concrete's own shear capacity.**

**Minimum shear reinforcement, and why it is required even when not needed by calculation:**

> **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevents SUDDEN diagonal tension failure** | Shear failure without stirrups is **brittle and gives no warning** |
| Holds the main bars in position | During concreting |
| Confines the concrete | Modest but real benefit |
| Resists unforeseen effects | Torsion, support settlement |

> **Shear failure is BRITTLE — it occurs suddenly, with little deflection and no warning**, unlike flexural failure in an under-reinforced beam, which announces itself through large deflections and wide cracks.

> **That is precisely why minimum stirrups are mandatory**: the failure they prevent is the one that gives no opportunity to evacuate.

**Maximum stirrup spacing:** the **least of 0.75d, 300 mm**, or the spacing required by calculation — chosen so that **any potential 45° crack is crossed by at least one stirrup.**

> **A crack that passes between two widely spaced stirrups is uncrossed and unrestrained**, which is the geometric reason behind the 0.75d limit.

**And the detailing consequence** of shear peaking at the supports: **stirrups are closely spaced near the supports and widely spaced at midspan** — the exact opposite of the main flexural steel, which is fullest at midspan and curtailed toward the ends.

examTip.trick: **Shear failure is really a TENSION failure** — shear produces principal tension on 45° planes, and concrete cracks there because its tensile strength is only 10–15% of its compressive. Stirrups cross those cracks.
examTip.trap: **Above τ_c,max the section is INADEQUATE and no amount of stirrup steel helps** — the concrete strut itself crushes. More reinforcement cannot fix an undersized beam; the depth must increase.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear failure is BRITTLE — sudden, with no warning** — which is exactly why minimum stirrups are mandatory even when calculation says none are needed. And spacing ≤ **0.75d** so every 45° crack is crossed.

questions.stem: The main reason for providing a minimum percentage of reinforcement in a concrete member is to:
options: Reduce the cost of the member
Ensure the member does not fail suddenly on first cracking, and to control shrinkage and temperature cracks
Allow a smaller concrete section to be used
questions.solution:
**To ensure the member does not fail suddenly on first cracking, and to control shrinkage and temperature cracking.**

**The first reason — avoiding sudden failure at first crack:**

> Before cracking, the **concrete itself carries the tension**. At the instant the section cracks, **all that tension transfers abruptly to the steel.**

> **If there is too little steel, it cannot carry what the concrete was carrying — and it yields or fractures immediately.**

| Steel provided | Behaviour at first crack |
|---|---|
| **Below the minimum** | **Steel fails the moment the concrete cracks — SUDDEN, brittle collapse with no warning** |
| **At or above the minimum** | **Steel carries the transferred force; the member cracks but continues to carry load, deflecting visibly** |

> **The minimum steel is therefore set so that the member's CRACKED capacity exceeds its CRACKING moment.**

> **A member with too little steel is more dangerous than an unreinforced one**, because it looks like a reinforced member and is designed as one, but fails as suddenly as plain concrete.

**The second reason — shrinkage and temperature:**

> **Concrete shrinks as it dries and moves with temperature.** Where that movement is restrained — and it almost always is, by adjacent members, foundations or friction — **tensile stresses develop.**

> **Minimum reinforcement does not prevent cracking; it distributes it** — turning what would be **a few wide cracks into many fine, harmless ones.**

> **That distinction is the essential point**: crack **WIDTH**, not crack existence, is what matters for durability. Reinforced concrete is designed on the assumption that it **is cracked in tension**.

**The IS 456 minimum values:**

| Member | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **Beam (tension steel)** | **A_s/(bd) = 0.85/f_y** |
| **Slab — main steel** | **0.12%** of gross area (Fe 415), **0.15%** (Fe 250) |
| **Slab — distribution steel** | **0.12%** of gross area |
| **Column** | **0.8%** of gross area |
| Maximum (beam) | 4% |

> **Note the column minimum (0.8%) is much higher**, and for a different reason again: it guards against **accidental eccentricity and bending**, and provides ductility in a member whose failure would be catastrophic.

**DISTRIBUTION steel in a one-way slab** illustrates the principle clearly:

> It carries **no calculated load**, yet it is mandatory. Its jobs are:

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Distribute concentrated loads** laterally | So a point load is shared by a width of slab |
| **Resist shrinkage and temperature stresses** | The main reason |
| **Hold the main bars in position** | During concreting |

> **A member can require reinforcement that no calculation demands** — which is exactly why minimum percentages exist as code requirements rather than as design outputs.

**Why the wrong options fail:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| Reduce cost | Minimum steel **adds** cost |
| Increase stiffness | Steel's contribution to stiffness before cracking is small; concrete provides it |
| Allow a smaller section | The **maximum** steel percentage is what limits how small a section can be, not the minimum |

**And the maximum limit, for contrast:**

> **4% in a beam** — a **practical** limit on congestion, not a strength one. **Above it the concrete cannot be placed and compacted around the bars**, and the section becomes unbuildable.

> **Bar spacing and cover requirements often bind before the 4% figure does**, which is why heavily reinforced sections are usually limited by detailing rather than by the percentage.

examTip.trick: At first crack, **all the tension transfers abruptly from concrete to steel.** Too little steel and it fails immediately — so the minimum ensures the **cracked capacity exceeds the cracking moment**.
examTip.trap: **A member with too little steel is MORE dangerous than an unreinforced one** — it is designed and treated as reinforced but fails as suddenly as plain concrete, with no warning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum steel does not prevent cracking — it DISTRIBUTES it**, turning a few wide cracks into many fine ones. Crack **WIDTH** is what matters (0.3 mm normally), not crack existence.

questions.stem: The slenderness ratio of a steel compression member is limited by the code primarily to:
options: Reduce the weight of the member
Prevent excessive lateral deflection and vibration, and avoid damage during handling and erection
questions.solution:
**To prevent excessive lateral deflection and vibration, and to avoid damage during handling and erection.**

**The limits (IS 800):**

| Member | Maximum λ |
|---|---|
| **Carrying loads resulting from dead and imposed loads** | **180** |
| **Compression member subject to reversal of stress** (wind or seismic) | **180** |
| **Member normally acting as a tie but subject to reversal under wind** | **250** |
| **TENSION member** (other than a pre-tensioned one) | **400** |

> **The limits are far more generous for tension members** — a tie cannot buckle, so its limit exists only for handling, sag and vibration.

**Why the limits exist — three practical reasons:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Handling and erection damage** | **A very slender member BENDS under its own weight when lifted** — it may be permanently deformed before it is ever loaded |
| **Vibration** | A slender member has a **low natural frequency** and can resonate under wind or machinery |
| **Excessive lateral deflection** | Visually alarming and can damage attached finishes |

> **The handling reason is the most practical and the most often overlooked.** A member that is perfectly adequate once in place can be ruined by being lifted at one point — and a bent compression member has a large initial imperfection, which reduces its capacity substantially.

**Why the limit is NOT primarily about strength:**

> **The buckling capacity is already accounted for by the design formulae** — Euler, Rankine, or the code's buckling curves. **A member at λ = 300 would simply have a very low capacity, correctly computed.**

> **The slenderness limit is a SERVICEABILITY and PRACTICALITY provision, not a strength one** — which is exactly what the question tests. **Option (d) has it backwards: limiting slenderness does not increase capacity, it just prevents members so slender as to be unusable.**

**The underlying buckling relations:**

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²** and **λ = L_e/r**, with **r = √(I/A)** taken about the **MINIMUM** axis.

| End conditions | L_e |
|---|---|
| **Both ends FIXED** | **0.5 L** |
| One fixed, one pinned | 0.707 L |
| **Both ends PINNED** | **1.0 L** |
| **One fixed, one FREE** | **2.0 L** |

> **A sixteen-fold range in capacity** across those four cases — and **codes use higher values than the theory** (0.65 L rather than 0.5 L for fixed–fixed), because **a real fixed end always rotates a little.**

**Where Euler's formula stops working:**

| Slenderness | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Low λ** | **CRUSHING** — the member squashes rather than buckles |
| **Intermediate λ** | **INELASTIC buckling — Euler OVERESTIMATES**, because yielding intervenes |
| **High λ (> ~100 in steel)** | Euler's elastic formula applies |

> **RANKINE's formula — 1/P = 1/P_crushing + 1/P_Euler — bridges both ends**, and is the safer general expression because **Euler alone is unsafe for intermediate slenderness**, which is where most real columns sit.

**And the practical lever:**

> **Bracing a column at midheight HALVES L and QUADRUPLES the buckling capacity** — almost always cheaper than enlarging the section.

> **Which is also why a TUBE is the ideal strut**: it has a **large radius of gyration in EVERY direction**, so it has no weak axis. A solid bar of the same area buckles at a fraction of the load, because its material sits near the centroid where it contributes little to I.

examTip.trick: **The slenderness limit is a SERVICEABILITY and PRACTICALITY provision, not a strength one** — buckling capacity is already handled by the design formulae. A very slender member is simply unusable.
examTip.trap: **The limits are far more generous for TENSION members (400) than compression (180)** — a tie cannot buckle, so its limit exists only for sag, vibration and handling.
examTip.mnemonic: **A slender member BENDS under its own weight when lifted** — ruined before it is ever loaded. And bracing at midheight **halves L and quadruples capacity**, almost always cheaper than a bigger section.

questions.stem: The main purpose of a service reservoir in a water supply system is to:
options: Balance the variable hourly demand against the steady rate of supply from the treatment works
Provide additional treatment to the water
Increase the pressure at the treatment works
Remove residual turbidity by further settlement
questions.solution:
**To balance the variable hourly demand against the steady supply from the treatment works.**

**The problem it solves:**

| Side | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Treatment works and pumping** | Most economical at a **STEADY rate**, running continuously |
| **Consumer demand** | **Highly VARIABLE** — peaks morning and evening, minimal at night |

> **The service reservoir absorbs that mismatch**: it **fills at night** when supply exceeds demand, and **empties during the peak hours** when demand exceeds supply.

> **Without it, the treatment works and every main would have to be sized for the PEAK HOUR demand — about 2.7 times the average.** That would mean plant standing largely idle most of the day, at nearly three times the necessary capital cost.

**The peak factors that create the problem:**

| Factor | Value |
|---|---|
| **Maximum daily demand** | **1.8 × average** |
| **Maximum hourly demand** | **1.5 × maximum daily** |
| **Peak hour** | **≈ 2.7 × average** |

> **The factors COMPOUND**, which is why the peak is so far above the mean — and why balancing storage is so valuable.

**The four components of service reservoir capacity:**

| Component | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **BALANCING (equalising) storage** | **The main component** — typically **one third to one half of the daily demand** |
| **BREAKDOWN (emergency) storage** | Supply during a **plant or pumping failure** — often 4 to 8 hours' demand |
| **FIRE storage** | A reserve for fire fighting |
| Dead storage | Below the outlet |

> **The balancing component is determined from a MASS CURVE** — cumulative supply plotted against cumulative demand over a day, with the **maximum vertical separation** giving the required storage. **It is the same Rippl construction used for sizing an impounding reservoir**, applied over a day instead of a year.

**The other functions a service reservoir performs:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maintains PRESSURE** in the distribution system | An elevated reservoir sets the hydraulic grade line |
| **Allows pumping at a uniform rate** | Cheaper plant, and off-peak electricity tariffs |
| **Provides emergency supply** | During breakdown or maintenance |
| Absorbs demand fluctuation | The main purpose |

> **Note that it maintains pressure in the DISTRIBUTION system, not at the treatment works** — which is why option (c) is wrong. **An elevated reservoir works by gravity on the network downstream of it.**

**Why options (b) and (d) are wrong, and instructively so:**

> **A service reservoir is NOT a treatment unit.** Water entering it is already treated and disinfected.

> **Storage can actually DEGRADE water quality** rather than improve it:

| Risk | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Chlorine residual DECAYS** with time | Long detention loses the protection |
| **Stagnation in dead zones** | Poor inlet/outlet arrangement creates unmixed corners |
| Contamination ingress | Through vents, covers, overflow pipes |
| Temperature rise | Encourages bacterial regrowth |

> **Which is why a service reservoir must be COVERED, properly ventilated with screened vents, regularly inspected and cleaned, and arranged so the inlet and outlet promote CIRCULATION rather than short-circuiting.**

> **A reservoir that short-circuits has stagnant corners where the residual dies** — the same problem as a dead end in the distribution network, and with the same consequence.

**Position in the system:** ideally at a **high point within or near the distribution area**, so it can supply by gravity and float on the system — filling when pressure is high and discharging when it falls, automatically and without control valves.

> **A reservoir at the far end of the network from the works is particularly valuable**, because it supplies the remote area during peak hours from the near side rather than through the whole length of main.

examTip.trick: **Supply is steady, demand is peaky** — the reservoir absorbs the mismatch, filling at night and emptying at the peak. Without it, everything upstream must be sized for **2.7 × average**.
examTip.trap: **A service reservoir is NOT a treatment unit** — and storage can **degrade** quality: chlorine residual decays, dead zones stagnate. Hence covered, ventilated, and arranged for **circulation not short-circuiting**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Balancing storage from a MASS CURVE** — the same Rippl construction as for an impounding reservoir, applied over a day instead of a year. Typically **⅓ to ½ of the daily demand**.

questions.stem: In an Initial Environmental Examination (IEE), which of the following is NOT required?
options: A formal scoping exercise producing Terms of Reference
questions.solution:
**A formal scoping exercise producing Terms of Reference** — this is required for an **EIA**, not for an IEE.

**IEE versus EIA:**

| | **IEE** | **EIA** |
|---|---|---|
| **For** | **SMALLER** projects with limited impacts | **LARGE or SENSITIVE** projects |
| **SCOPING required?** | **NO** | **YES — produces the Terms of Reference** |
| **Public hearing** | **Usually not required** | **REQUIRED** |
| **Depth** | **Preliminary** | **Full and detailed** |
| Duration and cost | Short, low | Long, high |
| Approving authority | Usually the concerned ministry | Higher-level (Ministry of Environment) |

> **Scoping is the step that distinguishes them.** An EIA's scope is not obvious in advance — it must be **determined, agreed and documented as Terms of Reference** before the study begins.

> **An IEE is a standard-format preliminary examination**, so there is nothing to scope: the content is known in advance.

**What an IEE DOES require** — the other three options:

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Project description** | What is proposed, where and how |
| **Baseline environment** | The existing physical, biological and socio-economic conditions |
| **Identification of likely impacts** | And their significance |
| **Mitigation measures** | How adverse impacts will be reduced |
| Environmental management plan | Who does what |
| Monitoring | — |

> **All three wrong options are genuine IEE requirements**, which is what makes this a real test rather than a guess.

**The screening decision — how the level is chosen:**

| Basis | Note |
|---|---|
| **Project type and SIZE** | Thresholds are set in schedules to the Regulations |
| **LOCATION** | **A project in a PROTECTED AREA requires an EIA regardless of size** |
| Sensitivity of the receiving environment | — |

> **The location override is important**: a small project in a national park, a wetland or a culturally significant site attracts a full EIA even though its scale would otherwise suggest an IEE. **Sensitivity trumps size.**

> **And an IEE can escalate**: if it reveals significant adverse impacts, the outcome may be a requirement to proceed to a full EIA.

**The EIA process, for contrast:**

> **SCREENING → SCOPING → EIA study → PUBLIC HEARING → review and CLEARANCE → MONITORING**

| Step | Decides |
|---|---|
| **Screening** | **WHETHER** an assessment is needed, and **at what level** |
| **Scoping** | **WHAT** the study must cover — the **Terms of Reference** |
| Study | The assessment itself |
| **Public hearing** | Affected people comment on the **findings** |
| Clearance | Approval, with conditions |
| **MONITORING** | Verifies the mitigation is actually implemented |

> **The order is forced by logic**: you cannot scope a study you have not decided to do, and the public cannot comment on findings that do not yet exist.

**The MITIGATION HIERARCHY**, which applies to both levels:

> **AVOID → MINIMISE → MITIGATE → COMPENSATE**, in that order of preference.

> **Avoidance is always better than compensation** — rerouting an alignment away from a forest costs less and achieves more than replanting elsewhere afterwards. **A great deal of poor practice consists of jumping straight to compensation**, because it is easy to quantify and easy to promise.

**And the step most often neglected in both:**

> **MONITORING.** An assessment not followed by monitoring and enforcement is **a document, not a safeguard**.

> **That is where environmental assessment most often fails in practice** — not in the prediction, but in whether the promised mitigation is ever built, operated and verified.

examTip.trick: **SCOPING is what distinguishes an EIA from an IEE.** An EIA's scope must be determined and agreed as **Terms of Reference**; an IEE follows a standard format, so there is nothing to scope.
examTip.trap: **All three wrong options are genuine IEE requirements** — project description, impact identification and mitigation are needed at both levels. Only the formal scoping step is EIA-only.
examTip.mnemonic: **A project in a PROTECTED AREA needs a full EIA regardless of size** — sensitivity trumps scale. And an IEE can **escalate** to an EIA if it finds significant adverse impacts.

questions.stem: The 'duty' of water in irrigation is best described as:
options: The area of land irrigated per unit discharge running continuously through the base period
The total depth of water supplied to a crop over its base period
The volume of water consumed by a crop each day
The efficiency with which water is conveyed through a canal
questions.solution:
**The area of land irrigated per unit discharge running continuously through the base period** — expressed in **hectares per cumec**.

**The three linked quantities:**

| Term | Meaning | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **DUTY (D)** | **Area irrigated per cumec** running continuously through the base period | **hectares/cumec** |
| **DELTA (Δ)** | **Total DEPTH of water** supplied over the base period | **metres or cm** |
| **BASE PERIOD (B)** | The period between the **first and last watering** of a crop | **days** |

> **Option (b) defines DELTA, not duty** — and it is the well-made distractor, since the two are inseparable in every irrigation calculation.

**The relation between them:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B / D** metres, with **B in days** and **D in hectares per cumec**

> **The 8.64 is simply 86 400 seconds per day ÷ 10 000 m² per hectare** — knowing where it comes from means never mis-remembering it.

**The relation is INVERSE, and this is the point candidates most often get backwards:**

> **A HIGH duty means LESS water per hectare.**

| Duty | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **High** | One cumec serves a **large area** → **little water per hectare** → **EFFICIENT** |
| **Low** | One cumec serves a small area → much water per hectare → thirsty crop or wasteful system |

> **A high duty is a sign of efficiency, not of thirst** — which reads backwards to most people, and is exactly why the definition matters.

**Why duty varies:**

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **Crop type** | A rice crop has a **low** duty; millet a high one |
| **Soil** | A sandy soil loses more to percolation → lower duty |
| **Climate** | Hot and dry → more evapotranspiration → lower duty |
| **Method of application** | **Drip raises duty greatly** over flood irrigation |
| **CANAL LINING** | **Raises duty** by cutting seepage losses |
| **Where it is measured** | **Duty at the FIELD is higher than duty at the canal HEAD** |

> **That last row is essential**: duty must always be quoted **with the point at which it is measured**, because losses accumulate between the head and the field.

> **Duty at the head < duty at the outlet < duty at the field** — since the same discharge serves progressively less area as losses mount.

**Typical deltas, for scale:**

| Crop | Delta |
|---|---|
| **Rice** | **1200 – 2000 mm** |
| Sugarcane | 1500 – 2000 mm |
| **Wheat** | **350 – 400 mm** |
| **Millet / maize** | **300 – 500 mm** |

**How duty enters canal design:**

> **Q = (Duty at the canal outlet, including all losses) × CCA ÷ (time factor × capacity factor)**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CCA** | **Culturable command area** — land that **can actually be irrigated** |
| **Time factor** | Actual operating period ÷ crop period |
| **Capacity factor** | Mean supply ÷ full designed capacity |

> **Both factors are less than 1, and both INCREASE the required capacity.**

**And the peak, not the average, governs:**

> The canal must carry the **maximum demand of all crops requiring water at any one time** — described by the **KOR DEPTH** (water needed at the crop's critical growth stage) over the **KOR PERIOD**.

> **Outlet discharge factor = 8.64 B/Δ** using the kor values gives the peak capacity directly.

**The efficiency chain that determines what must actually be supplied:**

> **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application** — and **efficiencies MULTIPLY, never average.**

> Two stages at 70% give **49%**, so the water delivered at the canal head can be **1.5 to 2 times** what the crop consumes. **Sizing on the crop's own requirement guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) defines DELTA — the DEPTH of water — not duty, which is an AREA per cumec.** The two are inseparable in calculations, which is why the distractor works.
examTip.trick: **Δ = 8.64 B/D**, where **8.64 = 86 400 s/day ÷ 10 000 m²/ha**. Knowing the origin of the constant means never mis-remembering it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A HIGH duty means LESS water per hectare — it signals EFFICIENCY, not thirst.** And always state **where** the duty is measured: duty at the field exceeds duty at the canal head.

questions.stem: A canal outlet (module) is said to be 'flexible' when:
options: Its discharge is independent of the water levels in both the distributary and the watercourse
Its discharge varies only with the watercourse level
Its discharge varies with the water level in the distributary
It can be physically moved to another location
questions.solution:
**When its discharge varies with the water level in the distributary.**

**The three types of canal outlet:**

| Type | Discharge depends on |
|---|---|
| **NON-MODULAR** | **BOTH the distributary AND the watercourse levels** — i.e. on the **difference** between them |
| **SEMI-MODULE (FLEXIBLE)** | **ONLY the DISTRIBUTARY level** — independent of the watercourse |
| **RIGID MODULE** | **NEITHER — the discharge is CONSTANT** within a working range |

> **Option (a) describes a RIGID MODULE**, which is the deliberate near-miss — and the more advanced device, which is why it is tempting.

**The essential distinction:**

| Outlet | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Non-modular** | A simple **submerged pipe**. If the cultivator raises the watercourse level, the discharge **falls** — so the supply can be interfered with |
| **FLEXIBLE (semi-module)** | Flow passes through **critical or free flow**, so **downstream conditions cannot propagate upstream** |
| **Rigid module** | A **mechanical arrangement (roller, baffle)** holds the discharge constant despite level changes |

> **The semi-module works on exactly the principle from open channel flow: in SUPERCRITICAL or FREE flow, disturbances cannot travel upstream**, so the watercourse level has no influence on the discharge.

> **That is why a free-falling or critical-flow outlet is independent of tailwater** — the same reason a broad-crested weir works as a discharge meter.

**Why the distinction matters practically — EQUITY:**

> **A canal outlet is where the public system meets the individual cultivator**, and it is the point at which water is either distributed fairly or not.

| Problem | Which outlet |
|---|---|
| **A cultivator can raise the watercourse level and reduce a neighbour's supply** | **Non-modular** |
| **A cultivator at the head of a distributary draws more when levels are high** | Non-modular and, partly, flexible |
| **Discharge stays as designed regardless of interference** | **RIGID MODULE** |

> **The rigid module is the fairest but the most expensive and most easily damaged or tampered with.** The **semi-module is the usual compromise** — it removes the watercourse's influence, which is the interference most easily arranged, while remaining simple and robust.

**The performance measures used to compare outlets:**

| Measure | Definition |
|---|---|
| **FLEXIBILITY (F)** | Rate of change of **outlet discharge** ÷ rate of change of **distributary discharge** |
| **PROPORTIONALITY** | **F = 1** — the outlet takes a **constant PROPORTION** of the distributary flow |
| **HYPER-proportional** | **F > 1** — takes a **larger share as the supply falls** |
| **SUB-proportional** | **F < 1** — takes a smaller share as supply falls |
| **SENSITIVITY** | Rate of change of outlet discharge ÷ change in distributary **water level** |
| **Setting** | Depth of the outlet crest **below** the distributary full supply level |

> **PROPORTIONALITY is the design ideal** for a distributary system: when the supply is short, **every outlet should share the shortage equally** rather than the head reach taking its full share and the tail getting nothing.

> **A hyper-proportional outlet at the head of a distributary is the classic cause of TAIL-END DEPRIVATION** — as the supply falls, it takes an increasing share, and the tail reaches run dry first.

> **That is one of the most persistent problems in canal irrigation**, and it is a design problem as much as a management one.

**Setting** controls the proportionality: an outlet set **deeper** below the full supply level is **less sensitive** to level changes and therefore closer to sub-proportional.

**The other canal structures**, for context: the **HEAD REGULATOR** controls flow into the distributary; the **CROSS REGULATOR** raises the parent canal's level so the offtake can draw; the **ESCAPE** disposes of surplus; and the **FALL** takes the bed down where the ground drops faster than the canal.

examTip.trick: Count what the discharge depends on: **non-modular = BOTH levels; flexible (semi-module) = distributary ONLY; rigid module = NEITHER.** Three outlets, three dependencies.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) describes a RIGID MODULE** — the more advanced device, hence tempting. A semi-module removes only the **watercourse's** influence, not the distributary's.
examTip.mnemonic: **A semi-module works by FREE or CRITICAL flow, so downstream conditions cannot propagate upstream** — the same principle as a broad-crested weir. And **PROPORTIONALITY (F = 1)** is the ideal, or the tail runs dry first.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme, 'pondage' refers to:
options: A small storage at the headworks allowing the plant to meet daily or weekly demand variation
Seasonal storage converting monsoon flow into dry-season supply
The dead storage reserved for sediment accumulation
The volume of water in the penstock
questions.solution:
**A small storage at the headworks allowing the plant to meet DAILY or WEEKLY demand variation.**

**Pondage versus storage — the distinction that matters:**

| | **PONDAGE** | **STORAGE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Timescale** | **DAILY or WEEKLY** | **SEASONAL or ANNUAL** |
| **Size** | Small — a pond at the headworks | Large — a reservoir behind a dam |
| **Purpose** | **Meet the daily demand PEAK** | **Convert monsoon surplus into dry-season supply** |
| Regulates | **Short-term fluctuation** | **Seasonal mismatch** |

> **Option (b) describes seasonal STORAGE**, which is the deliberate near-miss — and the distinction is not academic, because **the two solve completely different problems.**

**Why pondage is valuable:**

> A plain run-of-river plant generates **whatever the river gives at that moment**. But **demand is not constant** — it peaks in the evening and falls at night.

| Time | Without pondage | With pondage |
|---|---|---|
| **Night (low demand)** | Water **runs to waste** past the plant | Water is **STORED in the pond** |
| **Evening peak** | The plant can only generate the river's flow | The plant draws on the pond and **generates well above the river's flow** |

> **Pondage converts a plant that must sell whatever it happens to produce into one that can sell into the PEAK** — and peak power is worth substantially more.

> **That is the whole commercial case for a Peaking Run-of-River (PROR) scheme**, and it explains why so many Nepali projects are developed in that form.

**What pondage does NOT do:**

> **It cannot address the SEASONAL problem.** A pond holding a few hours' flow cannot carry monsoon water into January.

> **In Nepal about 80% of the flow arrives in four monsoon months**, while demand peaks in the dry winter evening. **Only STORAGE addresses that mismatch** — pondage, and pumped storage, shift energy **within a day**.

> **That is the structural problem of the Nepali power system in one sentence**, and it is why storage projects and cross-border trade both matter.

**The plant types:**

| Type | Storage | Firm power |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure run-of-river** | **None** | **LOW** — limited by dry-season flow |
| **PROR (with pondage)** | **Daily/weekly** | Low, but **peaking capability** |
| **Storage** | **Seasonal** | **HIGH** — the reservoir regulates |
| **Pumped storage** | Daily, by **reversible pump-turbine** | Not a net producer; a **time-shifting** device |

**Sizing pondage:**

> From the **daily load curve**: the pond must hold enough to supply the **excess of peak demand over the available river flow** for the duration of the peak.

> **Typically a few hours' worth of flow at full plant discharge** — modest in volume, but requiring a small barrage or weir at the headworks.

**The design consequence:**

> **Pondage means the water level at the intake VARIES through the day**, which affects the **available head** and must be allowed for. **It also means the river downstream sees a fluctuating discharge (hydropeaking)** — a genuine environmental concern, since rapid daily flow changes affect aquatic life and downstream users.

> **Environmental flow requirements** (a minimum release, commonly **10% of the minimum monthly average flow** in Nepali practice) constrain how far the flow may be manipulated.

**And the design discharge**, for context: a run-of-river plant is normally designed at about **Q40** — the flow available 40% of the time — because that **maximises annual ENERGY per rupee invested**, whereas designing at the firm flow Q95 would spill most of the monsoon.

examTip.trick: **Pondage is DAILY/WEEKLY; storage is SEASONAL/ANNUAL.** The two solve different problems — pondage lets a plant sell into the evening **peak**, storage carries monsoon water into the dry season.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) describes seasonal storage**, and the distinction is not academic: a pond holding a few hours' flow **cannot** carry monsoon water into January.
examTip.mnemonic: **80% of Nepal's flow arrives in four monsoon months, but demand peaks in the dry winter evening.** Only **STORAGE** fixes that; pondage and pumped storage shift energy **within a day**.

questions.stem: The load factor of a power system is defined as:
questions.solution:
**Average load ÷ maximum demand.**

**The family of power system factors**, which are constantly confused because they share numerators and denominators:

| Factor | Definition | Measures |
|---|---|---|
| **LOAD FACTOR** | **Average load ÷ MAXIMUM DEMAND** | **How STEADY the demand is** |
| **PLANT LOAD FACTOR (capacity factor)** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED capacity** | **How fully the PLANT is used** |
| **DEMAND FACTOR** | **Maximum demand ÷ CONNECTED load** | Not everything runs at once |
| **UTILISATION FACTOR** | **Maximum demand ÷ RATED capacity** | How fully the plant's rating is called on |
| **DIVERSITY FACTOR** | Σ individual maxima ÷ system maximum | **Always > 1** |
| Plant use factor | Energy ÷ (capacity × hours **in service**) | Excludes shutdown |

> **Every option here is a real factor** — so this is a four-way match, and the discriminator is **which denominator goes with which numerator.**

> **Load factor and plant load factor share the same numerator** (average load) and differ only in the denominator: **maximum DEMAND versus installed CAPACITY.** That is the pair most often swapped.

**What load factor tells you, and why it matters commercially:**

| Load factor | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HIGH (near 1)** | **Steady demand** — the peak is close to the average |
| **LOW** | **Peaky demand** — a high peak over a low average |

> **A high load factor allows cheaper generation**: plant runs continuously at its efficient point instead of cycling, and capacity is not built to stand idle.

> **A low load factor requires expensive PEAKING capacity that sits unused most of the time** — and someone must pay for that idle plant.

> **That is why industrial tariffs REWARD a high load factor**, and why **time-of-day tariffs** exist: they are attempts to make the consumer's incentive match the system's cost.

**Typical values:**

| System | Load factor |
|---|---|
| **Domestic** | **Low (~20–30%)** — evening peak, little night use |
| **Industrial (continuous process)** | **High (~70–90%)** |
| **Whole system** | 50 – 70% |

> **A continuous-process industrial consumer is the most valuable customer a utility can have**, because it uses the capacity that domestic consumers leave idle at night.

**DIVERSITY FACTOR** is the concept that makes electricity supply economically possible at all:

> **Not everyone's maximum demand occurs at the same instant.** The sum of individual peaks always exceeds the system peak, so the diversity factor is **always greater than 1**.

> **The whole system can therefore be built SMALLER than the sum of its consumers' demands** — often much smaller. **Without diversity, every supply system would have to be sized for everyone's peak simultaneously.**

**A caution about plant load factor:**

> **A low PLF is not necessarily bad.** A **peaking plant is MEANT to run rarely** — its value lies in being **available** at the daily peak, not in the energy it produces.

> **Judging a peaking plant by its capacity factor misunderstands its purpose entirely** — and the same applies to standby and reserve plant.

**For hydropower specifically:**

| Plant | PLF |
|---|---|
| **Base load thermal** | **60 – 80%** |
| **Run-of-river hydro (Nepal)** | **~40 – 60%** — limited by dry-season flow |
| Peaking plant | **10 – 20%** |
| Solar PV | 15 – 20% |

> **Nepal's run-of-river plants have a low PLF in the dry season, exactly when demand peaks** — which is the structural mismatch that storage, pondage and cross-border trade all exist to address.

examTip.trick: **Every option is a real factor** — this is a four-way match. **Load factor and plant load factor share the numerator (average load)** and differ only in the denominator: **maximum DEMAND versus installed CAPACITY.**
examTip.trap: **A low plant load factor is not necessarily bad** — a peaking plant is meant to run rarely, and its value is **availability**, not energy. Judging it by capacity factor misses its purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **DIVERSITY FACTOR is always > 1** — peaks do not coincide, so the system can be built smaller than the sum of its consumers' demands. **That is what makes electricity supply economically possible.**

questions.stem: A settling basin at the headworks of a run-of-river hydropower plant is designed primarily to remove:
options: Suspended sand particles above a specified size, to protect the turbine
questions.solution:
**Suspended sand particles above a specified size, to protect the turbine.**

**Why it matters so much in the Himalaya:**

> Himalayan rivers carry **very heavy sediment loads**, and the suspended fraction is largely **QUARTZ — harder than the steel of a turbine runner.**

| Damage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Erosion of the Pelton needle and bucket splitter** | At jet velocities above 100 m/s |
| **Erosion of Francis guide vanes and runner** | Loss of profile and efficiency |
| **Loss of efficiency, then loss of output** | Progressive |
| **A runner can lose its profile in a SINGLE MONSOON** | Without effective sediment exclusion |

> **Turbine erosion is the dominant operation and maintenance problem of Nepali hydropower**, and the settling basin is the principal defence against it.

**The design particle size:**

> Typically **0.2 mm** for a high-head Pelton scheme, and **0.3 mm or larger** for lower heads.

> **The higher the head, the finer the particles that must be removed** — because damage depends on the **velocity** at which the particles strike, and jet velocity rises with head.

> **A high-head plant therefore needs a larger and more effective settling basin than a low-head one of the same capacity**, which is a genuinely counter-intuitive design consequence.

**How it works — the same principle as a water treatment sedimentation tank:**

> **A particle is removed if its SETTLING velocity exceeds the OVERFLOW RATE: V_s = Q/A_surface**

> **Efficiency therefore depends on SURFACE AREA, not depth** — Hazen's law again — and the basin is made long and wide rather than deep.

| Design element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Long, wide, shallow** | Maximises surface area |
| **Low horizontal velocity (~0.2–0.4 m/s)** | So settled material is not scoured up |
| **Gradual inlet transition** | Avoids turbulence and short-circuiting |
| **Hopper and FLUSHING arrangement** | To remove what has settled |

> **The flushing arrangement is essential, not an accessory**: a basin that fills with sediment stops working, and it must be flushable **without shutting the plant down** — which is why continuous or periodic flushing systems (Bieri, Dufour, serpentine) are used.

**The sediment defences in ORDER along the water's path:**

| Structure | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Intake SITING** | The most, for free — outer bank of a bend, surface draw |
| **TRASH RACK** | **Floating debris, branches** — option (b) |
| **GRAVEL TRAP** | **Coarse BED LOAD — rolling stones** — option (c) |
| **SETTLING BASIN** | **Finer SUSPENDED sand** ← |
| Flushing | Removes what has settled |

> **COARSE FIRST, FINE SECOND.** A settling basin cannot handle boulders, which is precisely why the gravel trap precedes it — and why options (b) and (c) name real structures with different jobs.

**Intake siting is the cheapest measure of all:**

> Placing the intake on the **OUTSIDE of a river bend** exploits the **helical secondary current**, which sweeps bed load toward the **inside** of the bend and leaves cleaner water at the outer bank.

> **Drawing from near the SURFACE** avoids the highest sediment concentrations, which occur at the bed.

> **One siting decision removes more sediment than any structure downstream, and it costs nothing.**

**Why option (a) is wrong:**

> **Settling removes SUSPENDED matter, never DISSOLVED matter.** No amount of detention time causes a dissolved salt to settle out — that requires a chemical or membrane process, and it is irrelevant to turbine protection in any case.

**The economics:** a settling basin is a **large civil structure and a significant fraction of headworks cost** — but **runner replacement, lost generation during outage, and progressive efficiency loss are far more expensive.** The basin is a genuine investment rather than a compliance cost.

examTip.trick: **Coarse first, fine second**: trash rack (debris) → gravel trap (bed load) → **settling basin (suspended sand)**. Options (b) and (c) name real structures with different jobs earlier in the chain.
examTip.trap: **A HIGHER head needs a FINER design particle size** (0.2 mm for Pelton), because damage depends on **impact velocity** — which rises with head. Counter-intuitive, but it drives the basin's size.
examTip.mnemonic: **Efficiency depends on SURFACE AREA, not depth** (Hazen) — so the basin is long and wide, not deep. And **intake siting on the OUTSIDE of a bend removes more sediment than any structure, for free.**

questions.stem: In the New Austrian Tunnelling Method (NATM), the primary principle is to:
options: Support the tunnel with a heavy rigid lining immediately, preventing any ground movement
Excavate the full face in a single operation to minimise time
Allow the rock to deform slightly and mobilise its own load-carrying arch, supported flexibly and monitored
Line the tunnel with cast iron segments erected within a shield
questions.solution:
**Allow the rock to deform slightly so it mobilises its own load-carrying capacity, supporting it flexibly and monitoring the convergence.**

**The central idea, and it is genuinely a change of philosophy:**

> **The rock around a tunnel is not merely a LOAD to be carried — it is the principal STRUCTURAL ELEMENT.**

> By allowing a **small, controlled deformation**, the rock mass **redistributes stress around the opening and forms its own arch**. The support's job is then only to **help the rock support itself**, not to carry the full overburden.

| Approach | Support carries |
|---|---|
| **Traditional rigid lining** | **The full ground load** — a heavy, expensive structure |
| **NATM** | **Only what the rock cannot carry itself** — a light, flexible support |

> **Preventing deformation entirely (option a) is exactly wrong.** A rigid lining installed immediately attracts the **maximum possible load**, because the rock is never given the chance to arch. **It is both more expensive and less effective.**

**The support elements:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **SHOTCRETE** | Applied immediately; **seals the surface** and prevents loosening and ravelling |
| **ROCK BOLTS** | **Bind the rock mass into a self-supporting arch** |
| **Wire mesh** | Holds the shotcrete and small blocks |
| Steel ribs / lattice girders | Where the ground is weaker |

> **Sealing the surface promptly is more important than its strength.** Exposed rock **loosens and deteriorates** — it weathers, slakes and ravels — and once loosening starts, the arch is lost. **A thin shotcrete layer applied at once does more good than a thick one applied a day later.**

**MONITORING is integral, not optional:**

> **Convergence measurements are taken continuously**, and the support is adjusted in response.

| Reading | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Deformation decelerating and converging** | **The arch is forming — the support is adequate** |
| **Deformation continuing or accelerating** | **More support needed, urgently** |

> **NATM is a DESIGN-AS-YOU-GO method**: the ground's actual response determines the support, rather than the support being fixed in advance from an assumed ground condition.

> **That flexibility is its great strength and also its principal risk** — it depends on **competent, continuous monitoring and on the judgement to act on it.** Where that discipline is absent, the method is dangerous.

**The timing question, which is the whole art:**

| Support installed | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **TOO EARLY / too stiff** | **Attracts excessive load** — uneconomic, and the rock never arches |
| **TOO LATE / too flexible** | **The rock LOOSENS and the arch is lost** — collapse |
| **Correctly timed** | The rock carries most of the load; the support carries the remainder |

> **There is an optimum, and finding it is what the monitoring is for.**

**Why the other options describe different methods:**

| Option | Method |
|---|---|
| Heavy rigid lining immediately | **Traditional rigid support** — the approach NATM replaced |
| Full face in one operation | A **drill-and-blast SEQUENCE** choice, not a support philosophy |
| **Cast iron segments in a shield** | **SHIELD TUNNELLING — for SOFT, water-bearing ground**, an entirely different technique |

> **Shield tunnelling is the meaningful contrast**: it is used precisely **because the ground will NOT stand on its own** and cannot form an arch. **NATM depends on the rock's self-supporting capacity; a shield exists because there is none.**

> **The ground condition, not the diameter, chooses the method.**

**The other hard-rock methods**, for completeness: **drill and blast** (flexible, suits variable rock and any shape), **heading and benching** (a drill-and-blast sequence for a large section), **full face** (smaller sections in good rock), and **TBM** (fast and smooth-bored, but inflexible and very costly to mobilise).

> **And the practical constraint on progress in any tunnel**: the cycle time is set by the **slowest of drill – blast – MUCK – support**, with **muck removal and ventilation frequently controlling the advance rate.**

examTip.trick: **The rock is the STRUCTURE, not the load.** Allowing controlled deformation lets it arch and carry itself; the support only helps. A rigid lining installed at once attracts the **maximum** load.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), shield tunnelling with segments, is the meaningful contrast** — used where the ground will **NOT** stand alone. NATM depends on self-supporting capacity; a shield exists because there is none.
examTip.mnemonic: **Seal the surface FAST — timing beats thickness.** Exposed rock loosens and the arch is lost. And **MONITORING is integral**: converging deformation means the arch is forming; accelerating means act now.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a reaction turbine is most likely to occur at the:
options: Upstream face of the runner blades
Outlet (downstream) side of the runner blades and in the draft tube
questions.solution:
**At the outlet side of the runner blades and in the draft tube** — where the pressure is lowest.

**Why there:**

> In a reaction turbine the pressure **falls progressively through the machine** as energy is extracted. **The lowest pressure in the whole system is at the runner EXIT and in the upper draft tube** — and that is precisely where cavitation begins.

> **The draft tube deliberately creates SUCTION** (sub-atmospheric pressure) so that the turbine can be set above the tailwater without losing that head. **That same suction is what makes cavitation possible.**

> **The feature that gives the reaction turbine its efficiency also creates its principal vulnerability.**

**What cavitation is:**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1** | Local pressure falls to the **VAPOUR PRESSURE** of water |
| **2** | **Vapour bubbles form** |
| **3** | Bubbles are carried to a **higher-pressure region** |
| **4** | They **COLLAPSE implosively**, generating very high local pressures |

> **The damage comes from the COLLAPSE, not the formation** — and the implosion pressures are high enough to **pit steel and concrete**.

**The symptoms:**

| Symptom | Note |
|---|---|
| **Noise like gravel** passing through the machine | The bubbles collapsing |
| **Vibration** | — |
| **PITTING** of the runner and draft tube | The physical damage |
| **Loss of head and efficiency** | The performance cost |

**THOMA'S CAVITATION PARAMETER** is how it is controlled in design:

> **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s)/H**

> where **H_s** is the **suction head** — the height of the runner **above the tailwater**.

> **The turbine's setting must give σ greater than the critical value σ_c** for that machine, which depends on its **specific speed**.

| Turbine | Susceptibility |
|---|---|
| **Kaplan** (high specific speed) | **MOST susceptible** — needs the largest σ |
| Francis | Susceptible; σ_c rises with specific speed |
| **PELTON** | **CANNOT cavitate at all** |

> **A high-specific-speed machine may have to be set BELOW the tailwater level** — that is, in an excavated pit — to obtain sufficient σ. **Cavitation is therefore a civil works cost, not merely a mechanical one**, and it directly influences the powerhouse's foundation depth.

**Why a PELTON cannot cavitate:**

> It is an **IMPULSE** turbine: the runner operates at **ATMOSPHERIC pressure**, in air, with the whole pressure drop occurring in the nozzle.

> **The pressure never approaches the vapour pressure**, so cavitation is impossible — and a Pelton correspondingly has **no draft tube**, since there is no suction to create and no exit pressure to recover.

> **That single difference — does the pressure drop across the runner? — separates impulse from reaction machines and determines both the draft tube and the cavitation question.**

**Remedies and mitigation:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Set the turbine LOWER** relative to tailwater | The primary control — increases σ |
| **Cavitation-resistant materials** | **Stainless steel overlays** on vulnerable areas |
| Careful blade profiling | Avoids local low-pressure zones |
| Smooth surfaces, tight tolerances | **A small irregularity can trigger it** |
| **Air admission** to the draft tube | Cushions the collapse |
| Avoiding operation far off the design point | Part-load operation worsens it |

> **A Francis turbine run well below its design flow develops a strong draft tube vortex and cavitates readily** — which is one reason Francis machines perform poorly below about 40% load, and why Kaplan's **double regulation** (adjustable guide vanes **and** runner blades) is worth its cost at low head.

**And the same physics elsewhere:** cavitation limits a **pump's suction lift** (hence **NPSH available > NPSH required**), damages **valve throats**, and attacks **spillway surfaces** where the nappe lifts off above the design head — which is why ogee crest profiles are built to millimetre tolerances.

> **Vapour pressure RISES with temperature**, so hot liquids cavitate far more readily — relevant to pumps, though not to hydro turbines.

examTip.trick: Cavitation occurs where the pressure is **LOWEST** — the runner exit and draft tube, where the machine deliberately creates **suction**. The feature that gives the turbine its efficiency creates its vulnerability.
examTip.trap: **A PELTON cannot cavitate at all** — it runs at atmospheric pressure in air, and has **no draft tube**. Both facts follow from the same difference: does the pressure drop across the runner?
examTip.mnemonic: **Thoma's σ sets the turbine's HEIGHT above tailwater** — and a high-specific-speed Kaplan may have to sit **below** it, in an excavated pit. **Cavitation is a civil works cost, not just a mechanical one.**

questions.stem: In highway alignment through hilly terrain, the first and most important consideration is:
options: Stability of the hillside along the alignment
Providing the highest possible design speed
questions.solution:
**Stability of the hillside.**

**Why stability outranks everything else:**

> **A road on unstable ground will not survive, however good its geometry.**

| Consequence of an unstable alignment | Note |
|---|---|
| **Repeated landslides** | Every monsoon |
| **Continuous reconstruction cost** | Often exceeding the original construction cost within a few years |
| **Route closed when it is most needed** | During and after heavy rain |
| **Risk to life** | Both from slides and from vehicles stranded |

> **Choosing a stable alignment is worth more than any amount of retaining wall.** A road placed on a moving slope needs rebuilding every monsoon; one placed on sound ground needs almost nothing.

> **That is the single most valuable decision in hill road engineering, and it costs nothing at the alignment stage** — but it is irreversible once construction begins.

**The special considerations in hill roads:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stability of the hillside** | **The first consideration** |
| **DRAINAGE** | **On a hill road, water does more damage than traffic** |
| **Geometric standards** | Relaxed, but hairpins need **grade compensation** |
| **Resisting length** | The total rise, which governs the ruling gradient |
| Avoid | **Landslide zones, unstable talus, springs, deep cuts** |
| Balanced cut and fill | Minimises spoil and borrow |
