> **The instruction to avoid springs is worth noting**: a spring line marks where groundwater emerges, and it is very often the head of an existing or incipient slide. **Building across it invites failure.**

**Why DRAINAGE comes second only to stability:**

> Water is what makes slopes fail — it **raises pore pressures, reduces effective stress, and adds weight.**

> **Seepage roughly HALVES the factor of safety of a cohesionless slope** (**FoS = (γ_sub/γ_sat) × tanφ/tan i**, and γ_sub ≈ γ_sat/2).

> **So drainage is the first and cheapest slope stabilisation measure** — and the two considerations are really one: **a stable alignment is one where water is controlled.**

**The minimum gradient requirement** follows from this:

> **1 in 200 (0.5%) on a lined side drain, 1 in 100 (1%) unlined** — below which water stands, infiltrates the formation and softens the subgrade.

> **A road too flat is as defective as one too steep**, and on a hill road that is not a theoretical point.

**Why the other options are subordinate:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Shortest route** | The shortest route in hills is usually the **steepest and least stable** — and often the most expensive to build and maintain |
| **Fewest curves** | Curves are how a hill road gains height at an acceptable gradient. **Fewer curves means steeper grades** |
| **Highest design speed** | Design speed is **relaxed in hilly terrain** (Class I: 120 in plain, **60 in steep**) precisely because terrain governs |

> **All three describe genuine objectives that are deliberately SUBORDINATED in hill terrain** — which is exactly what the question tests.

**The requirements of a good alignment**, in general:

> **SHORT, EASY, SAFE and ECONOMICAL** — and **they conflict.** The shortest route is frequently the steepest; the easiest gradient is usually the longest.

> **Alignment design is the RESOLUTION of that conflict**, not the satisfaction of any one criterion. **In hills, stability and drainage are the constraints within which the resolution must be found.**

**GRADE COMPENSATION on curves**, since hairpins are unavoidable:

> A vehicle on a curve already faces **curve resistance** from tyre scrub. Adding a steep gradient makes the total excessive, so the gradient is **eased**:

> **Grade compensation = (30 + R)/R percent, maximum 75/R**, and **not applied on gradients flatter than 4%.**

> **Failing to compensate is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends** — one of the most commonly observed design failures on Nepali hill roads.

**And the survey sequence** that reaches the alignment: **map study → reconnaissance → preliminary survey → detailed survey**, each **costing more per kilometre and covering less ground** than the one before.

examTip.trick: **A road on unstable ground will not survive, however good its geometry.** Choosing a stable alignment costs nothing at the planning stage and is irreversible once built — which is why it comes first.
examTip.trap: **All three wrong options are genuine objectives** — short, few curves, high design speed. In hill terrain they are deliberately **subordinated** to stability, which is what the question tests.
examTip.mnemonic: **On a hill road, water does more damage than traffic** — and **seepage roughly HALVES a slope's factor of safety**. Stability and drainage are really one consideration. Avoid **springs**: they mark incipient slides.

questions.stem: The 85th percentile speed observed in a spot speed study is used mainly to:
options: Determine the geometric design speed of the road
Estimate the capacity of the road
Fix the speed limit for the road
questions.solution:
**To fix the SPEED LIMIT for the road.**

**What the 85th percentile speed is:**

> The speed **at or below which 85% of vehicles travel** — read from the cumulative frequency curve of a spot speed study.

> **It represents the speed adopted by the great majority of reasonable drivers**, excluding only the fastest 15%.

**Why it is used for speed limits:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Most drivers choose a safe speed for the conditions** | The road itself communicates what is appropriate |
| **A limit set far BELOW it is widely disobeyed** | Which undermines enforcement generally |
| **A limit set at it is largely self-enforcing** | Most drivers already comply |
| **Crash risk is lowest near the mean/85th percentile** | Both much slower and much faster vehicles are over-represented in collisions |

> **That last point is the strongest justification**: it is **SPEED VARIANCE, not speed alone, that correlates with crash risk.** A vehicle travelling much slower than the traffic stream is a hazard just as one travelling much faster is, because both generate overtaking and conflict.

> **Setting the limit near the 85th percentile MINIMISES the variance**, which is a safety argument rather than merely a practical one.

**The other percentiles and their uses:**

| Percentile | Use |
|---|---|
| **15th** | **MINIMUM speed limit**, where one is imposed |
| **50th (MEDIAN)** | **Average speed**; used in some design work |
| **85th** | **SPEED LIMIT**; also used for geometric design in some jurisdictions |
| **98th** | **GEOMETRIC DESIGN** in Indian practice |

> **Note that option (a) is not absurd** — the 85th percentile **is** used for design in some countries, and the two purposes are related. **But Indian and Nepali practice uses the 98th percentile for design** and the 85th for the limit, which is what makes (d) the intended answer.

**The essential distinction between DESIGN SPEED and SPEED LIMIT:**

| | **DESIGN SPEED** | **SPEED LIMIT** |
|---|---|---|
| **Set by** | **The designer, before construction** | **The authority, from observed behaviour** |
| **Basis** | Road class and terrain (**Class I plain 120, steep 60**) | **85th percentile of actual speeds** |
| **Purpose** | Fixes the **geometry** — radii, sight distances, superelevation | Regulates **behaviour** |

> **They are chosen by different bodies, at different times, for different purposes — and they need not agree.**

> **A road may be designed for 100 km/h and posted at 60** because of roadside development, pedestrian activity or accident history. **Conversely, a limit should never exceed what the geometry safely permits.**

**The spot speed study itself:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **Measures** | Speed at a **specific point** — not journey speed |
| Methods | Radar, enoscope, pneumatic tubes, video |
| **Sample** | Taken under **free-flow** conditions, so drivers choose their own speed |
| Output | **Frequency and CUMULATIVE frequency curves** |

> **The free-flow requirement matters**: in congested conditions drivers cannot choose their speed, so the observations would measure the congestion rather than the road.

**Other uses of spot speed data:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Speed limits** | The 85th percentile |
| **Accident investigation** | Before-and-after studies |
| **Justifying geometric improvements** | Where speeds are inappropriate |
| **Signal timing** | Approach speeds |
| Assessing the effect of a change | Traffic calming, resurfacing |

**And why the other options belong to different studies:**

> **Capacity** comes from **volume** studies and the level-of-service analysis; the **vehicle damage factor** comes from **AXLE LOAD** surveys and the **fourth power law** — neither has anything to do with speed observations.

examTip.trick: **A limit far below the 85th percentile is widely disobeyed; one set at it is largely self-enforcing.** And crash risk correlates with **speed VARIANCE**, so matching the limit to actual behaviour minimises it.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is not absurd** — the 85th percentile is used for design in some countries. But **Indian and Nepali practice uses the 98th percentile for DESIGN** and the 85th for the limit.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design speed is set by the DESIGNER before construction; the speed limit by the AUTHORITY from observed behaviour.** Different bodies, different times, different purposes — and they need not agree.

questions.stem: In a flexible pavement, the primary purpose of the sub-base course is to:
options: Provide the wearing surface for traffic
Distribute the load further, act as a drainage layer, and prevent intermixing of the subgrade with the base
questions.solution:
**To distribute the load further, act as a drainage layer, and prevent intermixing of the subgrade with the base course.**

**The three functions, each genuinely necessary:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Load distribution** | Spreads the stress further before it reaches the subgrade |
| **DRAINAGE** | A permeable layer that **carries water out of the pavement laterally** |
| **SEPARATION** | **Prevents the fine subgrade from pumping up into the coarse base** |

> **The separation function is the one most often overlooked and the most damaging when it fails.**

**Why separation matters — PUMPING:**

> Under repeated wheel loading with water present, **fine subgrade material is pumped upward into the voids of the base course.**

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **The base loses its interlock** | Contaminated with fines, it no longer behaves as a granular layer |
| **The subgrade loses material** | Voids and settlement below |
| **Progressive failure** | Both layers degrade together |

> **A sub-base of intermediate grading — or a geotextile separator — breaks that migration**, and it is why the sub-base's grading is specified rather than merely its strength.

**Why DRAINAGE matters so much in a flexible pavement:**

> **A flexible pavement transmits load by GRAIN-TO-GRAIN contact**, so **the subgrade ultimately carries everything** — and a **wet subgrade is a weak subgrade.**

> **The CBR is measured after FOUR DAYS' SOAKING** precisely because the design must assume the worst condition the pavement will meet. **In Nepal that is unambiguously the saturated monsoon state.**

> **Keeping water out of the pavement is worth as much as building it thicker** — side drains, camber, a sealed surface and a draining sub-base are all pavement structure in effect, not accessories.

**The flexible pavement layers and their roles:**

| Layer | Function | Material |
|---|---|---|
| **Wearing (surface) course** | **Riding quality, SKID RESISTANCE, waterproofing** | **Bituminous concrete** |
| **Binder course** | Distributes load to the base | DBM, BM |
| **BASE course** | **The main load-spreading layer** | WBM, WMM, crushed aggregate |
| **SUB-BASE** | **Load distribution, DRAINAGE, SEPARATION** ← | Granular material, GSB |
| **Subgrade** | The natural or prepared soil — **carries everything** | Compacted soil |

> **Options (a), (b) and (d) all describe the WEARING COURSE's functions** — surface, waterproofing and skid resistance. **All three are real, but they belong to a different layer.**

> **Recognising that three options describe one layer and only one describes the sub-base** settles the question.

**The design principle behind the layering:**

> **Stress reduces with depth**, so the **strongest and most expensive material goes on TOP** and progressively cheaper material below.

> **That is the whole economic logic of a flexible pavement**: it uses expensive bituminous material only where the stress is highest, and cheap local granular material where it is not.

**Design (IRC 37):**

> **Thickness is read from charts as a function of the subgrade CBR and the traffic in msa** (million standard axles of 8160 kg).

> **The relationship is steeply non-linear in both** — which is why **improving a weak subgrade is often cheaper than building a thicker pavement over it**, and why a subgrade below about 2% CBR usually needs replacement, stabilisation or a capping layer.

**And the traffic side:**

> **The FOURTH POWER LAW: damage ∝ (axle load)⁴.** A truck at twice the legal axle load does **sixteen times** the damage — which is why **axle load control matters more than traffic volume** for pavement life, and why overloading is the greatest single cause of premature failure in Nepal.

**Contrast with a RIGID pavement**, which distributes load by **SLAB ACTION** and therefore **bridges over** weak spots — making the subgrade far less critical, and the concrete's **flexural strength (f_cr = 0.7√f_ck)** the governing property instead of the subgrade's CBR.

examTip.trick: **Options (a), (b) and (d) all describe the WEARING COURSE** — surface, waterproofing, skid resistance. Three options for one layer, one for the sub-base: that alone identifies the answer.
examTip.trap: **SEPARATION is the most overlooked function.** Without it, fines are **PUMPED up from the subgrade into the base**, destroying the base's interlock and voiding the subgrade — a progressive failure of both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stress reduces with depth, so the best material goes on TOP** — that is the economic logic of layering. And a **wet subgrade is a weak subgrade**, which is why CBR is measured after **four days' soaking**.
